title: Perceptions of quality in e-learning:a case study
authors:
- Cação, Maria do Rosário Santos Cruz Andrade
supervisors:
- Figueiredo, António Dias de
date: '2010-07-22'
keywords:
- E-learning
- Educação à distância
abstract_pt: ''
abstract_en: "Departing from an online survey targeted at trainees of e-learning courses\
  \ intended for\r\nprofessional training, which was preceded by an exploratory qualitative\
  \ study, we\r\npropose future utility as an important dimension in the appraisal\
  \ of the quality of elearning.\r\nOur results show that future utility is the second\
  \ most important dimension of\r\nquality in e-learning for professional training,\
  \ following satisfaction. We also conclude\r\nthat three major factors explain the\
  \ perception of quality: training attitudes, training\r\nprocess, and training utility.\
  \ Additional conclusions are that final motivation and\r\nperceptions of quality\
  \ are affected by the length of the course, that professional\r\ncertification courses\
  \ lead to higher perceptions of immediate and future utility, and that\r\nperceptions\
  \ of value are also related to utility. These findings are particularly useful for\r\
  \nthose who plan or design e-learning courses and are interested in the impact of\
  \ the\r\ntraining processes."
source_url: https://estudogeral.uc.pt/handle/10316/14225
rights: openAccess

Chapter 1  
Introduction 
q
Whileqcompaniesqwantqtalentedqresourcesqwhoqcanqcopeqwithqtheqstrategicqobjectivesqofq 
theqcompany,qworkers,qstudents,qandqtheqgeneralqpopulationqareqeagerqtoqknowqmore,qtoq 
beqandqhaveqmore,qtoqbecomeqbetterqinqlife,qorqjustqtoqsurvive.qERlearningqisqseenqasqaq
solutionqforqthatqandqhasqbecomingqmoreqandqmoreqpopular.qBut,qasqinqeveryqbusiness,q 
theqlongRtermqsurvivalqandqtheqcompetitivenessqofqeRlearningqcompaniesqdependqonqtheirq 
abilityq toq satisfyq andq retainq theirq customers,q whichq dependsq onq theirq abilityq toq offerq
coursesq withq quality.q Theseq companiesq faceq twoq majorq challenges:q theq firstq isq toq dealq 
withq openq marketsq thatq allowq consumersq toq accessq aqwholeq rangeq ofq suppliersq andq eR
learningqproducts;qtheqsecondqisqthatqconsumersqareqbecomingqmoreqsophisticated,qmoreq
informedqthanqever,qandqmoreqawareqandqdemandingqinqtermsqofqquality.qQualityqisqnotq 
objective,q asq itq dependsqonq theq perceptionsq ofq theqcustomers.q Moreover,q itq isq aq multiR
dimensionalqvariable,qasq severalq factorsqcanq contributeq toq it.q Therefore,q evaluatingq theq
qualityqofqaqproductqisqnotqanqeasyqtask.qWhenqservicesqareqbeingqconsidered,qtheqtaskq 
becomesq harder:q servicesq areq entangledq andq areq influencedq byq theq customer,q whoq
participatesq andq affectsq theq service.q Inq addition,qunlikeq products,q theq resultsq ofq theq 
serviceq areq asq importantq asq theq processq ofq providingq them.q Whenq theq serviceq isq anq 
educationalq service,q anq additionalq problemq isq introduced,q asq oneq ofq itsq majorq outputs,q 
learning,qisqtheqresultqofqaqprocessqcarriedqoutqbeqtheqcustomers,qandqnotqsoqmuchqbyqtheq
companyq thatq offersq theq serviceq (Ehlers,q 2004).q ERlearningq servicesq areq mainlyq anq 
educationalq service,q butqtheq qualityq ofq anq eRlearningqcourseqcanq alsoq beq influencedqbyq 
severalq factors,q suchq asq theq technologyq usedq orq theq psychologicalq andq geographicalq 
distanceqbetweenqtheqtrainerqandqtheqtrainees.qqq
q
Theqproblemqis,qtherefore,qwhatqisqanqeRlearningqcourseqwithqquality.qWhatqareqtheqmostq 
importantqdimensionsqofqquality?qAndqhowqcanqcompaniesqmeasureqtheqqualityqofqtheirq 
eRlearningqcoursesqinqorderqtoqimproveqthem?qWeqbelieveqthatqifqweqareqableqtoqanswerq 
theseqquestionsqweqwillqableqtoqhelpqeRlearningqcompaniesqtoqdeliverqservicesqwithqmoreq 
qualityqandqimproveqtheirqlongRtermqcompetitiveness.qq
q
Ourqaimqisqtoqinvestigateqtheq contemporary phenomena qofqqualityqinqeRlearningqwithinq 
itsq real-life context (Yin,q1994,qp.q13).qWequseq mixed methods q(Creswellq&qClark,q2007;q 
Tashakkoriq &q Teddlie,q 2003)q andq focusq ourq attentionq onq trainees,q asq “ofq allq theq 
dimensionsqandqaspectsqofqeRlearningqquality,qtheqperspectiveqofqtheqlearnerqisqprobablyq 
theq mostq important”q (Ehlers,q 2004).q Ourq researchq isq heldq atq EVOLUI.COM,q aq 
PortugueseqproviderqofqasynchronousqeRlearningqforqprofessionalqtraining,qwithqtenqyearsq 
ofqexperienceqinqtheqconsumerqeRlearningqmarketqandq50.000qclientsqfromq26qcountries.q 
EVOLUI.COMqoffersqmoreqthanq160qshortRtermqcoursesqthatqrangeqinqlengthqfromq1qtoq9q
weeks.qWeqfirstqusedqaqqualitativeqstudyqconductedqatqtheqonlineqforumsqofqtheqcourses,q 
andqinqthisqstudyqweqcombinedqparticipant observation (Angrosino,q2005,qp.q732)qandq 
someq elementsq ofq interviewq (Creswell,q 2002,q pp.q 178R181)q andq digitalq ethnographyq 
(Patton,q 1990,q pp.q 265R266;q Ruhleder,q 2000).q Basedqonq theq mainq conclusionsq ofq thisq 
study,qweqthenqconductedqaqquantitativeqstudyqtoqexploreqtheqdimensionsqofqqualityqinqeR
learning.q Forq thatq purpose,q weq usedq theq satisfactionq surveyq thatq theq traineesq normallyq 
answerqatqtheqendqofqtheqcourse.qAtqtheqsameqtime,qweqconductedqaqsecondqquantitativeq 
studyqtoqexploreqtheqmotivationalqdriversqofqtheqtrainees,qtheirqperceptionsqofqvalue,qandq

q
Thisqdocumentqisqstructuredqinqfourqparts.qq
q
Chapterq2qisqdedicatedqtoqaqreviewqofqtheqliterature.qAfterqaqgeneralqintroductionqtoqtheq 
challengesqofqqualityqinqbusinessqperformance,qsectionq2.2.qgivesqanqoverviewqonqwhatq 
qualityq isq andq whatq theq philosophyq ofq totalq qualityq managementq means.q Amongq theq 
majorq approachesq toq quality,q weq focusq ourq attentionq onq Juran’sq (1951,q Sectionq 2R2)q
definitionq ofq qualityq asq fitness for use ,q whichq heq describedq asq theqextentq toq whichq theq 
productqorqserviceqservesqtheqpurposesqofqthequser,qduringqusage.qThisqsectionqendsqwithq 
theqdiscussionqofqtheqconceptualqapproachqtoqqualityqproposedqbyqGarvinq(1987,q1988).qqq
q
Sectionq 2.3.q isq focusedq onq eRlearningq asq aq service.q Itq startsq byq discussingq theq 
idiosyncraticq characteristicsq ofq services,q theq relationq betweenq quality q andq satisfaction ,q 
andqtheqinfluenceqofq expectations .qItqthenqpresentsqtheqmajorqdimensionsqandqmodelsqofq 
qualityq inq services,q namelyq Juran’sq (1951q pp.2R4)q dimensionsq ofq qualityq inq services,q 
Grönroos’q (1982,q 1988,q 1990,q 2007)q modelq ofq perceivedq quality,q SERVQUALq 
(Parasuraman,qZeithaml,q&qBerry,q1985,q1988),qandqotherqrelevantqmodelsqofqqualityqinq 
services.q Thisq sectionq endsq presentingq theq leverageq roleq thatq technologyq hasq inq theq 
qualityqofqtheqservice.qq
q
Sectionq2.4.qisqdedicatedqtoqqualityqinqeducation.qItqbringsqtogetherqallqtheqconcernsqthatq 
existq inq educationq inq generalq andq inq higherReducationq inq particular,q inq vocationalq 
educationqandqtrainingq(VET),qandqinqeRlearning.qItqalsoqpresentsqanqextendedqdiscussionq 
ofqtheqmodelsqofqtrainingqevaluationqandqtheqroleqofqtheqaccreditationqandqstandards,qasq 
wellq asq otherq instrumentsq ofq qualityq assuranceq andqseveralq proposalsq forq aq commonq 
frameworkqofqqualityqinqeRlearning.q
q
Inq sectionq 2.5.q weq approachq twoq majorq conceptsq thatq areq relatedq toq quality,q namelyq 
motivation qandqperceptionqofq value .qMotivationqreflectsqaqdesireqtoqlearnqandqtoquse qtheq
acquiredqknowledge,qskills,qandqattitudes.qIfqthereqisqaq stimulus to use ,qthereqmustqbeqaq 
perceptionq ofq fitness for use (Juran,q 1951,q Sectionq 2R2),q which,q inq turn,q suggestsq thatq 
motivation qisqsomehowqrelatedqtoq quality .qEvenqso,qweqpresentqaqhigherRorderqconstruct,q 
value ,qtoqbetterqunderstandqquality .qAfterqpresentingqtheqseveralqexistingqapproachesqtoq
value ,q weq focusq ourq attentionq onq valueq asq an interactive relativistic preference 
experience q q (Holbrook,q 1999c,q pp.q 5R9)q andq onq aq specialq typeqofq value:q utility .q Thisq 
sectionqendsqpresentingqtheqroleqofqutilityqinqeducation,qtheqcontributionqofqHoltonq(1996)q
andqNoeqandqSmittq(1986)qtoqthatqdiscussion,qandqtheqdifferenceqbetweenq immediate qandq 
future utility .qq
q
Chapterq3qdetailsqourqchoicesqinqtermsqofqresearchqapproachqandqpresentsqEVOLUI.COMq 
asqourqcaseqstudyqandqthequnitsqofqanalysisqthatqweqused.qItqalsoqpresentsqourqresearchq 
questionsq andq theq statementsq ofq purposes,q asq wellq asq someq detailsq concerningq theq 
research,qsuchqasqtheqsubjectsqofqstudy,qtheqsampleqconcernsqthatqweqhad,qtheqprocessqofq 
research,qandqourqresearchqcronogram.q
q
Inq Chapterq 4q weq explainq theq threeq studiesq thatq weq haveq carriedq out.q Theq first,q wasq aq 
qualitativeqstudyqthatqwasqheldqatqEVOLUI.COM’sqonlineqforumsqandqwhichqwasqusedq 
toqexploreqtheqkindqofqissuesqthatqtheqtraineesqreferredqtoqwhenqaskedqwhatqqualityqinqeR
learningq is.q Theq conclusionsq ofq thisq studyq suggestedq utilityq asq aq node q thatq weq shouldq

explore.q Theq secondq study,q aq quantitativeq one,q wasqbasedq onq anq onlineq survey,q alsoq

mostq importantqdimensionqofq qualityq inqeRlearningq forq professionalq training,q followingq

andq future utility qareqaffectedqbyqtheqlengthqofqtheqcourseqandqbyqtheqtypeqofqcourse.qTheq 
lastqstudy,qalsoqquantitative,qconcludesqthatqtheqmotivationsqofqtheqtrainee’sqareqmostlyq 
relatedqtoq ends-in-view (Dewey,q1939)qbutqthatqthereqareqdifferencesqinqtheqmotivationq 
regardingqwhoqhadqtheqideaqofqattendingqtheqcourseqandqwhoqpaidqforqit.qThisqlatterqstudyq 
showsq thatq perceptionsq ofq valueq areq mainlyq selfRoriented,q active,q andq extrinsic,q andq 
mostlyqrelatedqtoq utility qandq job opportunities .qItqalsoqshowsqthatq immediate utility qisqaq 
factorqofqcomfortqforqtheqtraineeqwhenqherqcompanyqprovidesqtheqtrainingqcourses.qYet,q
theqabsenceqofq future utility qisqaqfactorqofqdiscomfortqwhenqtheqtrainingqisqnotqprovided:q 
whenqtheqcompanyqdisregardsqtheqprovisionqofqtrainingqcourses,qtheqtraineesqperceiveqaq 
lossqofq future utility qthatqmakesqthemqfeelqunmotivated.qqqq
q
Weq endq upq withq generalq conclusionsq andq suggestionsqforq furtherq research,q andq aq 
discussionqonqtheqlimitationqofqourqresearch.qq

2.2.3.  Quality As The Right Set of Characteristics 
q
Theqconceptqofqqualityqisqnotqabsolute.qAsqFeigenbaumq(1961,qp.q13)qemphasises,q“theq 
wordq qualityq doesq notq haveq theq popularq meaningq ofq ‘best’q inq anyq absoluteq sense.q Toq 
industry,q itq meansq best for certain customer conditions ”.q Amongq theseq customerq 
conditions,qFeigenbaumqidentifiesqtwoqimportantqones:qtheqactualqendquseqandqtheqsellingq 
priceqofqtheqproduct.qInqturn,qtheseqconditionsqareqreflectedqinqfiveqadditionalqconditionsq 
thatqheqalsoqidentifies:qq
q
R Theqspecificationqofqdimensionsqandqofqoperatingqcharacteristics;q
R Theqlifeqandqreliabilityqobjectives;q
R Theqmanufacturingqandqengineeringqcosts;q
R Theqproductionqconditionsqunderqwhichqtheqarticleqisqmanufactured;q
R Theqfieldqinstallationqandqmaintenanceqobjectives.qq
q
Inqotherqwords,qperfectionqisqnotqtheqfinalqaim.q“Theqaimqisqratherqtheqlevelqofqqualityqthatq 
establishesqtheqproperqbalanceqbetweenqtheqcostqofqtheqproductqandqtheqserviceqitqrenders”q 
(Feigenbaum,q1961,qp.q13).qq
q
Qualityqhasqbeenqdefinedqasqaqsetqofqcharacteristicsqandqasqaqsingleqfactorqconcept.qInqthisq 
sense,q qualityq isq aq compositeq ofq severalq characteristicsq thatq mustq beq combinedq inq theq 
rightq way.q Theseq individualq characteristicsq areq thoseq thatq makeq upq theq compositeq ofq 
productq quality.q Shewhartq (1931,q p.q 38)q exemplifiesq thisq ideaq whenq heq arguesq that,q 
althoughqwaterqisqdefinedqasqaqchemicalqcombinationqbetweenqhydrogenqandqoxygen,qitsq 
qualityqisqexpressedqinqtermsqofqitsqchemicalqandqphysicalqproperties.qFeigenbaumq(1961,q 
p.q 14)q goesq further,q emphasizingq theq importanceq ofqprovidingq theq rightq combination:q 
“theq keyq requirementq inq establishingq whatq isq toq beqtheq ‘quality’q ofq aq givenq productq 
requiresq theq economicq balancingq ofq theseq variousq individualq qualityq characteristics”.q
Whenqallqtheqcharacteristicsqareq“balancedqin,qtheqright qualityqbecomesqthatqcompositeq 
whichqprovidesqtheqintendedqfunctionqwithqtheqgreatestqoverRallqeconomy…qandqisqtheq 
totalqconceptqofq‘quality’qthatqmustqbeqcontrolled’.qShewhartq(1931)qhasqaqsimilarqideaq 
thatqisqrevealedqwhenqheqdefendsqthatq“theqqualityqofqaqthingqisqthatqwhichqisqinherentqinq 
it,qsoqthatqweqcannotqalterqtheqqualityqwithoutqalteringqtheqthing.qItqisqthatqfromqwhichq 
anythingq canq beq saidq toq beq suchq andq suchq andq may,q forq example,q beq aq characteristicq 
explainableq byq anq adjectiveq admittingq degreesq ofq comparison”q (p.q 38).q He,q therefore,q
concludesqthatq“aqthingqhasqqualitiesqandqnotqaqquality”q(pp.q39R40).qForqinstance,qaqpieceq 
ofqmaterialqhasqweight,qdensity,qdimensions,qlength,qvelocity,qresistanceqandqsoqon,qandq 
theseqqualitiesqcanqevenqbeqgeometricallyqpositionedq[P=q f(x 1qx2,qx 3…)],qwhereqPqisqtheq 
productqorqserviceqandqx iq areqtheqqualities.qq
q
Yet,q theq magnitudeq ofq theseq characteristicsq isq notqtheq onlyq importantq factor.q Theq 
relationshipsqbetweenqthemqareqalsoqsignificant.qShewhartq(1931,qp.q49)qalsoqalertsqtoqtheq 
importanceq ofq theq relationshipq amongq theseq characteristics.q “Inq tryingq toq defineq theq 
qualityqofqaqthingqinqtermsqofqthoseqcharacteristicsqwhichqmakeqitqwhatqitqis,qweqcalledq 
attentionqtoqtheqfactqthatqweqmakequseqofqwhatqareqperhapsqsecondaryqcharacteristics.qForq 
example,q inq expressingq theq qualityq ofq aq thingq inq respectq toq strengthq weq makeq useq ofq 
measuresq ofq ductility,q brittleness,q andq hardnessq –qcharacteristicsq whichq areq likelyq 
dependentqtoqaqcertainqdegreequponqsomeqcommonqfactorqmoreqelementalqinqnature”.qq
Theseqcharacteristicsqallowqusqtoqdefineqtheqqualityqofqaqproductqorqserviceqinqsuchqaqwayq 
thatq wellq definedq quantitativeq andq qualitativeq measuresq canq beq reached.q Inq turn,q theseq

2.2.3.1.   Garvin’s Quality Dimensions 
q
Davidq Garvinq (1987,q 1988,q pp.q 49R61)q developedq aq meaningfulq conceptualq viewq ofq 
quality.qHeqsuggestsqthatqeightqdimensionsqcomposeqtheqqualityqofqaqproductqorqservice.q 
Productsqandqservicesqcanqbeqrankedqhighqonqoneqofqthoseqdimensions,qwhileqbeingqlowq 
onqanother.qDimensionsqarequsuallyqinterrelated,qandqsometimesqanqimprovementqinqoneq 
mayq beq achievedq onlyq atq theq expenseq ofq another.q Otherq times,q twoq dimensions,q likeq 
reliability andq conformance ,qmayqmoveqtogetherq(Garvin,q1988,qp.q50).qq
q
Thoseqdimensionsqare:qq
q
R Performance :q Theq primaryq characteristicsq ofqaq product/serviceq(forq example,q theq 
accelerationqofqaqcar,qtheqclarityqandqcolourqofqaqTVqpicture,qorqtheqspeedqofqserviceq 
inqfastqfoodsqandqairlines).q
R Features :qAddRons,qsupplements,qorqsecondaryqcharacteristicsqthatqsupplementqtheq 
product’sq basicq functioningq (forq example,q theq studyq guideq forq aq course,q orq 
automaticqtuningqonqaqTVqset).q
R Reliability :qTheqprobabilityqofqmalfunctioningqorqfailingqwithinqaqspecifiedqperiodq 
ofqtime.q
R Conformance :qThereqareqtwoqdistinctqapproachesqtoqconformance.qTheqfirstqrelatesq 
conformanceqtoqtheqdegreeqtoqwhichqtheqdesignqandqoperatingqcharacteristicsqofqaq 
productq meetq specificationsq andq establishedq standards.q Forq example,q aq product’sq 
partq mustq beq withinq 0,05q inchesq ofq theq standard.q Thisq approachq hasq aq tolerance 
stack-up, asqthereqcanqbeqaqmatchingqproblemqevenqifqpartsqmeetqspecification.qForq 
example,qifqoneqpartqfallsqatqtheqlowerqlimitqofqitsqspecificationqandqitsqmatchingq 
partq isq atq theq upperq limit.q Inq thisq situation,q aq tightq fitq isq unlikely.q Theq otherq 
approachq equatesq conformanceq withq theq degreeq ofq variabilityq (inversely,q theq 
degreeqofquniformity)qaroundqtheqtargetqdimensionqorqcentralqline.qq
R Durability :q Aq measureq ofq aq products’q life.q Durabilityq hasq bothq economicq andq 
technicalq dimensions.q Technically,q durabilityq isq theq amountq ofq useq thatq oneq getsq 
fromq aq productq beforeq itq physicallyq deteriorates.q Ifq repairq isq possible,q durabilityq 
becomesqtheqamountqofquseqthatqoneqgetsqfromqaqproductqbeforeqitqbreaksqdown.q
R Serviceability :q Theq speed,q courtesy,q competence,q andq easeq ofq repair.q Consumersq 
areqconcernedqnotqonlyqaboutqaqproductqbreakingqdownqbutqalsoqaboutqtheqelapsedq 
timeqbeforeqserviceqisqrestored,qorqtheqtimelinessqwithqwhichqserviceqappointmentsq 
areq kept.q Reactionsq toq downtime,q forq instance,q canqbeq quiteq complex,q andq rapidq 
responseqcanqbecomeqcriticalqinqcertainqcircumstancesq(forqexample,qtheqdowntimeq 
ofqrepairingqequipmentqduringqtheqharvestqseason).q
R Aesthetics :qTheqlook,qfeel,qsound,qtaste,qandqsmellqofqaqproduct.qItqisqaqmatterqofq 
personalqjudgmentqandqaqreflectionqofqindividualqpreferences.q
R Perceived quality :qQualityqasqviewedqbyqaqcustomer,qclient,qorqstudent.q

2.3.1.  The Idiosyncratic Characteristics of Services 
q
Theqliteratureqonqmarketingqofqservicesqprovidesqaqhandfulqofqinsightsqonqtheqqualityqofq

service:qtheqeRlearningqservice.qq
q
Marketeers q assumeq thatq servicesq “areq –q inq theq extremeq –q differentq fromq goods”q 
(Schneiderq &q White,q 2004,q p.q 4)q andq areq “deeds,q processesq andq performances”q 
(Zeithaml,q Bitner,q &q Gremler,q 2006,q p.q 4).q Becauseqservicesq areq performancesq ratherq 
thanqobjectsq(Parasuramanq et al .,q1985),qtheyqdifferentiateqthemselvesqinqtheirq threshold, 
range, and order (Lamprecht,q 1994,q pp.q 61R62) . Theyq alsoq haveq idiosyncraticq search ,q 
experience ,q andqcredence propertiesq (Bloomq &q Pailin,q 1995;q Darbyq &q Karni,q 1973;q 
Nelson,q1974).qAlthoughqservicesqareqalsoq perishable qandq lack ownership ,qtheqliteratureq 
isqfrequentlyqfocusedqonqthreeqmainqfeaturesqofqservices:qintangibility,qheterogeneity,qandq

Appendixq 2q presentsq anq extendedq analysisq ofq theseq characteristicsq ofq servicesq andq

q
Theqliteratureqonqserviceqqualityqdevelopsqanqextendedqdiscussionqaroundqtheqdifferenceq

1992;qParasuramanq et al .,q1985,q1988).qq
q
Juranq andq Grynaq (1993,q p.q 3)q mentionq aq dictionaryq definitionq ofq qualityq asq “ customer 
satisfaction”,qwhichqmakesqunclearqtheqdifferenceqbetweenqtheqtwoqconcepts.qHowever,q 
thereqseemsqtoqbeqsomeqtendencyqtoqagreement,qinqtheqliterature,qasqOliverq(1981),qBitnerq 
(1990),qBoltonqandqDrewq(1991a;q1991b),qandqParasuramanq et al. q(1985,q1988)qconcurq
thatq perceivedq serviceq qualityq isq aq formq ofq attitude ,q aq longRrunq overallq evaluation,q

Satisfactionq isq presentedq asq “ an evaluation of the surprise inherent in a product

is a form of overall evaluation, similar to attitude . Oliverq (1981)q summarizesq theq

consumer’sq relativelyq enduringq affectiveq orientationq forq aq product,q store,q orq processq 
(e.g.,q customerq service),q whileq satisfactionq isq theq emotionalq reactionq followingq aq

specific.qAttitudeqisqthereforeqmeasuredqinqtermsqmoreqgeneralqtoqproductqorqstoreqandqisq

q
Parasuramanq et al. q (1985,q 1988)q alsoq suggestq thatq theq differenceq betweenq theseq twoq 
constructsqliesq inq theq wayq disconfirmationsq areq operationalized.q Theyq argueq thatq thereq 
areqdifferencesqinqtermsqofqwhatqisqmeasured:qwhenqmeasuringqperceivedqserviceqquality,q

Besidesq theq problemsq inq theq distinctionq betweenq theq twoq constructs,q thereq areq alsoq 
problemsq inq theq relationship q betweenq themq andq theq directionality q ofq thatq relationship.q 
Parasuramanq et al. q(1988)qrecallqthatqcustomersqcanqbeqsatisfiedqwithqaqspecificqserviceq 
butqnotqfeelingqthatqtheqserviceqisqofqhighqquality.qSomeqliteratureq(CroninqJr.q&qTaylor,q 
1992;qJ.qL.qHeskett,q1987;qParasuramanq et al .,q1985,q1988)qdefendsqthatqhigherqlevelsqofq 
perceivedqserviceqqualityqresultqinqincreasedqconsumerqsatisfaction,qwhileqotherqauthorsq 
suggestq thatq satisfactionq isq anq antecedentq ofq serviceq qualityq (Bitner,q 1990;q Boltonq &q 
Drew,q1991a;q1991b),qandqthatqsatisfactionqjudgmentsqwillqcollapseqintoqoverallqserviceq 
qualityqjudgementsqoverqtime.q
q
Boltonq andq Drewq (1991a)q defendq thatq perceivedq serviceq qualityq dependsq onq theq 
consumers’qperceptionqofqtheqqualityqofqtheqservice,qfromqaq previous period ,qandqtheirq 
levelqofq(dis)satisfactionqwithqtheqcurrentqlevelqofqserviceqperformance,qsuggestingqthatq 
satisfactionq isq aq distinctq constructq thatq mediatesqpreviousq andq currentq perceptionsq ofq 
serviceqquality.qYet,qtheirqempiricalqevidenceqrevealedqthatqperceivedqserviceqqualityqisq 
stronglyq affectedq byq current performance q andq thatq disconfirmationq hasq littleq impact.q 
ThisqinfluenceqofqexperienceqandqpastqexperienceqisqalsoqstressedqbyqOliverq(1980),qwhoq 
suggestsqthatqattitudeqisqinitiallyqaqfunctionqofqexpectationsqand,qinqfurtherqexperiences,qaq 
functionq ofq prior attitudes q andq current levels of satisfaction .q Inq theq absenceq ofq priorq 
experiencesqwithqaqserviceqprovider,qexpectationsqwillqdefineqtheqattitudeqandqtheqlevelqofq 
perceivedqserviceqquality.qAccordingqtoqBoltonqandqDrewq(1991a),qcustomerqsatisfactionq 
isqonlyqtheqmediatorqbetweenqtheqpreviousqperceptionqofqserviceqqualityqandqtheqrevisedq

Perceivedqserviceqqualityqandqcustomerqsatisfactionqareqalsoqdifferentqinqtermsqofqtheirq 
impact on purchase intentions .q Forq Heskettq (1987),q serviceq qualityq affectsq consumerq

argueq thatq managersq shouldq focusq onq customerq satisfactionq overq serviceq qualityq 
strategies,qasqtheqformerqexertsqaqstrongerqinfluenceqonqpurchaseqintentionsqthanqserviceq

intentions.q
q
Thisq relationshipq betweenq customerq satisfactionq andq perceivedq quality,q asq wellq asq theq

q
Theq traditionalq literatureq onq qualityq distinguishesq betweenq performance quality q andq 
conformance quality q(Kotlerq et al. ,q1996,qpp.q456R457):qq
q
R Performance quality qrefersqtoqtheqlevelqatqwhichqaqproductqorqserviceqperformsqitsq 
functionsq(forqexample,qMercedesqcarsqprovideqhigherqperformanceqqualityqthanq 
Volkswagen:qtheyqrideqmoreqsmoothly,qhandleqbetter,qandqlastqlonger);q
R Conformance quality q refersq toq freedomq fromq defectsq andq theq consistency q withq 
whichq aq productq deliversq aq specifiedq levelq ofq performanceq (forq examples,q 
Mercedesq andq Volkswagenq canq offerq equivalentq conformanceq qualityq ifq theyq 
consistentlyqdeliverqwhatqtheirqmarketqexpects).qq
q
Inq theq servicesq industry,q theq evaluationq ofq performance quality q (and,q therefore,q theq 
evaluationq ofqserviceq quality)qisq commonlyqbasedqonq perceived q quality:q consumersq doq 
notqalwaysqhaveqcompleteqinformationqaboutqtheqattributesqofqaqproductqorqservice,qand,q 
frequently,q theyq relyq onq indirectq measures,qcues,q andq otherq signallingq devicesq toq drawq
inferencesq aboutq qualityq (Lambert,q 1980,q quotedq inqGarvin,q 1988,q p.q 59).q Images,q 
advertising,qandqbrandqnamesq–qperceptionsqofqqualityqratherqthanqtheqrealityqitselfq–qcanq 
beq criticalq inq theq creationq ofq aq judgmentq ofq qualityq (Garvin,q 1988,q p.q 60).q Perceived q
qualityq is,q therefore,q theq consumer’sq judgmentq aboutq anq entity’sq overallq excellenceq orq 
superiorityq (Zeithaml,q 1987),q andq itq isq quiteq differentq fromq objective q qualityq 
(Parasuramanq et al .,q1988).q
q
Corporateqimageqactsqasqaqfilterqofqperceivedqqualityq(Grönroos,q2007,qp.q74),qandqbrandq 
name,qandqevenqprice,qcanqbeqseenqasqqualityqindicatorsq(Brucks,qZeithaml,q&qNaylor,q 
2000).q Corporateq reputationq isq pointedq outq asq oneq ofq theq primaryq contributorsq toq 
perceivedq quality,q andq itsq powerq comesq fromq anq unstatedq analogy:q thatq theq qualityq ofq 
productsq manufacturedq byq aq companyq todayq isq similarq toq theq qualityq ofq productsq itq

Gummessonq wasq probablyq theq firstq serviceq marketingqresearcherq toq talkq aboutq serviceq

Theqideaqofqhavingqproductsqandqservicesqthatqmeetqorqexceedqcustomers’qexpectationsqisq

Expectations ,qinqtheqliteratureqonqquality,qareqviewedqasqdesiresqorqwantsqofqconsumersq–q
whatq theyq feelq aq serviceq providerq should q offer.q Onq theq contrary,q inq theq literatureq onq 
satisfaction,q expectations q areq definedq asq probabilitiesq ofq theq occurrenceq ofqpositiveq orq 
negativeqeventsqwhenqtheqconsumerqengagesqinqsomeqbehaviour,qandqareqviewedqasqwhatq 
consumersqfeelqaqserviceqproviderq would qofferq(Oliver,q1981;qWoodruffq et al .,q1983).q

Inqevaluatingqtheqqualityqofqtheqservice,qconsumersqcompareqtheqserviceqtheyqexpectqwithq 
perceptionsqofqtheqserviceqtheyqreceiveq(Grönroos,q1982),qandqtheqperceivedqqualityqofq 
theqserviceqisqtheq degree qandq direction of discrepancyqbetweenqconsumers’qperceptionsq 
andqexpectations(Parasuramanq et al .,q1988).qThisqideaqofqmeetingqtheqexpectationsqalsoq 
emergedq inq theq literatureq onq productq quality:q Feigenbaumq (1961,q p.q 13),q forq instance,q

expectations q ofq theq consumer”.q Thisq ideaq isq basedq onq theq disconfirmation paradigm q
(Churchillq &q Surprenant,q 1982;q Oliver,q 1980),q accordingq toq whichq theq comparisonq 
betweenqexpectationsqandqperceptionsqresultsqinqsatisfactionqifqthereqisqaqconfirmationqorq 
aqpositiveqdisconfirmationqofqexpectations,qandqperceivedqserviceqqualityqisqtheqresultqofq 
theqconsumer’sqcomparisonqofqexpectedqserviceqwithqperceivedqservice.qWhenqexpectedq 
serviceqisqbetterqthanqperceivedqservice,qtheqperceivedqqualityqisqlessqthanqsatisfactory,q 
andqwillqtendqtowardqtotallyqunacceptableqqualityqasqtheqdiscrepancyqbetweenqexpectedq 
serviceqandqperceivedqserviceqincreasesq(Parasuramanq et al.,q1985).q

Someqliteratureq(Liljanderq&qStrandvik,q1993;qNadiriq&qHussain,q2005;qParasuramanqetq

minimumqsheqisqwillingqtoqaccept.qTheqconceptqofq zone of tolerance qsuggestedqbyqBerryq 
&q Parasuramanq (1991)q assumesq thatq customersq doq notqhaveq expectationsq ofq aq serviceq

2.3.4.1.   Juran’s Quality Dimensions 
q
Amongqtraditionalqauthorsqdedicatedqtoqqualityqissues,qJuranq(1951,qp.q2.2)qisqoneqofqtheq 
fewqthatqproposedqaqsetqofqparametersqorqdimensionsqtoqevaluateqquality,qdefendingqthatq 
theqconceptqofq fitness for use, isqaquniversalqconceptqapplicableqtoqgoodsqandqservices.qq
AccordingqtoqJuranq(1951,qpp.q2.4R2.9)q“Fitness for use ”qisqdefinedqbyqcustomersqandqisq 
theqresultantqofqfourqparameters,qcalledq quality characteristics :q1)q quality of design, 2)q 
quality of conformance, 3) the abilities andq4)  field service. 
 
Quality of design qisqaqcompositeqofqthreeqsteps:q quality of market research ,q quality of 
concept q (Masing,q 1966,q quotedq inq Juran,q 1951q (1974q edition),q p.q 2.5)q andq quality of 
specification .q Itq startsq withq theq identificationq ofq whatq constitutesq fitness for use q toq theq 
user.qTheqchoiceqofqtheqconceptqofqaqproductqorqserviceqtoqrespondqtoqtheqidentifiedqneedsq 
ofqthequserqisqtheqnextqstep.qFinally,qthereqisqaqtranslationqofqtheqchosenqconceptqintoqaq 
detailedqsetqofqspecificationsqtoqbeqexecutedq(Juran,q1951,qp.q2.5).qq
 
Quality of conformance ,qalsoqknownqasq“qualityqofqproduction”qorq“qualityqofqproduct”,q 
refersq toq theq extentq toq whichq theq productq conformsqtoq theq design,q andq isq theq resultq ofq 
technology,qresources,qandqmanagementqabilities.qqq
q
Theq abilities qareqespeciallyqimportantqforqlongRlivedqproductsqandqincludeq(Juran,q1951,q 
pp.q2.6R2.8):qq
q
R Availability, whichqisqtheqextentqtoqwhichqthequserqcanqsecureqserviceqwhenqsheq 
wantsqit;qq
R Reliability ,q whichq wasq definedq byq Juranq asq freedom from failure q andq canq beq 
measuredq byq theq probabilityq ofq performanceq withoutqfailureq forq aq specifiedq 
periodqofqtimeqandqunderqgivenqandqknownqconditions;qq
R Maintainability ,qwhichqrefersqtoqtheqneedqforqcontinuityqofqservice,qandqcanqeitherq 
beq theq easeq ofq conductingq preventiveq andq scheduledqinspectionsq andq servicingq 
(alsoqknownqasq serviceability)qorqtheqeaseqofqrestoringqserviceqafterqfailureq(alsoq

whatqgoesqonqpriorqtoqtheqsaleqofqtheqproductqorqserviceqtoqthequser.qFieldqserviceqisqalsoq

2.3.4.2.1.   Technical versus  Functional Outcomes in Services 
q
Grönroosq (1990a)q madeq anq importantq contributionq toqtheq studyq ofq serviceq qualityq byq 
distinguishingq betweenq theq technical q orq outcome q componentq ofq servicesq andq theq 
functionalqorqprocessRrelatedqcomponentq(seeqFigureq1).qTheqtechnicalqdimensionqisq what q
theq customerq isq leftq withq whenq theq serviceq productionq processq andq theq buyerRsellerq 
interactionqareqover;qitqisqwhatqcustomersqreceiveqinqtheirqinteractionsqwithqtheqfirm.qItq 
canq beq measuredq objectivelyq byq theq customers,q becauseq ofq itsq characteristicsq asq aq 
technicalq solutionq toq aq problemq (Grönroos,q 2007,q p.q 74).q Thisq technicalq dimensionq ofq 
qualityqisqoftenqthoughtqofqasqtheqqualityqofqtheq service delivered .qq
q
However,qtheqoutcomeqorqendqresultqofqtheqprocessqdoesqnotqcountqforqtheqtotalqqualityq 
thatqcustomersqperceiveqasqreceived,qasqitqisqjustqoneq dimension of qquality .qTheqcustomerq 
isq alsoq influencedq byq theq wayq theq technicalq qualityq isq transferredq toq her:q sheq isq alsoq 
influencedqbyq how qsheqreceivesqtheqservice,qandqhowqsheqexperiencesqtheqsimultaneousq 
productionqandqconsumptionqprocess.qThisqfunctionalqcomponentqofqservicesqRqtheq how q
ofqtheqserviceqRqconcernsqtheqserviceqdeliveryqitself.qq
Theq accessibilityq toq theq service,q theq appearanceq ofq theq staffq andq howq theq serviceq 
employeesqperformqtheirqtasks,qwhatqtheyqsay,qandqhowqtheyqdoqit,qalsoqinfluencesqtheq 
viewq ofq theq customerq aboutq theq service.q Theq how q ofq theq serviceq isq “theq processesq 
involvedqinqbeingqseated,qinqorderingqtheqmeal,qtheqmealqbeingqbroughtqtoqtheqtableqandq

wouldqbe.qImageqis,qtherefore,qaqfilterqofqperceivedqquality.qq

2.3.4.4.   Service Quality after SERVQUAL 
q
Theq literatureq onq serviceq qualityq hasq changedq afterq SERVQUAL,q andq whileq someq 
authorsqproposeqmodificationsqtoqtheqSERVQUALqmodel,qothersqhaveqdevelopedqtheirq 
ownq approaches.q Itq hasq beenq acknowledgeq thatq SERVQUAL’sq methodologyq canq helpq 
determineqwhere,qandqhow,qseriousqtheqgapsqare,qandqitqisqprobablyqtheqmostqworldwideq 
usedq serviceq qualityq instrument,q butq itq hasq alsoq beenq widelyq criticizedq (forq example,q 
CroninqJr.q&qTaylor,q1992;qOliver,q1993;qPattersonq&qJohnson,q1993;qPeter,qChurchill,q 
&qBrown,q1992).q
q
Parasuramanq et al. q (1988)q referq thatq withq appropriateqadaptation,q SERVQUALq canq beq 
usedq toq evaluateq serviceq qualityq amongq differentq industries.q Theyq alsoq suggestq thatq 
SERVQUALqcanqbequsedqbyqcompaniesqwithqseveralqpointsqofqsaleqtoqtrackqtheqlevelqofq 
serviceq providedq byq eachq storeq inq theirq chain.q And,q inq fact,q SERVQUALq hasq beenq 
applied,q forq instance,q toq internalq services,q leadingq toq aq modelq calledq INTSERVQUALq 
(Frostq &q Kumar,q 2000),q whichq isq probablyq theq mostq appropriateq modelq forq eRlearningq 
servicesq thatq areq deliveredq byq aq companyq toq itsq ownq employees,q i.e.q internalq training.qq 
Otherq adaptationsq ofq SERVQUALq forq specificq industriesq haveq alsoq beenq made:q forq 
example,qParaskevasq(2001a,q2001b)qadaptedqitqtoqHotel’sqinternalqserviceqchains.qq
q
Parasuraman,qBerryqandqZeithamlq(1991a)qlaterqfoundqthatq tangibles qwasqsplittingqintoq 
twoq factorsq ( physical facilities/equipment q andq employees/communication materials ),q 
whileq responsiveness qandq assurance qwereqmergingqintoqoneqdimension.qq

2.3.4.5.   SERVPERF 
q
CroninqandqTaylorq(1992)qdoqnotqagreeqwithqtheqconceptualizationqofqserviceqqualityqonq 
theqbasisqofqtheqexpectancyRdisconfirmationqparadigm,qasqproposedqbyqParasuramanq et 
al. q(1985,q1988).qTheirqmainqcritiqueq(1994)qtoqSERVQUALqisqthatqParasuramanq et al. q
makeqanqabusiveqgeneralizationq ofq Oliver’sq (1980,q 1993)q disconfirmationq paradigmq toq 
serviceqquality,qwhichqwasqcreatedqtoqevaluateqcustomerqsatisfaction,qnotqserviceqquality.qq 
Theyqargueqthatqtheqperformanceq minus qexpectationqisqanqinappropriateqbaseqforquseqinq 
theqmeasurementqofqserviceqquality,qandqthatqtheqexpectationsRperformanceqgapqtheory,q
uponq whichq SERVQUALq wasq basedq on,q hasq littleq theoreticalq orq empiricalq evidenceq 
support.q Forq thatq reason,q theseq authorsq suggestq aq performanceRbasedq onlyq paradigm,q 
calledqSERVPERF,q overq theq disconfirmationRbasedq modelq(SERVQUAL).q Theirq pointq 
ofqviewqwasqsupportedqbyqMazis,qAhtola,qandqKlippelq(1975),qChurchillqandqSurprenantq 
(1982),q Woodruffq et al. q (1983),q Carmanq (1990),q Boltonq andq Drewq (1991a,q 1991b),q 
Babakusqandqhisqcolleaguesq(Babakusq&qBoller,q1992;qBabakusq&qMangold,q1992),qandq 
alsoqbyqBrown,qChurchillqandqPeterq(1992),qbut,qevenqso,qSERVPERFqexhibitsqtheqsameq 
factorqinstabilityqacrossqserviceqindustriesqasqSERVQUALq(CroninqJr.q&qTaylor,q1994).q

2.3.4.7.  Other Relevant Contributions 
q

Fourq yearsq later,q Lehtinenq andq Lehtinenq (1982)q proposeq threeq qualityq dimensions:q 
physical quality q(whichqincludesqphysicalqaspectsqofqtheqserviceqasqtheqbuildingqorqtheq 
equipments),q corporate quality q (whichq includesq theq company’sq imageq orq profile)q andq 
interactive quality q(thatqderivesqfromqtheqinteractionqbetweenqserviceqpersonnelqandqtheq 
customer,qandqbetweenqtheqcustomerqandqotherqcustomers).q

regardingqtheqqualitativeqapproachesqthatqmostqofqtheqmodelsquse,qbutqalsoqinqtermsqofq 
qualityqdimensionsqthatqcouldqbeqexploredqinqtermsqofqourqresearchqcontext.qq
q
q
2.3.5.  Quality in Technology-Based Services 
q
Servicesqthatqareqbasedqonqtechnologyqhaveqadditionalqconcernsqthatqareqrelatedqtoqtheq 
qualityqofqtheqtechnology.qTheqmoreqtechnologyRorientedqtheqfirmqis,qtheqbiggerqisqtheq 
riskq toq defineq qualityq tooq narrowly,q andq toq considerq technicalq specificationsq ofq theq 
serviceqtheqonlyqorqtheqmostqimportantqfeatureqofqperceivedqqualityq(Grönroos,q2007,qp.q 
73).q ERlearningq servicesq are,q mostly,q andq educationalq services.q Yet,q theyq areq basedq inq 
technologicalqinfrastructures,qand,qtherefore,qadditionalqconsiderationsqhaveqtoqbeqmade,q 
toqincludeqthisqtechnologicalqside,qnamelyqtheqfactqthatqtechnologyqcanqhelpqorqinjureqtheq 
customer’sqperceptionqofqtheqqualityqofqtheqservice.q
q
Itqhasqbeenqclaimedq(S.qMcConnell,q2002)qthatqtechnology,qnamelyqsoftware,qcanqhaveq 
qualityqcharacteristicsqthatqthequserqisqawareq(theqexternalqcharacteristics)qandqothersq(theq 
internalqones)qthatqsheqwillqneverqnotice.qQualityqmodelsqofqinformationqsystemsqincludeq 
notqonlyqqualityqconcernsqwithqtheqsoftware,qbutqalsoqwithqtheqinfrastructure,qtheqdata,q 
theqadministrativeqprocedures,qandqtheqserviceqitself.qAndqforqservicesqthatqareqprovidedq 
online,q suchq asq eRlearningq services,q thereq areq additionalq concernsq thatq includeq theq 
usability ,q accessibility, communication, credibility, and appearance qofqtheqwebsite.qq
q
InqAppendixq4qweqprovideqanqextendedqreviewqofqtheqleverageqroleqthatqtechnologyqhasq 
inq perceptionq ofq qualityq andq theq concernsq withq qualityq thatq canq beq foundq inq softwareq 
developmentq andq inq informationq systems.q Inq thisq Appendix,q weq alsoq reviewq theq mostq 
relevantqapproachesqtoqqualityqforqwebRbasedqservices.qq

2.4.1.  Quality in Education 
q
Knowledge,qskills,qandqattitudesq–qtheqoutputqofqeducationqRqcanqoccurqwithoutqaqqualityq 
educationalq systemq –q theq process,q asq individualsq doq notq needq aq formalq educationalq 
systemqtoqlearnq(J.qCross,q2007).qHowever,qwheneverqaqformalqeducationalqsystemqexistsq 
andqisqbeingqusedqbyqaqperson,qtheqeducationalqprocessqisqplannedqinqorderqtoqprovideqaq 
qualityqoutput.qq
q
Qualityqinqeducationqmayqevenqbeqmoreqdifficultqtoqdefineqthanqinqmostqotherqsectors,qasq 
theq output q andq theq process q areq intimatelyq connectedq andq evenq moreq dependentq onq theq 
trainee.qMoreover,qqualityqconcernsqinqeducationqareqexpressedqinqmanyqways,qrangingq

q
Mostqofqtheqliteratureqofqqualityqinqeducationqisqdedicatedqtoqhigherqeducation.qEvenqso,q 
allqkindsqofqeducationalqinstitutionsqhaveqqualityqconcerns.qTheqliteratureqonqqualityqinq

higherq educationq institutionsq haveq alreadyq reached,q inq orderq toq dealq withq recognitionq 
issuesqthatqhasqbeenqfacingq(AssociationqofqPublicqandqLandRGrantqUniversitiesq&qSloanq 
NationalqCommissionqonqOnlineqLearning,q2009a,q2009b).qq

2.4.1.1.  Education Stakeholders and Their Perceptions of Quality 
q
Inq theqeducationalqcontext,q qualityq isq alsoq aq relativeq term:q Itq meansq differentq thingsq toq 
differentqpeople,qwhichqraisesqtheqissueqofqinq whose qqualityqshouldqweqfocusqwheneverq 
researchingqaboutqqualityqinqeducationq(Harveyq&qGreen,q1993).qq
q
Oneq commonq approachq toq qualityq inq higherq educationqisq theq stakeholderq approach,q 
whichqrecognizesqtheqpotentialqforqaqnumberqofqdifferentqperspectivesqofqquality,qwhichq 
reflectqtheqviewsqofqaqvarietyqofqstakeholdersqwho,qasqVroeijenstijnq(1991)qclaims,qhaveq 
legitimateq authorityq toq voiceq theirq perspectives.q Burrowsq &q Harveyq (1992,q quotedq inq 
Harveyq &q Green,q 1993)q identifiedq aq varietyq ofq stakeholdersq inq higherq education,q 
includingq students,q employers,q teachingq andq nonRteachingq staff,q governmentq andq itsq 
fundingqagencies,qaccreditors,qvalidators,qauditors,qandqassessorsq(includingqprofessionalq 
bodies),qandqeachqoneqofqtheseqstakeholdersqhasqaqdifferentqperspectiveqonqquality.qq
q
Havingq inq mindq theseq differentqperspectivesqonqquality,q Greenq (1994)q arguesq thatq itqisq 
necessaryqtoqdefineqasqclearlyqasqpossiblyqtheqcriteriaqthatqeachqstakeholderqusesqwhenq 
judgingqqualityqandqtakeqallqtheseqcompetingqviewsqintoqaccount:q
q
R Providers (funding bodies and community at large) q interpretq qualityq asq “valueq 
forqmoney”,qasqtheyqareqlookingqforqaqgoodqreturnqonqinvestments;qq
R Users of products (e.g. current and prospective students) qinterpretqqualityqasqofq 
excellence,qasqtheyqwantqtoqensureqaqrelativeqadvantageqinqcareerqprospects;qTheq

interpretationqofqqualityqasqexcellenceqisqtheqinterpretationqthatqbestqdescribesqtheq 
student’sqviewqofqqualityq(Lagrosen,qSeyyedRHashemi,q&qLeitner,q2004);qq
R Users of outputs (e.g. the employers) qseeqqualityqasq“fitnessqforqpurpose”,qasqtheyq

Althoughq recognizingq theq existenceq ofq severalq stakeholders,q Telfordq (2005)q attenuatesq

Amongqstudents,qthereqmayqalsoqbeqdifferencesqinqtermsqofqqualityqevaluations.qLagrosenq

q
Theqfirstqapproachesqtoqcreateqaqdefinitionqofqqualityqinqhigherqeducationqbeganqwithqdeq 
Grootq(1983,qquotedqinqVroeijenstijn,q1991),qwhoqdefendsqthatqqualityqisqdeterminedqbyq

Discussingq qualityq inq higherq education,q Harveyq andqGreenq (1993)q proposeq fiveq 
interrelatedqwaysqofqthinkingqaboutqquality:q
q
R Quality as exceptional :qQualityqisqregardedqinqtermsqofqexcellence,qwhichqmeansq 
somethingq distinctive,q specialq or,q inq aq weakerq perspective,q exceedingq highq 
standards;q
R Quality as perfection or consistency :q Theq focusq isq onq processesq andq 
specificationsqthatqareqaimedqtoqbeqperfectlyqmet.qExcellence,qinqthisqcase,qmeansq 
zeroqdefectsqandqgettingqthingsqrightqatqtheqfirstqtime;  
R Quality as fitness for purpose :q Qualityq hasq meaningq onlyq inq relationq toq theq 
purposeq ofq theq productq orq service.q Itq meansq theq extentq toq whichq aq productq orq 
serviceqmeetsqtheqspecificationsqofqtheqcustomerqandqtheqneedsqthatqwillqexistqinq 
theqfuture.qTheqnotionqofq fitness for purpose qasq“meetingqcustomerqrequirements”q 
inq educationq isq problematic,q dueq toq theq contentiousnessq ofq theq notionq ofq 
customer”qandq theq difficultyq studentsq haveq inq specifyingq whatq isqrequired.q Theq 
trickyqissueqofqdeterminingqwhoqareqtheqcustomersqofqhigherqeducation,qandqwhatq 
theirq requirementsq are,q leadsq Harveyq &q Greenq toq suggestq definingq fitnessq forq 
purposeqinqtermsqofqtheqinstitutionqfulfillingqitsqownqstatedqobjectives,qorqmission.qq
R Quality as value for money :q Qualityq isq relatedq toq valueq and,q inq particularq withq 
cost.q“Qualityqatqaqpriceqyouqcanqafford”qorq“youqgetqwhatqyouqpayqfor”qexpressq 
thisqnotionqofqaccountabilityqofqquality;q
R Quality as transformation :qTheqprocessqshouldqideallyqbringqaboutqaqqualitativeq 
change,qaqfundamentalqchangeqofqform,qsuchqasqtheqphaseqtransitionqwhenqwaterq 
transformsq intoq iceq asq theq temperatureq isq lowered.qTheq authorsq claimq thatq thisq 
viewqcanqbeqfoundqinqtheqthinkingqofqmajorqWesternqphilosophers,qasqwellqasqinq 
Easternq philosophies.q Inq education,q theq transformationq canq takeq theq formq ofq 
enhancementqandqempowerment.q
q
Inq hisq studyqwithqaccountingq students,qWattyq (2005)q usedq HarveyqandqGreen’sq(1993)q
classificationq schemeq toqrankq respondentqbeliefsqandqattitudes.qTheqattributeq rankedq inq 
firstqplaceqwasqdesigningqaqprogramqtoqsuitqtheqrequirementsqofqtheqprofession,qandqtheq 
finalq resultsq showedq thatq theq dimensionsq ofq quality,q inq orderq ofq importance,q andq 
accordingqtoqHarveyqandqGreenq(1993)qclassification,qwhereq fitness for purpose ,q value 
for money ,q excellence ,qand,qforqlast,q transformation .q

2.4.2.  Quality in Vocational Education and Training (VET) 
q
Qualityq concernsq inq vocationalq educationq andq trainingq (VET)q haveq beenq madeq 
operationalqbyq evaluation models andq quality assurance frameworks .qq
q
q
2.4.2.1.  EU Quality Assurance Framework for VET 
q
Theq Europeanq Unionq developedq aq Commonq Qualityq Assuranceq Frameworkq (CQAF)q 
(Europeanq Commission,q 2004)q toq theq vocationalq educationq andq trainingq sector.q Thisq 
frameworkq (Figureq 6)q wasq designedq toq supportq theq developmentq andq reformq ofq theq 
qualityqofqVETqatqsystemsqandqprovidersqlevels,qwhileqfullyqrespectingqtheqresponsibilityq 
andqautonomyqofqMemberqStatesqtoqdevelopqtheirqownqqualityqassuranceqsystemsq(p.q3).q 
Theq CQAFq (2004,q p.q 4)q constitutesq aq Europeanq referenceq frameworkq toq ensureq andq 
developq qualityq inq VET,q buildingq onq theq keyq principlesq ofq theq mostq relevantq existingq 
qualityqassuranceqmodels.qThisqframeworkqcanqbeqappliedqatqbothqtheqsystemqandqVETq 
providerqlevels,qandqcan,qtherefore,qbequsedqtoqassessqtheq effectiveness qofqVET.qInqthisq 
model,qtheqqualityqemphasisqisqinqeffectiveness,qasqitqgivesqaqparticularqemphasisqtoqtheq 
improvementqandqevaluationqofqtheq outputs qandq outcomes qofqVETqinqtermsqofqincreasingq 
employability,qimprovingqtheqmatchqbetweenqdemandqandqsupply,qandqpromotingqbetterq 
accessqtoqlifelongqtraining,qinqparticularqforqdisadvantagedqpeople.q
q
Theq CQAFq comprisesq 1)q aq model,q toq facilitateq planning,q implementation,q evaluation,q
andqreviewqofqsystemsqatqtheqappropriateqlevelsqinqMemberqStates,q2)qaqmethodologyqforq 
assessmentqandq reviewq ofqsystems,q whichq emphasizesqselfqassessment,qcombinedq withq 
externalqevaluation,q3)qaqmonitoringqsystem,qatqnationalqorqregionalqlevel,qorqcombinedq 
withq voluntaryq peerq reviewq atq Europeanq level,q and,qfinally,q 4)q aq measurementq tool,q 
whichq includesq aq setq ofq referenceq indicatorsq aimingq atq facilitatingq Memberq Statesq toq 
monitorqandqevaluateqtheirqownqsystemsqatqnationalqorqregionalqlevels.qTheqCQAFqmodelq
includesq theq fourq interrelatedq elements:q planning,qimplementation,q evaluationq andq 
assessment,q andq review.q Forq eachq oneq ofq theseq elements,q theq coreq qualityq criteria,q 
consideredqasqtransversalqtoqanyqVETqsystem,qhaveqbeenqidentified.qq

2.4.2.2.  Models of Training Evaluation 
q
Trainingq evaluation qisqtheqprocessqofqfindingqoutqwhetherqallqtheqmoney,qtime,qandqeffortq 
putq intoq designingq andq deliveringq trainingq coursesqorq otherq learningq experiencesq wasq 
worthqitq(Donovanq&qTownsend,q2004,qp.q6).qKirkpatrickqandqKirkpatrickq(2006,qp.q19)q
focusqtheqreasonsqforqtheqexistenceqofqevaluationqinqtheqimprovementqofqfutureqprogramsq 
andqtoqdetermineqwhetherqaqprogramqshouldqbeqcontinuedqorqdropped.qq
q
Trainingqevaluationqisqaqprocessqthatqisqtimeqdispersed,qasqitqisqsupposedqtoqoccurqbefore,q 
during,qandqafterqtheqtrainingqcourseqhasqoccurred,qalthoughqmostqofqtheqtimesqitqisqdoneq 
onlyqinqtheqendqofqtheqcoursesqandqinqanqincompleteqwayq(Tamkin,qYarnall,q&qKerrin,q 
2002,qp.qix).qItqcanqbeqprognosticqorqofqimpact,qalthoughqtheqlatterqisqmoreqfrequent:qTheq 
prognosticqevaluationqprovidesqaqglimpseqonqhowqtrainingqobjectivesqwillqbeqdevelopedq 
andq theq kindq ofq impactq theq trainingq courseq willq haveq inq theq company;q Theq impactq 
evaluationq isq madeq someq timeq afterq theq courseq hasq endedq andq intendsq toq previewq theq 
resultsqthatqtheqcourseqpromotedqinqtermsqofqknowledge,qskills,qandqattitudesqandqaimsqtoq 
determineq theq impactq theq courseq hadq inq theq traineesq andq inq theq organization.q Ehlersq 
(2006,q p.q 159)q claimsq thatq theq differentiationq betweenq formativeq andq summativeq 
evaluationq isq alsoq often:q Formativeq evaluationsq mainlyq serveq purposesq ofq qualityq 
assurance q andq itsq goalq isq theq uncoveringq ofq weakq pointsq inq aq process.q Summativeq 
evaluationsqarequsedqtoqcontrolqtheqquality,qtheq impact ,qorqbenefitqofqanqeducationalqoffer.q
q
Theqevaluationqmodelsqofqvocationalqtrainingqareqfocusedqon  results ,qratherqthanqinqtheq 
trainingq process .q Asq Stoneq (1967,q p.q xi)q claims,q organizationalq stakeholdersq areq 
interestedqinqdemonstratedqresultsqRqmeasuresqofqhowqtrainingqexpendituresqcontributeqtoq 
theq organization.q Globalq competitionq andq investors,q heq argues,q areq increasingq theq 
demandq forq accountabilityq forq results,q asq wellq asq prudentq expenditures,q andq forq that,q 
emphasisqisqputqonqtrainingqresults.qq
q
PhillipsqandqStoneq(2002,qpp.q1R2)qjustifyqthisqemphasisqonq training results qforqseveralq 
reasons:qq
q
- Trainingq andq performanceRimprovementq initiativesq mustq beq integratedq intoq theq 
overallqstrategicqandqoperationalqframeworkqofqtheqorganization;qtheyqcannotqbeq 
isolatedq eventRbasedq activities,q unrelatedq toq theq mainstreamq functionsq ofq theq 
business;qq
- Thereqmustqbeqaqcomprehensiveqmeasurementqandqevaluationqprocessqtoqcaptureq 
theqcontributionsqofqhumanqresourcesqdevelopmentqandqestablishqaccountability;qq
- Partnershipqrelationshipsqmustqbeqestablishedqwithqkeyqoperatingqmanagers.qq
q
q
2.4.2.2.1.  Kirkpatrick’s Model 
q
Theq mostq widelyq usedq frameworkq ofq trainingq evaluationq isq theq Kirkpatrickq modelq 
(1959a).q Theq modelq consistsq ofq fourq stages,q originallyq describedq asq stepsq and,q laterq
(1996),qasqlevelsq(Figureq7):qq
q
- Levelq 1Rq Reaction:q whatq theq participantsq thoughtq ofq theq course,q measuredq byq 
reactionqquestionnaires;qq
- Levelq2qRqLearning:qtheqchangesqinqknowledge,qskills,qorqattitudesqwithqrespectqtoq 
theqtrainingqobjectives,qmeasuredqbyqperformanceqtests;qq

PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
53 
- Levelq 3q Rq Behaviour:q changesq inq jobq behaviourq resultingq fromq theq course,q toq 
identifyq whetherq theq learningq isq beingq applied,q measuredq byq observation,q 
productivityqdata,qandqinterviews;qq
- Levelq4qRqResults:qtheqbottomRlineqcontributionqofqtheqcourse,qmeasuredqbyqcosts,q 
quality,qandqreturnqonqinvestment.qq
q

q
Kirkpatrick’sq modelqisq simpleqandq pragmatic,qandq promotesq theqevaluationq ofq trainingq 
programsq(Alligerq&qJanak,q1989).qYet,qitqhasqbeenqwidelyqcriticized,qmostlyqdueqtoqtheq 
factqthatqtheqlevelsqareqarrangedqinqaqhierarchicalqway,qalthoughqitqwasqnotqmeantqtoqbeq 
seenqasqsuchqwhenqitqwasqfirstqproposed.qThatqpromotedqtheqideaqthatqthereqisqaqcausalq 
relationshipqbetweenqeachqlevel,qwhichqhasqnotqbeenqprovedq(forqexample,qS.qH.qLeeq&q 
Pershing,q1999;qWarr,qC.,q&qBirdi,q1999).q
q
Bernthalq (1995)q andq Holtonq (1996)q areq someq ofq theq authorsq thatq criticizeq theq 
Kirkpatrick’sq model.q Bernthalq (1995)q arguesq thatq theq modelq mixesq evaluationq andq 
effectiveness,q andq thatq theq proposedq levelsq doq notqformq aq continuum,q whileq Holtonq 
(1996)qarguesqthatqtheqKirkpatrick’sqlevelsqareqaqtaxonomyqofqoutcomes,qratherqthanqaq 
model,q dueq toq theq lackq ofq constructsq identifiedq andq theq assumptionq ofq causalq 
relationships.q
q

2.4.2.2.3.  Alternative Models 
q
Otherq modelsq haveq emergedq withq aq differentq approachq thanq Kirkpatrick’s,q andq areq 
focusedqonqtheq purpose qofqevaluation.qq
q
Stufflebeamq et al. q(1971)qargueqthatqevaluationqisqessentialqtoqprovideqanqexplanationqforq 
theq outcome,q whichq hasq someq similaritiesq withq theq CIROq Model.q Theyq distinguishq 
betweenq context evaluation q (thatq helpsq inq planningq andq developingq objectives),q input 
evaluation q(thatqhelpsqtoqdetermineqtheqdesignqbyqexaminingqcapability,qresources,qandq 
differentq strategies),q process evaluation q (thatq helpsq toq controlq theq operationsq byq 
providingqonRgoingqfeedback),qandq product evaluation q(thatqhelpsqtoqjudgeqandqreactqtoq 
theqcourse’sqattainmentsqinqtermsqofqoutputsqandqoutcomes).q
q
Newbyq (1992)q focusq hisq attentionq inq theq contextsq ofq evaluationq andq arguesq thatq 
evaluationqcanqtakeqplaceqwithinqtheqtrainingqevent,qinqtheqworkplaceqafterqtheqevent,qinq 
theq contextq ofq performanceq measures,qandq usingq criteriaq notq relatedq toqtheq workplace,q 
suchqasqsocietal,qmoral,qorqpoliticalqcriteria.q
q

Pulleyq(1994)qclaimsqthatqtheqobjectiveqofqevaluationqshouldqbeqtoqprovideqevidenceqsoq 
thatq decisionRmakersq canq determineq whatq theyq wantq toq knowq aboutq theq trainingq 
programme.q Hisq modelq isq focusedq onq theq needsq forq qualitativeq orq quantitativeq 
informationqofqtheqdecisionRmakers.qPulley’sqworkqhasqbeenqsupportedqinqsomeqliteratureq 
(forq example,q Abernathy,q 1999)q thatq statesq thatq evaluatorsq mustq findq whatq internalq 
customersq wantq toq know,q ratherq thanq collectingq dataq definedq byq aq preRexistingq 
framework.q Thisq suggestsq thatq eachq stakeholderq mayqlookq forq aq differentq evaluationq 
model.qq
q
OtherqmodelsqthatqhaveqaqdifferentqapproachqfromqKirkpatrick’squseqdifferentq measures q
ofqevaluation:qq
q
- Kraigerq et al. q(1993)qemphasizeqtheqimportanceqofqlinkingqtrainingqevaluationqtoq 
learningq outcomes.q Theyq distinguishq threeq types of outcomes q (cognitive ,q skill-
based ,qandq affective )qandqargueqthatqtheqgoalsqofqtrainingqmustqbeqlookedqfromq 
theseq threeq perspectives,q whichq inq turnq willq makeq theq evaluationq measuresq 
clearer;q
- KaplanqandqNortonq(1996)qproposedqaqbalancedqscorecardqandqsuggestqdifferentq 
perspectivesqofqevaluation:q finance ,q customers ,q internal business processes ,qandq

areqasqimportantqasqfinancialqmeasures;qq
- Leeq(1994)qsuggestsqtheq pay back, pay forward qapproachqwhereqaqseparationqisq 
madeqbetweenqpayqbackqandqpayqforwardqresults.qPayqbackqincludesqtheqfinancialq 
benefits,q whereasq payq forwardq includesq thoseq benefitsq thatq flowq fromq training,q 
whichqcannotqbeqexpressedqdirectlyqinqfinancialqtermsq(indirectqreturns).q
q
Laterq (pageq 101),q weq willq discussq anotherq alternativeq modelq ofq evaluationq thatq wasq

2.4.3.  Quality in e-Learning 
q
2.4.3.1.  Defining What e-Learning Is 
q
TheqtermqeRlearningqhasqitsqrootqinqdistanceqeducationqandqinqcomputerRbasedqtraining,q 
whichqappearedqinqtheqearlyq80’sqandqusedqCDRROMsqtoqteachqmostlyqtechnicalqskillsqtoq 
mostlyq technicalq peopleq (ACTq Center,q 2007).q Aroundq1995,q electronicq learningq wasq 
calledqInternetqbasedqtrainingq(IBT).qToqclarifyqthatqtheqlearningqprocessqcouldqalsoqbeq 
withinq anq Intranet,q itq wasq thenq calledq WebRbasedq Trainingq (WBT).q Later,q theq conceptq 
evolvedq toq online learning q andq finallyq eRlearning,q “adoptingq theq inq vogueq useq ofq "eR"q 
duringqtheqdotqcomqboom”(ERlearningqGuru,q2007).qNowadays,qitqisqgenericallyqacceptedq 
thatqeRlearningqisq the delivery of learning by electronic means ,qalthoughqtoqsomeqauthorsq 
suchq asq Deweyq (1902,q 1910,q 1916),q Vygotskyq (1978),qandq Pauloq Freireq (1970,q 1992,q 
1996,q 1998),q theq ideaq ofq learningq asq somethingq thatq canq beq delivered q andq transferred q
fromqoneqheadqtoqanotherqmakesqnoqsense.qq
q
ERlearningqhasqbeenqusedqinqtheqcontextqofqhigherqeducation,qinqvocationalqeducationqandq 
training,qcorporateqtraining,qandqinformalqlearning.qItqincludesqaqwideqrangeqofqlearningq 
formatsq thatq includeq tutorialsq (selfRstudy)q andq instructorRled,q asynchronousq orq 
synchronous,q“pure”qorqblendedqlearning,qsmallqgroupqonlineqcollaboration,qknowledgeq 
databasesq (alsoq knownq asq repositories),q onRdemandq eRlearning,q onlineq coaching,q andq 

PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
q
q
58 
'jukeboxes'q ofq granularq chunksq ofq learningq material.q Itq alsoq includesq moreq recentq 
conceptsq andq trendsq suchq asq podcasting,q blogs,q wikis,q andq academicq usesq ofq socialq 
communitiesqsuchqasqTwitterqandqFacebook.qq
Asq mentioned,q eRlearningq hasq developedq fromq twoq mainq origins,q oneq ofq whichq isq 
distanceq education,q whichq inq turn,q hasq sinceq itsq veryq startq “alwaysq representedq anq 
alternativeqtoqtraditionalq andq training,qand,q therefore,qhasq hadqtoqbattleq forq recognitionq 
andqconsequentlyqdevelopedqproceduresqforqdemonstratingqqualityqearlyqon”q(Rekkedal,q 
2006,qp.q12).q
q
q
2.4.3.2.  Stakeholders and Profiles of Quality in e-Learning 
q
EhlersqandqPawlowskiq(2006,qp.q6)qalertqthatqcurrentlyqthereqareqnoqgenerallyqrecognizedq 
approachesqforqqualityqmanagementqinqeRlearning.qThisqdoesqnotqmeanqthatqthereqareqnoq 
qualityq concernsq inq eRlearning,q althoughq itq isq “difficultq toq 'fix'q duringq aq periodq ofq 
significantq changeq andq innovation;q andq constancyq ofq purposeq isq neededq toq maintainq 
momentumq inq assuringq quality”q (ICCA,q 2004a).q Inq orderq toq copeq withq thisq unclearq 
scenario,qEhlersqandqPawlowskiq(2006,qp.q2)qproposeqqaqdifferentqapproachqtoqqualityqinq 
eRlearningq basedq onq threeq criteria:q differentq interpretationsq ofq quality,q differentq 
stakeholdersqwithqdifferentqperspectivesqonqquality,qandqdifferentqformsqofqqualityq(alsoq 
knownqasqinputR,qprocessR,qoutputRquality).q
q
Kazmerq &q Haythornthwaiteq (2005),q whileq discussingq theq stakeholder’sq pointq ofq view,q 
defineqtheqprimaryqconcernsqofqeach:q
q
R Forq educators ,qtheqprimaryqconcernqhasqbeenq“whetherqonlineqprogramsqresultqinq 
learningq outcomesq thatq areq asq goodq asq thoseq achievedq throughq traditionalq 
means”;q
R Forq faculty and instructors ,qtheq primaryq concernq isq“howq doq weqteachq online?q 
Whatqworksqandqwhatqdoesqnot?qLikeqanyqotherqeducationalqenterprise,qthereqareq 
betterqandqworseqpracticesqinqonlineqteaching.qTranslatingqcoursesqintoqtheqonlineq 
environmentq successfullyq requiresq newq pedagogicalq techniques,q syllabi,q 
assessmentq mechanisms,q andq understandingq ofq theq particularq needsq ofq adultq 
distanceqlearners”;qq
R Forq administrators ,qtheqconcernqis:q“afterqspendingqtheqeffortqandqmoneyqtoqputqaq 
wholeqdegreeqorqprogramqonline,qwillqitqbeqaccepted?”q
q
Theq conceptq ofq individual qquality profiles (Pawlowski,q 2004)q inq eRlearningq hasq beenq 
suggested,qandqfourqtypesqofqqualityqprofilesqinqeRlearningqhaveqbeenqidentifiedq(Ehlers,q 
2004):q
q
R Theq individualist ,q thatq isq contentRorientedq andq prefersq individualisedq learningq 
scenarios;qqq
R Theq result-oriented ,q thatq isq independentq andq goalRoriented.q Learningq isq workq 
integratedqandqthereqisqanqinstrumentalqpurposeqattitude;q
R Theq pragmatic ,q thatq needsq toq beq oriented,q requiresq tutorq support,q information,q 
andqadvise;q
R Andq theq avant-gardist ,q thatq isq interactionRoriented,q electsq discussionsqandq 
communication,qandqexpectsqtechnologyqvanguard.q
q

q
59 
2.4.3.3.  Attitudes and Beliefs Related to Quality in e-Learning 
q
Overallq ratingsq ofq onlineq coursesq areq significantlyq moreq positiveq thanq theq inRclassq 
versionsqofqtheqsameqcourses,qandqonlineqstudentsqareqmoreqwillingqtoqrecommendqtheq 
courseq toq others,q thanq theq inRclassq students,q whichq reflectsq theq students’q skillRlearningq 
ratherqthanqrequirementRfulfilmentqmotivationqforqtakingqtheqcoursesq(Kleinmanq&qEntin,q 
2002).q Attitudesq andq satisfactionq ofq studentsq inq eRlearningq areq alsoq generallyq positiveq 
(Kleinmanq &q Entin,q 2002;q Phippsq &q Merisotis,q 1999,qquotedq inq Kleinmanq &q Entin,q 
2002).q Theseq studiesq provideq someq insightsq aboutq overallq satisfactionq onq eRlearning,q 
buyingq intentions,q wordRofRmouthq promotionalq potential,qandq generalq perceptionsq that,q 
asqdiscussedqabove,qareqrelatedqtoqquality.qq
q
ERlearningq quality,q byq now,q shouldq beq equalq toq faceRtoRfaceq learningq (Theq Sloanq 
Consortium,q2003,qpp.q10R11)qbutqthisqdoesqnotqmeanqthatqspecificqqualityqdimensionsq 
cannotq haveq completelyq differentq perceptionsq inq onlineq andq faceRtoRfaceq education.q Inq 
fact,qsimilarqoverallq perceptions of quality qcanqalsoqmeanqdifferentqqualityqproblemsqandq 
qualityqconcerns.qMoreover,qaqwiderqrangeqofqlearningqreasonsqalsoqmakesqexpectationsq 
ofq anq onlineq courseq different,q andq differentq expectations,q can,q asq alreadyq discussed,q 
createqdifferentqperceptionsqofqoverallqquality.qq
q
Althoughq eRlearningq qualityq specificq literatureq isqfrequentlyq tryingq toq compareq onlineq 
learningqwithqtraditionalqfaceRtoRfaceqlearning,qdemographicqandqsocialqdifferencesqthatq 
existqbetweenqtheqstudentsqofqeRlearningqcoursesqandqfaceRtoRfaceqcoursesqmustqbeqtakenq 
inq considerationq whenq comparingq both.q Inq fact,q thereq areq notq onlyq socioRdemographicq 
differencesq butq alsoq differencesq inq theq reasonsq forq takingq onlineq courses:q studentsq areq 
muchq moreq likelyq toq beq takingq theq courseq forq theq learningq experienceq (theq internally 
motivated reason )qwhereasqinRclassqstudentsqareqmoreqlikelyqtoqbeqinqtheqcourseqbecauseq 
itqisqaqrequirementqforqtheirqprogramq( externally motivated reasons )q(Kleinmanq&qEntin,q 
2002).qBesidesqthat,qpeopleqexpectqaqmoreqinformalqtypeqofqinstructionq–qandqlearningq–q
inqonlineqcoursesqthanqinqfaceRtoRfaceqcourses:qNotqonlyqstudentsqfeelqthatqtheyqdependq 
muchqmoreqonqtheirqownqeffortsqandqthatqtheyqhaveqmuchqmoreqcontrolqofqtheirqlearningq 
process,qbutqtheyqalsoqexpectqtoqtakeqanqactiveqpartqofqtheqinstructionalqprocess.qAqmoreq 
participativeqinstructionalqapproach,qfilledqwithqdiversifiedqcontentqmediaqsupportsqandq 
friendlyqandqinformalqcontexts,qisqalsoqexpected.qq
q
Differencesqinq learning outcomes qforqonlineqeducation,qinqcomparisonqwithqfaceRtoRfaceq 
traditionalq education,q areq alsoq subjectq ofq attention.q Inq thisq field,q theq literatureq hasq 
pacificallyq acceptedq thatq theq learningq outcomesq forq onlineq educationq areq equalq orq 
superiorq toq thoseq ofq faceRtoRfaceq instructionq (Kleinmanq &q Entin,q 2002;q Phippsq &q 
Merisotis,q1999,qquotedqinqKeinmanq&qEntin,q2002;qTheqSloanqConsortium,q2003,qp.q10)q
q
Ehlersq et al. q(2005,qp.q25)qfoundqoutqthatqforqhalfqofqtheqstudents,q‘qualityqinqeRlearning’q 
isq theq best learning achievements .q Thisq means,q theyq claim,q thatq qualityq inq theq 
educationalq senseq requiresq notq justq averageq performance,q butq theq bestq performanceq 
imaginable.q Thisq isqcloselyq connectedq withq somethingq beingq excellentq inq performanceq 
(exceptionality );qAqfifthqofqallqrespondentsqcallqforq excellence in performance ,qalthoughq 
thisq mayq meanq notq onlyq successfulq learningq butq also,q forq example,q ‘carryingq outq andq 
navigatingq aq learningq programme’q orq ‘applyingq whatqhasq beenq learntq inq practice’;q 
Anotherq fifthq ofq respondentsq expectq qualityq toq meanq fulfillingq aq certainq minimumq 
standard,qsomethingqthatqmeetsqtheqstandardqrequirement;qAndqfinally,qonlyq4,5%qofqtheq 
respondentsqassociateq‘quality’qwithqreceivingqtheqbestqvalueqforqmoney.q

2.4.3.4.  Types of Methods and Instruments of Quality in e-Learning 
q
Donabedianq(1980,qquotedqinqUlfRDanielqEhlersq&qPawlowski,q2006,qp.4)qsuggestedqtheq 
followingqqualityqtriadqtoqapproachqqualityqinqeRlearning:qq
q
R ERlearningq prerequisitesq (inputq orq structureq quality),q whichq includeq theq 
availabilityqorqcapabilityqofqtheqtechnologicalqinfrastructure,qandqqualificationqofq 
tutors,qamongqothers;qq
R Theq learningq processq (processq quality),q whichq includesq theq interactionq ofq 
learners,q learningq formats,q corporateq learningq culture,q learningq content,q andq 
desiredqtrainingqgoals;q
R Theq resultq (output/outcomeq quality),q whichq includesq theq increaseq inq theq

2.5.  Motivations,qPerceptionsqofqValue,qandqUtility,qandqTheirqRelationq

2.5.1.  Insights From Motivational Theories 
q
2.5.1.1.  Quality and Motivation 
q
Motivationq isq composedq ofq energizing,q directing,q andq maintenanceq components.q Inq aq 
trainingqsituation,qmotivationqcanqbeqseenqasqaqforceqthatqinfluencesqenthusiasmqaboutqtheq 
programq(energizer),qaqstimulusqthatqdirectsqparticipantsqtoqlearnqandqattemptqtoqmasterq 
theq contentq ofq theq programq (director),q andq aq forceqthatq influencesq theq useq ofq newlyq 
acquiredq knowledgeq andq skills,q evenq inq theq presenceq ofq criticismq andq lackq ofq 
reinforcementqforquseqofqtheqtrainingqcontentq(maintenance)q(Noeq&qSchmitt,q1986,qp.q 
498).qqIndividualsqmayqorqmayqnotqbeqmotivatedqtoqattendqanqeRlearningqcourse,qandqafterq 
that,qtheyqmayqbeqmotivated,qorqnot,qtoquseqallqtheqknowledgeqandqskills,qthatqtheyqcreatedq 
duringqthatqcourse,qinqtheirqworkqorqinqtheirqlife.qTheqattributesqofqmotivationqidentifiedq 
byqNoeqandqSchmittq(1986,qp.q498)qrelateqmotivationqtoqbehaviour,qwhich,qinqaqtrainingq 
situation,q reflectq theq use qofq acquiredq knowledge,q skills,q andqattitudes.q Thisq meansqthatq 
theq presenceq ofq motivationq suggestsq thatq thereq isq aq stimulusq to  use q theq acquiredq 
knowledge,qskills,qandqattitudesqafterqtheqcourseqisqcompleted.qInqthisqsense,qtheqstimulusq 
toquse,qorqmotivation,qmightqbeqhypothesizedqtoqbeqrelatedqtoqqualityqasqfitness for use q
(Juran,q1951,qSectionq2R2).qInqotherqwords,qifqthereqisqaqstimulus to use ,qthereqmustqbeqaq 
perceptionqofq fitness for use ,qwhich,qinqturn,qsuggestsqthatqmotivationqisqsomehowqrelatedq 
toqquality.q
q
Onqtheqsupplyqside,qthereqareqalsoqreferencesqtoqtheqroleqofqmotivationqinqquality:qTQMq 
literatureq (forq instance,q ISO/TCq 176:q Qualityq Managementq andq Qualityq Assurance,q 
2007)q emphasizes,q inq itsq principlesq (Appendixq 1),q theq needq ofq involvementq ofq 
individuals:q motivated qindividualsqwillqbeqcommittedqandqinvolved,qwillqbeqaccountableq 
forqtheirqownqperformance,qandqwillqbeqeagerqtoq participateqandqcontribute.qMoreover,q 
thoseq individualsq willq activelyq seekq opportunitiesqtoq enhanceq theirq competence,q 
knowledge,qandqexperienceqwithinqtheqcompany,qandqtheyqwillqcontributeqtoqqualityqwithq 
theirqmotivationqandqinvolvement.q
q
Severalqauthorsq(forqexample,qFok,qFok,qHartman,q&qPatti,q2001;qTalaqq&qAhmed,q2003)q
haveq beenq dedicatingq theirq attentionq toq theq influenceq thatq theq motivationq ofq theq 
company’sq employeesq hasq onq quality.q Lessq often,q othersq (forq example,q Holton1996)q
focusqtheirqattentionqinqtheqinfluenceqthatqtheqmotivationqofqtheqclientqhasqonqtheqqualityq 
ofq theq goodq orq serviceq delivered.q Inq thisq lastq case,q educationalq literatureq hasq theq mostq 
extensiveq contributeq asq itq isq recognizedq thatq theq student’sq motivationq isq anq importantq 
pieceqofqtheqlearningqprocess.qInqtheqfollowingqpages,qweqwillqbrieflyqdescribeqtheqmajorq 
explanationsqtoqmotivation,qinqorderqto,qafterqthat,qunderstandqwhyqindividualsqvalueqaq 
goodq orq aq serviceq inq general,q andq anq eRlearningq courseq inq particular.q Weq willq relateq 
motivation qtoq perception of value qandqexploreq utility qasqanqidiosyncraticqtypeqofqvalue.q 
Theqrelationshipqbetweenq motivation qandq utility qwillqalsoqbeqmadeqmoreqexplicitqwhenq 
weqfocusqourqattentionqinqtheqparticularqcaseqofqeRlearning.q

2.5.1.2.  The Decision of Acquisition and the Sources of Needs and Motivation 
q
Ifqweqaskqwhyqpeopleqbuyqaqproduct,qoneqofqtheqmostqobviousqanswerqisqtoq own q(Oliver,q 
1997,qp.q136).qIfqtheqproductqisqanqonlineqtrainingqcourse,qownershipqcanqrangeqfromqpureq 
tangibleq detailsq asq theq courseq manuals,q orq tangibleq elementsq asq theq trainingq certificateq 
thatq hasqaq greatq amountq ofq psychologicalq meaning,q toq pureq intangibleqelementsq asq theq 
trainingqexperienceqandqtheqknowledge,qskills,qandqattitudesqthatqwereqcreatedqduringqtheq 
trainingqprogram.qOwnership,qinqturn,qisqpursuedqtoqfulfilqaqperceivedq need qtoqown.qq
q
AccordingqtoqOliverq(1997,qp.q136),qthereqareqtwoq sources of need :qq
q
• Theqfirstqisqaqdeficitqthatqexistsqinqtheqconsumer’sqlifeqthatqsheqwantsqtoqremove.q 
Inqthisqcase,qtheqpurposeqofqtheqpurchaseqisq restoration ,qinqorderqtoqbringqherqbackq 
toqtheqwholeness;qqq
• Theqsecondqsourceqisqtheqconsumerqdesireqtoqincreaseqtheqpositiveq value qofqherq 
life.q Inq thisq case,q theq deficitq isq createdq inq theq consumer’sq imaginationq ofq theq 
future utility qofqpossession.qq
q
Restoration qandq enhancement qareqtheqtwoqcasesqofqreinforcementqspecifiedqbyqSkinnerq 
(1969),q inq operant conditioning ,q theq termq heq usesq toq describeq theq effectsq ofq theq 
consequencesqofqaqparticularqbehaviourqonqtheqfutureqoccurrenceqofqthatqbehaviour.qq
q
Besidesq positiveq andq negativeq reinforcements,q operant conditioning q alsoq includesq 
positiveqandqnegativeqpunishmentsqandqextinctionqoptionsq(Skinner,q1969):qq
q
- Positive reinforcement q occursq whenq aq behaviourq (response)q isq followedq byqaq 
favourableqstimulusq(commonlyqseenqasqpleasant)qthatqincreasesqtheqfrequencyqofq 
thatqbehaviour.qInqtheqSkinnerqboxqexperiment,qaqstimulusqsuchqasqfoodqorqsugarq 
solutionq canq beq deliveredq whenq theq ratq engagesq inq aq targetq behaviour,q suchq asq 
pressingqaqlever;qq
- Negative reinforcement qoccursqwhenqaqbehaviourq(response)qisqfollowedqbyqtheq 
removalq ofq anq aversiveq stimulusq (commonlyq seenq asq unpleasant),q therebyq 
increasingq theq frequencyq ofq thatq behaviour.q Inq theqSkinnerq boxq experiment,q 
negativeq reinforcementq canq beq aq loudq noiseq continuouslyq soundingq insideq theq 
rat'sqcagequntilqitqengagesqinqtheqtargetqbehaviour,qsuchqasqpressingqaqlever,quponq 
whichqtheqloudqnoiseqisqremoved;qq
- Positive punishment q(alsoqcalledq"punishmentqbyqcontingentqstimulation")qoccursq 
whenq aq behaviourq (response)q isq followedq byq anq aversiveq stimulus,q suchq asq 
introducingqaqshockqorqloudqnoise,qresultingqinqaqdecreaseqinqthatqbehaviour;qq
- Negative punishment q (alsoq calledq "punishmentq byq contingentq withdrawal")q 
occursqwhenqaqbehaviourq(response)qisqfollowedqbyqtheqremovalqofqaqfavourableq 
stimulus,q suchq asq takingq awayq aq child'sq toyq followingq anq undesiredq behaviour,q 
resultingqinqaqdecreaseqinqthatqbehaviour;qq
- Extinction  isq theq lackq ofq anyq consequenceq followingq aq response.q Whenq aq 
responseq isq inconsequential,q producingq neitherq favourableq norq unfavourableq 
consequences,qitqwillqoccurqwithqlessqfrequency.q
q
Bothq positive qandq negative reinforcements qstrengthenqbehaviour,qwhileq punishment andq 
extinction qweakenqit.q Negative reinforcement qisqusuallyqconfusedqwithq punishment ,qbutq 
theyqareqveryqdifferentqconcepts:q negative reinforcement qstrengthensqbehaviour,qbecauseq 
aq negativeq conditionq isq stoppedq orq avoidedq asq aq consequenceq ofq theq behaviour;q 

PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
67 
punishment ,q onq theq otherq hand,q weakensq behaviourq becauseq aq negativeq conditionq isq 
introducedq orq experiencedq asq aq consequenceq ofq thatqbehaviour.q Reinforcement q isq aq 
rewardq thatq hasq theq propertyq ofq sustainingq behaviour,q or,q atq least,q increasingq theq 
likelihoodq ofq behaviour.q Losingq theq stableqjobq thatq oneq hadqforq yearsq isq theq triggerq toq 
searchqforqaqtrainingqprogram,qinqorderqtoq restore qanqemployment,qandqlifestyleqsituation.q 
Theqtrainingqprogramqwillqactqasq negative reinforcement q–qtheqmechanismqofqremovalqofq 
anq aversive/negativeq situationq andq toq restoreq theq neutralityq status.q Asq soonq asq thisq 
restorationqoccurs,qaqfeelingqofqreliefqisqachieved.qInqcontrast,qattendingqaqtrainingqcourseq 
toq increaseq currentq jobq performanceq isq aq positive reinforcement ,q asq itq resultsq inq anq 
addition,qorqenhancement:qaqmovequpqfromqtheqneutralityqstatus.qItqproducesqpleasureqandq 
lifeq enrichment,q ratherq thanq lifeq restore.q Theq distinctionq betweenq theseq twoq 
interpretationsqofqfulfilmentqofqneedsq–qrestoration qandq enhancement ,qalsoqprovidesqanq 
easyq wayq toq distinguishq needs q fromq wants .q Needs q areq moreq relatedq withq deficitsq andq 
restoration,qandqareqconsideredqmoreqessentialqtoqhumanqexistence,qwhileq wants qderiveq 
fromq desiredq enhancements,q andq tendq toq beq viewedq asq superfluousq desires.q Oneq mayq 
considererqaqjobqrelatedqtrainingqcourseqasqaq need ,qwhileqconsideringqaqjobqnonRrelatedq 
trainingqcourseqonqhousingqstorageqsystemqandqdecorationqasqaq want .qq
q
Asqdiscussedqabove,q reinforcement qisqaqcoreqconceptqofqoperantqconditioning,qinqwhichq 
theq consequencesq areq usedq toq modifyq theq frequencyq ofq aq “voluntary”q behaviour.q Thisq 
meansq thatq aq personq willq attendq aq trainingq programqforq theq consequencesq ofq thatq 
frequency.q Yet,q operantq conditioningq opposesq toq classical conditioning ,q alsoq calledq 
respondent conditioning ,qorq Pavlovian conditioning q(C.qD.qGreen,q2008;qPavlov,q1927),q 
whereqbehaviourqisqmotivatedqbyq antecedent conditions .qThisqwouldqmeanqthatqaqpersonq 
wouldqattendqaqtrainingqprogramqnotqforqitsqconsequencesqbutqforqitsqantecedents.qThisq 
wouldq beq theq caseq ofq attendingq aq trainingq courseq becauseq ofq aq positiveq earlyq schoolq 
experienceq (eitherq withq aq specificq trainingq companyq orq aq specificq trainer).q Negativeq 
antecedentsqareqalsoqcommonqandqnegativeqschoolqexperiencesqproduceqnegativeqeffectsq 
inqlaterqeducationalqexperiencesq(Ahl,q2006).q
q
q
2.5.1.3.  Needs versus  Motivations 
q
Thereq areq severalq kindsq ofq servicesq (D.q P.q Cook,q Goh,q &q Chung,q 1999):q restorative q
servicesq(suchqasqhomeqrepairsqandqdentalqcavityqcare),q status quo maintenance qservicesq 
(suchq asq commonq residentialq utilities),q andq services that add value toq anq existingq

status quo qmaintenanceqservices,qtheqneedqextinguishes,qwhileqinq value-adding qservicesq 
theq motivationq isq reinforced.q Thisq isq whatq differentiatesq need q fromq motivation .q Inq 
motivationqtheories,qindividualsqareqdescribedqinqtermsqofqkindsqofqeffectsqtheyqareqtryingq 
toqbringqabout,qandqnotqinqtermsqofqsatiatingqneedsq(Oliver,q1997,qpp.q139R140).qq

2.5.1.4.  Motivation to Learn and Its Temporary Barriers 
q
Motivationq toq learnq canqbeqdescribedqasq aq specificqdesireq onqtheq partq ofq theqtraineeqtoq 
learnqtheqcontentqofqtheqtrainingqprogramqandqdevelopqtheqplannedqskillsqandqattitudes.qq
Mostq need/motivationq andq educationalq theoriesq takeqforq grantedq thatq humansq haveq anq 
intrinsicq motivationq toq learnq (Cropley,q 1985;q P.q K.q Cross,q 1981;q Knowles,q 1980;q 
Wlodkowski,q1999),qand,qtherefore,qmotivationqtoqstudyqandqlearningqareqalwaysqseenqasq 
latent.q
q
Evenq so,q althoughq generallyq motivatedq toq learn,q adultsq mayq notq beq motivatedq toq aq 
specific  trainingq programq andq notq motivatedq toq another.q Inq otherq words,q adultsq revealq 
interestq inq aq specificq trainingq courseq ifq itq offersq themq someq concrete,q specificq benefitq
(Ruberson,q1977).q
q
Motivationqtoqlearnqhasqaqdirectqrelationshipqwithqlearningq(Holton1996,qp.q11).qYet,q pre-
training motivation q andq traineeq attitudesq haveq notq receivedq enoughq attentionq inq theq 
literatureq(D.qJ.qCohen,q1990).qEvenqso,qfourqcategoriesqofqvariablesqareqhypothesizedqtoq 
beqtheqprimaryqinfluencesqonq motivation to learn q(Holton1996,qpp.q11R12):qq
q
- Readiness for the intervention :q Hicksq &q Klimoskiq (1987)q foundq thatq givingq 
traineesqtheqchoiceqtoqattendqtrainingqorqnot,qincreasedqtheirqmotivationqtoqlearnq 
andq improvedq learningq outcomes;q Baldwin,q Magjuka,q andq Loherq (1991)q foundq 
thatqtraineesqwhoqwereqgivenqaqchoiceqregardingqtheqtrainingqcontentqhadqgreaterq 
motivationq toq learn.q However,qthoseq whoq wereqallowedq toq chooseqbutqthenq notq 
givenqtheirq choiceq becameq lessqmotivatedq thanq thoseq whoq wereq notqallowedq toq 
chooseqatqall.qThus,qtheqdegreeqtoqwhichqaqtraineeqisqinvolvedqinqtheqprocessqofq 
needsqassessment,qandqgivenqchoicesqaboutqtraining,qcanqbeqexpectedqtoqinfluenceq 
motivationq toq learn.q Readiness q includesq suchq variablesq asq theq degreeq toq whichq 
traineesq areq involvedq inq assessingq needs,q theq involvementq inq planningq theq 
training,qtheqdegreeqtoqwhichqexpectationsqareqclarified,qandqtheqdegreeqofqchoice,q 
amongqothers;q
- Job attitudes :qemployeesqwhoqexhibitqmoreqpositiveqjobqattitudesqtendqtoqbeqmoreq 
motivatedqtoqlearn,qand,qinqturn,qhaveqmoreqpositiveqoutcomes.qNoeqandqSchmittq 
(1986)q foundq aq significantq relationshipq betweenq jobq involvementq andq learning,q

Thisqmeansqthatqhumanqinnateqneedqtoqlearnqisqhomeostatic:qmotivationqexistsqinitiallyq

2.5.1.5.  Searching for a Better Construct  
q
Thereqareqseveralqreasonsqthatqcouldqleadqusqtoqexcludeqmotivationqasqaqrelevantqfactorqofq 
qualityqinqeRlearning.qq
q
Firstqofqall,qbecauseqitqisqassumedqthatqeveryqhumanqbeingqhasqtheqinnateqneedqtoqlearn,qaq 
generalq presenceq versus q absenceq ofq innateq needq differenceq inq thatq needq cannotq beq 
assumedq toqjustifyq differentq perceptionsq ofq quality,qalthough,qatqaq lowerq level,qatqeachq 
course,qmotivationqmayqbeqexpressedqinqdifferentqlevels,qandqnotqjustqasqsimpleqpresenceq
orqabsence.qq
q
Theq secondq reasonq isq thatq mostq motivationalq theoriesq privilegesq individualq needs,q inq 
detrimentqofqsocialqneeds,qandqinqtheqspecificqcontextqofqeducation,qexternalqrecognitionq 
ofq one’sq abilitiesq orq knowledgeq isq relevantq (forq instance,q toq applyq forq aq job,q orq toq aq 
promotion).q Forq example,q Maslowq (1943,q 1954,q 1968)qputsq social needs q inq theq thirdq 
placeq fromq theq bottomq ofq hisq hierarchy,q McClellandq(1975)q doesq notq considerq affinity 
needs q asq contributorsq toq theq developmentq ofq theq society,q Herzbergq (1966,q 1968;q 
Herzbergq et al .,q1959)qaccountsq social needs qasqanqhygienicqneed,qandqDeciqandqRyanq 
(Deci,q 1975;q Deciq &q Ryan,q 1985)q privilegeq inner motivation q ratherq thanq outer 
motivation .qMoreover,qalthoughqthisqgeneralqprivilegeqofqindividualqneedsqisqcommonqinq 
westernq societies,q eastq societiesq areq constructedq withq strongq valuesq basedq onq theq 
communityqandq socialqweb.q Duties,q dependency,qandq theq ideaqofq beingq controlled,qareq 
notq wellq acceptedq inq westernq societies,q butq areq seenq asq naturalq inq eastq cultures.q Thisq 
meansq thatq mostq motivationalq theoriesq mayq notq giveqtheq deservedq attentionq toq theq 
social/collectiveqfactorqincludedqinqtheqtrainees’qmotivation.q
q
Theq thirdq reasonq isq thatq nobodyq isq justq ‘motivated’q becauseq motivationq isq aq relationalq 
conceptqthatqdependsqonqotherqobjectsqorqactionsqandqcannotqbeqstudiedqbyqalone.qq
q
Finally,qtheqrelationshipqbetweenqmotivationqandqbehaviourqisqalsoqquestioned.q Attitudes q
areq definedq asq predispositionsq toq behaveq inq aq characteristicq mannerq withq respectq toq 
specifiedqsocialqobjectsqorqclassesqofqsuchqobjects.qYet,qthereqisqveryqlittleqevidenceqforqaq 
relationshipqbetweenq attitudes qandq action (behaviour) q(Ahl,q2006).q
q
Forq theseq reasons,q weq willq approachq nowq axiologyq toq betterq understandq notq onlyq 
motivation,qbutqmainly,qperceptionsqofqqualityqinqtheqcontextqofqeRlearningqcourses:q value q
willqbeqpresentedqasqaqhigherRlevelqconstructqthatqcanqhelpqusqtoqunderstandqbetterqbothq 
motivationqandqperceptionsqofqquality.qqq

2.5.2.  Quality and Axiology 
q
2.5.2.1.  Introduction 
q
Thereqisqnotqaqgeneric,qwidelyqacceptedqopinionqaboutqtheqproperqinterpretationqtoqbeqputq 
uponq factsq andq uponq behaviours,q and,q therefore,q uponq theq perceptionsq ofq qualityq thatq 
traineesqcreateqonqeRlearningqcourses,qandquponqtheirqmotivationqtoqattendqthoseqcourses.q 
Weq haveq beenq presentingq severalq perspectivesq fromq whichq qualityq perceptionsq canq beq 
lookedq at,q asq theq serviceq marketingq andq theq motivationq perspectives.q Anotherq majorq 
theoreticalq frameworkq thatq canq provideq usefulq insightsq onq thoseq interpretationsq isq theq 
theoryq ofq valuation.q Inq theq endq ofq theq day,q facts,qbehaviours,q andq motivationsq canq beq 
explainedqbyq perceptions of value qandqobjectivesqandqso,qperceptions of quality qcanqbeq 
rootedqinqvalueqpropositions.q
q
 
2.5.2.2.    Quality and Value: Why Look Into Value? 
q
Axiologyq hasq beenq usedq asq anq inspirationq forq severalq managementq approachesq andq 
concepts.qForqinstance,qaccordingqtoqWoodall  (2003),q customer value qisqaqperceptionalq 
phenomenon,qassessesqtheqperceptionqthatqaqcustomerqhasqofqtheq goodwill qthatqaqproductq 
orq aq serviceq mayq bringq toq her.q Woodallq (2003)q suggestsq thatq corporateq decisionsq areq 
madeqonqtheqbasisqofqcustomer’sqpredictionsqconcerningqtheqvalueqofqaqfutureqproductqorq 
service.q Customer value q isq commonlyq usedq toq createq corporateq objectives,q supportq 
severalqproductqdecisions,qdesign,qmarketing,qandqsellingqapproaches.qMoreover,qvalueq 
hasq beenq relatedq withq customerq satisfaction,q loyalty,q andq corporateq profitabilityq (forq 
example,qqHallowell,q1996,qp.q28)qand,qtherefore,qitqisqnotqdifficultqtoqrelateqitqtoqquality.qq
q
Theq conceptq ofq qualityq becomesq clearerq asq weq distinguishq itq fromq satisfaction,q asq weq 
discussedq previouslyq (pageq 27).q Theq sameq happensq whenq relatingq itq toq theq conceptq ofq 
value:qasqsoonqasqitqbecomesqclearqwhatqaxiologyqmeansqandqstandsqfor,qtheqconceptqofq 
qualityqbecomesqclearer.qAsqHolbrookqandqCorfmanq(1985,qp.q40)qrecognize,q“weqcannotq 
adequatelyqcomprehendqtheqmeaningqofqqualityqwithoutqrelatingqitqtoqotherqtermsqwithinq 
theqbroaderqsphereqofqnormativeqdiscourse.qWeqcannotqunderstandqqualityqunlessqweqcanq 
specifyq howq itq comparesq withq beauty,q convenience,q fun,q andq otherq typesq ofq valueq 
judgment”.qq
q
Thisqsuggestsqthatqtheqmeaningqofqqualityqmustqbeqanalyzedqwithinqtheqoverallqnatureqofq 
value .q
 
 
2.5.2.3.    Value and Motivation 
q
Itqisqnowqtheqappropriateqmomentqtoqexplainqwhyqitqisqsoqimportantqtoqlookqintoq value q
theories,qafterqmakingqanqoverviewqstateRofRtheRartqonqmotivation.qTheqeasiestqwayqisqtoq 
lookqintoqmotivation,qandqunderstandqthatqnobodyqisqonlyq‘motivated’.qAsqAhlq(2006,qp.q 
402)q argues,q motivationq mustq notq beq regardedq asq anqentity,q residingq withinq theq 
individual,q butq ratherq asq aq relationalq concept,q asqitq isq hardq toq speakq aboutq motivationq 
withoutqrelatingq itqtoqsomething:q oneqcanq beq motivated to work,qtoqstudy,q toq play,q butq 
neverqjustqmotivated,qexceptqwhenqusingqitqasqaqsynonymqofqenergetic.qAlthoughqAhl’sq 
pointqofqviewqmakesqsense,qitqisqnotqenoughqtoqsayqthatqaqpersonqisqmotivatedqtoqlearnqorq 
isq motivatedq toq attendq anq eRlearningq course.q Itq isqimportantq toq understand  why sheq isq

q
ForqHolbrookq(1999c,qpp.q5R9)qconsumerqvalueqisqaq relativistic (comparative,qpersonalq

someqobject.q
