Valueqisq interactive qbecauseqitqentailsqanqinteractionqbetweenqsomeqsubjectq(aqconsumer,q 
orq trainee)q andq someq objectq (aq productq or,q inq ourq case,q aq trainingq service).q Theq 
collaboration q betweenq theq subjectq andq theq objectq inq theq constitutionq ofq valueq isq seenq 
differentlyqamongqsubjectivistsqandqobjectivists.qTheqformerqdefendqthatqvalueqdependsq

theq objectq itselfq andq inq itsq properties.q Anq intermediateq positionq suggestsq thatq valueq 
involvesq anq interactionq betweenq theq subjectq andq anqobject.q Inq thisq perspective,q valueq

R Valueqisq comparative qbecauseqtheqvalueqofqanqobjectqisqonlyqstatedqinqreferenceqtoq

ratherqthanqutilityqcomparisonsqamongqpeople.qInterpersonalqutilityqcomparisonsqasq

thisqisqclearlyqaqsubjectivistqapproachqtoqvalue;qq
R Andq valueq isq situational ,q asq itq dependsq onq theq contextq inq whichq theq evaluativeq 
judgmentq isq made.q Thisq situationRspecificq natureq ofq valueq occursq becauseq theq 
standardsq onq whichq evaluativeq judgmentsq hingeq tendqtoq beq contextRdependent,q

2.5.3.  Utility as a Multidisciplinary Concept 
q
2.5.3.1.  Expected Value and Expected Utility 
q
Asqdiscussedqsoqfar,qmotivationqisqrelatedqtoqvalueqperceptions:qindividualsqareqmotivatedq 
toq somethingq becauseq theyq perceiveq valueq inq itq andqthereq areq severalq interpretationsq 
aboutq whatq isq value ,q namelyq theq oneq thatq relatesq valueq toq useq andq utility.q Yet,q otherq 
approachesqdoqnotqconsiderq utility asqaqspecialqkindqofq value ,qbutq value qasqaqspecialqcaseq 
ofq utility .q Expected value qandq expected utility qareqconfrontedqinqtheqeconomicqtheoryqofq 
choiceq between  uncertain q alternativesq (vonq Neumannq &q Morgenstern,q 1944),q whichq 
explainsq howq peopleq makeq choices.q Theq theoryq ofq expectedq utilityq providesq theq 
foundationqofqthisqtheoryqofqchoiceqandqitqstatesqthatq“theq expected utility qofqaqgambleqisq 
theq expected value q ofq theq utilitiesq ofq eachq ofq itsq possibleq outcomes”q (Frank,q 1991,q p.q 
181).qTheqcentralqpremiseqofqthisqdecisionqtheoryqisqthatqpeopleqchooseqtheqalternativeq 
thatqhasqnotqtheqhighestq expected value ,qbutqtheqhighestq expected utility .qq
q
Rabinq (1996,q p.q 10)q alsoq differentiatesq expected utility q fromq expected value q andq 
accordingqtoqhim,qtheq expected value qisqaqspecialqcaseqofqtheqtheoryqofqexpectedqutilityq 
wherequtilitiesqareqassumedqtoqbeqlinearq(i.e.,qriskqneutrality).qRabinq(1996)qclaimsqthatqitq 
isqbetterqthequseqofq expected utility qratherqthanq expected value qbecauseqmostqindividualsq 
areqnotqriskqneutrals,qbutqratherqriskqaverse.qThisqsuggestsqthat,qtheqsameqwayqthatqvalueq 
perceptionq isq aq betterq indicatorq thanq motivation,q expectedq utilityq mayq alsoq beq aq betterq 
indicatorqthanqexpectedqvalue.qq
q
 
2.5.3.2.   Use, Usage, Usefulness, and Utility 
q
Someq ofq theq approachesq discussedq aboveq relateq valueq toq use,q usefulnessq andq utility.q 
Deweyq(1939,qp.q36)qdefendsqthatqgenuineqvalueqisqfocusedqonqends,qandqthatqtheqvalueq 
ofqaqgoodqorqserviceqisqinqitsq usefulness qthatqitqgivesqforqattainingqthequltimateqobjective.q 
Inq thisq approach,q value q isq relatedq toq usefulness .q Meanwhile,q Susanq Boztepeq (2007)q
providesqaqusefulqrelationshipqbetweenquseqandqvalue:q“ Use value qrelatesqtoqtheq utility qofq 
theqphysicalqpropertiesqofqaqproduct,qwhichqisqrealizedquponqitsq use ”.qUse qisqdefinedqasqanq 
effectiveq practice:q Whenq somethingq isq beingq used,q itq meansq thatq thatq thingq isq beingq 
employedq forq aq purposeq (Theq Freeq Dictionary,q 2009).q Thisq isq differentq fromq usage ,q 
whichq isq relatedq toq theq mannerq ofq using.q Ifq someone,q historically,q hasq beenq usingq 
somethingq inq theq sameq way,q thatq becomesq aq usage.q Theq conceptq ofq usage q assumes,q 
therefore,qseveralquses,qaqtraditionqinqtheqwayqofqusing.qUtility ,qinqturn,qisqdefinedqasq“theq 
qualityq ofq beingq usable”.q Thisq meansq thatq somethingq mayq beq perceivedq hasq havingq 
utility,q butq notq reallyq beingq used.q Inq otherq words,q theq conceptq ofq utilityq includesq 
perceptionsqofqaq hypothetical use ,qanqexpectationqofqaq future quse,qwhileqtheqconceptqofq 
use qimpliesqanq effective use ,qandqutility qisqanqexpectationqthatqifqconfirmedquponqeffectiveq 
use .q Thisq suggestsq thatq utilityq isq closerq toq expectations,q whileq useq isq closerq toq 
performance,qandqaq disconfirmation q(Churchillq&qSurprenant,q1982;qOliver,q1980,q1993)q
couldqbeqevaluated.qItqalsoqsuggestsqthat,qsincequtilityqisqanqexpectation,qthequseqofqtheq 
wordq‘expected’qinqtheqexpressionq‘expectedqutility’qisqaqredundancy.qq

q
Economicsqdistinguishesqpresent value q(PV)qfromqexpected value q(EV),qandqcombinesq
theseqtwoqconceptsqinq expected-present-value q(EPV)qforqcasesqwhereqdecisionsqinvolveq
future qcashq flowsq andqareq madeqinqanq uncertain qenvironment.qTheq differenceq betweenq 
theseqtwoqconceptsqisqbasedqonqtheqtemporalqdispersionqofq value .qq
q
Theq expected value q ofq anq outcomeq isq theq valueq ofq thatq outcomeq multipliedq byq theq 
probabilityqofq thatq outcomeq occurring.qSinceq severalq outcomesq areq possibleq underq riskq 
andquncertainty,qtheq expected value qofqaqdecisionqisqtheqsumqofqtheqexpectedqvaluesqofqallq 
theqpossibleqoutcomesqthatqmayqfollowqtheqdecision.qAsqtheqactualqoutcomeqwillqnotqbeq 
knownquntilqafterqtheq“investment”qisqmadeqandqallqtheqreturnsqareqin,qtheqexpectedqvalueq 
isqanq a priori qmeasureqofqdecisionqthatqallowsqtheqprobabilityqdistributionqofqoutcomesqtoq 
beq summarizedq asq aq singleq numberq (Douglas,q 1992b,q pp.q 18R19).q Theq analysisq ofq theq 
expected present value qisqrequiredqwheneverqthereqareqcostsqandqrevenueqimplicationsqofq 
theq decisionq thatq fallq inq bothq theq presentq periodq and,q atq least,q oneq futureq period.q Theq 
analysisqisqmoreqcomplexqwhenqthereqisqalsoqaqprobabilityqdistributionqofqoutcomesqinq 
eachqperiod,qbecauseqtheqoutcomesqinqtheqsecondqandqsubsequentqperiodsqwillqhaveqjointq 
probabilitiesq ofq occurring.q Toq makeq aq decision,q individualsq evaluateq theq expectedR
presentRvalueqofqtheqprofitsqpromisedqbyqeachqalternative,qassigningqprobabilitiesqtoqeachq 
scenario.q Then,q anq opportunity q discountq rateq isq usedq toq evaluateq futureq profitsq inq theq 
presentqperiodqandqexpectedqpresentqvalueqwillqbeqtheqsumqofqtheqpresentqvalueqofqfutureq 
expectedqvaluesq(Douglas,q1992a,qp.q3).qq

Thequtilityqfunctionqhasqseveralqquestionsqthatqhaveqtoqbeqdealt,qnamelyqtheqriskqinvolvedq 
inqeachqalternativeqdecision,qtheqmeasurementqorqperceptionqofqthatqrisk,qandqtheqproblemq 
ofq incompleteq informationq aboutq outcomes,q whichq sometimesq existsq whenq decisionsq 
haveqtoqbeqmadeq(thatqis,qtheq uncertainty qofqoutcomes,qwhichqisqanqadditionalqproblemq 
besidesq risk ).q Asq Douglasq (1992b,q p.q 17)q putsq it,quncertainty q existsq whenq aq decisionq 
mightqleadqtoqoneqofqseveralqoutcomesqandqtheqexactqoutcomeqisqnotqknownqinqadvance.q 
Instead,qthereqwillqbeqaqprobabilityqdistributionqofqpossibleqoutcomes,qwhichqtheqdecisionq 
makerq mustq identify.q Theq conceptq ofq risk q canq beq regardedq asq aq subcategoryq ofq 
uncertaintyqinqwhichqtheqprobabilitiesqofqeachqoutcomeqcanqbeqassignedqonqanqobjectiveq 
bases.q Accordingq toq Douglasq (1992a,q p.q 35),q theq riskq associatedq withq aq particularq 
decisionqisqdefinedqasqtheqdispersionqofqtheqpossibleqoutcomesqthatqmightqoccur.qq
q
Theqprobabilityqofqhavingq‘heads’qwhenqflippingqaqcoin,qorqtheqprobabilityqofqhavingqaq 
pairq ofq numbersq whenq throwingq twoq dices,q isq knownq a priori .q Inq otherq cases,q thatq 
probabilityq cannotq beq determinedq a priori .q Anotherq classq ofq riskq situationsq isq thatq inq 
whichqprobabilitiesqareqassignedq a posteriori ,qorqonqtheqbasisqofqpastqexperiencequnderq 
similarqcircumstances.qForqinstance,qbasedqonqpastqexperiences,qinsuranceqcompaniesqareq 
ableqtoqformqanqexpectationq(orqassignqaqprobability)qofqtheqchancesqofqaqspecificqdriverq 
havingq anq accidentq inq aq specificq car.q Yet,q inq theq greatq majorityq ofq decisionRmakingq 
problems,q theq potentialq outcomesq cannotq beq foreseenq clearlyq inq advanceq andq decisionq 
makersqmustqestimateqaqrageqofqpotentialqoutcomesqandqassignqprobabilitiesqsubjectively,q 
basedqonqexperience,qintuition,qandqjudgmentq(Douglas,q1992b,qpp.q17R18).qq

2.5.3.4.3.  Utility and the Observable Choices and Preferences 
q
Kahnemanq andq Vareyq (1991,q p.q 127)q claimq thatq theq standardq approachq toq utilityq inq 
decisionqscienceqisqanqobjectivistqview,qwhichqfocusesqonqtangibleqgoodsqasqtheqcarriersq 
ofq utility,q andq onq observable preferences q asq theq properq measureq ofq it.q Inq contrast,q aq 
“psychological”qview,qasqtheyqcallqit,qtendsqtoqfocusqonq interpreted objectsqandqevents,qasq 
theq carriersq ofq utility,q andq onq experiences of pleasure or satisfaction q asq theq properq 
measureqofqit.qq
q
Theseq authorsq relateq utilitarianismq toq utility,q andq makeq aq clearq retrospectiveq onq theq 
evolutionq ofq theq conceptq ofq utility,q formerlyq relatedq toq hedonismq andq currently,q theyq 
argue,qmoreqrelatedqtoqobservableqchoicesqandqpreferencesq(pp.q127R128):qq
q
“[Bernoulli’s]qargumentqandqhisqreferencesqtoqearlierqwritingsqbyqGabrielqCramer,qidentifyq 
utilityq asqsatisfactionq –qaqsubjectiveqstateq orqexperience.qJeremyq BenthamqandqJohnq Stuartq 
Millqalsoqusedqtheqtermqutilityqtoqreferqtoqtheqhedonicqqualityqofqexperience.qBenthamqspokeq 
ofqtheqtwoqsovereignqmastersqthatqgovernqmankindq–qpleasureqandqpainq–qandqdevelopedqtheq 
notionqofqaq‘hedonicqcalculus’.qIndeedqtheqbasicqtenetqofqutilitarianismqisqvariouslyqreferredq 
toqasqtheq‘principleq ofqutility’q andqasq‘theq greatestqhappinessqprinciple’q(…)qHowever,q theq 
modernq viewq ofq utilityq hasq abandonedq anyq explicitq referenceq toq hedonicq experienceq ofq 
happiness.qTheqpositivisticqmovementqthatqsweptqtheqsocialqsciencesqbetweenqtheqtwoqworldq 
warsq gaveq usq behaviourism,q strictq operationalq definitions,q andq aq suspiciousq attitudeq toq 
mentalistq notions.q Inq thisq spiritq itq wasq naturalq toq seekq aq definitionq ofq utilityq inq termsq ofq 
observableqchoicesq–qrevealedqpreferences.qTheqdefinitionqofqutilityqinqtermsqofqchoicesqstillq 
rulesqtheqsciencesqofqdecisionq(…).”q
q
Twoq conceptsqofq utility,q oneq moreq positivistqandq anotherq moreq constructivist,q seemq toq 
coRexist.qAsqKahnemanqandqSnellq(1990,qquotedqinqKahnemanq&qVarey,q1991,qp.q128)q
putq it,q “inq referringq toq Bentham’sq conceptq weq shallq speakq ofq experience utility :q theq 
hedonicq qualityq ofq experience,q broadlyq construedq toq includeq satisfaction q asq wellq asq 
pleasure .qTheqvalueqassociatedqwithqaqparticularqconsequenceqinqaqdecisionqcontextqisqitsq 
preference utility. Theq distinctionq betweenq experience andq preference utility q suggestsq 
anotherq notion:q predicted utility :q theq individual’sq reflectiveq assessmentq ofq futureq
experiencequtility”.qq

Theq objectivistq positionq favoursq aq notionq ofq utilityq basedq onq publiclyq (objectively)q

analysisqisqrejected.qSenq(1986,qquotedqinqKahnemanqandqVarey,q1991,qp.129)qnotesqthatq 
“theq popularityq ofq thisq viewq inq economicsq mayq beq dueq toq aq mixtureq ofq anq obsessiveq

pp.q129R130)qaddqthatq“theqsubstantiveqargumentqforqmeasuringqutilityqfromq choices qisq 
thatqpeopleqknowqwhatqisqgoodqforqthem.qThus,qtheqobjectivistqstanceqrequiresqfaithqinqtheq

Theqpsychologicalq stanceq onqtheseq mattersq isq different:q Psychologistsq tendq toq beq moreq 
tolerantqofqmeasuresqofqsubjectiveqexperienceqandqmoreqinclinedqtoqdoubtqtheqrationalityq 
ofqagentsq–qandqtheqwisdomqofqtheirqchoices.qThus,qtheqobjectivistqandqtheqpsychologicalq

objectivelyqidentifiableqaspectsqofqtheqdecisionqmaker’sqsituationqatqaqgivenqtime.qEvenq 
thoughq thatq notq allq economicq analysisq areq objectivistq inq thisq sense,q thereq isq aq distinctq 
tendencyqinqeconomicsqandqdecisionqtheoryqtoqviewqmaterialqassetsqasqtheqmainqcarriersq 
ofqutilityqq(Kahnemanq&qVarey,q1991,qp.q130).qTheqpsychologicalqstanceqonqtheqcarriersq 
ofqutilityqputsqmoreqweightqonqintangiblesqasqfactorsqofqutility.qThequtilitiesqofqoutcomesq

2.5.3.5.5.  Immediate vs.  Future Utility 
q
Theq presentq evaluationq ofq theq possibleq future utility q isq notq anq easyq task,q sinceq itq isq 
differentqtoqmakeqaqjudgmentqaboutqsomethingqthatqisqexpectedqtoqexistqinqtheqfuture,qandq 
somethingq thatq alreadyq exists.q Deweyq (1939)q expressesq similarq concernsq whenq heq 
confrontsqwhatqisqexpectedqtoqhappenqandqwhatqreallyqhappened.qWhenqdifferentiatingq 
appraisal q fromq evaluation ,q Deweyq (1939,q pp.q 20R21)q statedq thatq appraisal q refersq toq 
somethingq inq theq futureq thatq hasq notq beenq accomplishedq butq whichq shallq orq shouldq 
happen,qwhileq evaluation qrefersqtoqanqaccomplishedqfactq(detailedqinqpageqAppendixq8).qq
Inqthatqappraisal,qtheqlevelsqofqmotivationqandq future utility qareqtakenqintoqconsideration.qq
q
Theqeconomicqapproachqtoq utility qdealsqwithqtheqdifferentqmomentsqinqtimeqwherequtilityq 
willqbeqeffective,q namelyq throughq presentRvalue.q Inq thisq approach,qallqfutureqoutcomesq 
areqdiscountedqintoqtheqpresentqmomentqinqorderqtoqachieveqaqcurrentqvalueqofqthatq future 
utility qandqvalueqisqtheq(discounted)qcumulativeqfutureqreturn.qThisqmeansqthatqtheqlongerq 
theq timeq frameq betweenq theq momentq ofq expectedq utilityq andq theq momentq whenq theq 
decisionqisqmade,qmoreqinterferenceqwillqexist.qMoreover,qinqtheqeconomicqapproach,qtheq 
precisionqofqtheqcalculationqofqfutureqoutcomesqisqquestionableqandqseveralqdoubtsqariseq 
regardingqtheqmostqsuitableqopportunityqdiscountqrate.qqq

Someqauthorsqalertqtoqtheqpredictabilityqofq future utility ,qandqtheqmaintenanceqofqcurrent 
tastes .q Kahnemanq &q Snellq (1990,q p.q 133),q forq instance,q claimq thatq rationalq decisionsq 
aboutq delayed outcomes qrequireqaccurateqpredictionsqofq future tastes ,qandqtheqpredictionq 
ofqadaptationqisqanqimportantqpartqofqtheqtask.qTheyqargueqthatqdecisionsqcannotqbeqmadeq 
reasonablyqwithoutqconsideringqtheqpossibilityqofq tastes qandq sensibilities qbeingqmodifiedq 
byqcontinuedqexposure.qMoreover,q unpredictable tastes qmustqbeqtakenqinqconsideration.q 
Yet,qtheqindividual’sqabilityqtoqpredictqherqfutureqtastesqisqquiteqpoorqandqtheqcorrelationq 
betweenq actualq andq predictedq changesq inq likingq isq closeq toq zero,q althoughq thatq isq notq 
enoughqtoqsayqthatqpeopleqcannotqpredictqfutureqtastes.qq
q
Loewenstein,q O'Donoghue,q andq Rabinq (2003)q claimq thatq individualsq exaggerateq theq 
degreeq toq whichq theirq future tastes q willq resembleq theirq current tastes .q Theseq authorsq 
demonstratedq theq prevalenceq ofq suchq projection bias q andq showedq that,q whenq peopleq 
exhibitqhabitqformation,qprojectionqbiasqleadsqthemqtoqconsumeqtooqmuchqearlyqinqlife,q 
andqtoqdecide,qasqtimeqpasses,qtoqconsumeqmoreq(andqsaveqless)qthanqoriginallyqplanned.q 
Projectionqbiasqalsoqleadsqtoqmisguidedqpurchasesqofqdurableqgoods.qTheqsameqisqtoqsayq 
thatqpeopleqareqtooqoptimistqaboutq future utility .qInqaqtrainingqcontext,qthisqmayqmeanqthatq 
peopleqtendqtoqenrolqinqtrainingqcoursesqhavingqinqmindqaqtooRoptimistq future utility qofq 
thatqexperience.qq
q
Kahnemanq&qVareyq(1991,qp.q141)qbroughtqintoqthisqdiscussionqrelevantqfactorsqsuchqasq 
prior experience q andq theq abilityq ofq future retrieval .q Theyq argueq thatq utilityq shouldq beq 
viewedqasqaqdimensionqofq experience qand,qasqsuch,qitqisqexpectedqtoqobeyqthequsualqlawsq 
ofq perception q andq memory .q Theyq alsoq pointq outq twoq setsq ofq factorsq thatq areqlikelyq toq 
affectqtheqexperiencequtility:qtheqhistoryqofq prior experiences qandqtheq context toqwhichq 
theqrelevantqobject,qstate,qorqeventqwillqbeqcompared.qqImmediate utility qisqnotqonlyqeasierq
toqappraiseqbutqisqalsoqlessquncertainqandqwithqlessqriskqthanq future utility ,qwhichqsoundsq 
asqaqhypotheticalqoccurrence.qInqaddition,q future utility qalsoqincludesqretrievingqproblemsq 
thatqweqwillqapproachqnext.qq

Theq length q andq deepness q ofq theq trainingq courseq alsoq provideq inputsq toq theqforgettingq 
curve.qOnqoneqhand,qlongerqandqdeeperqcoursesqtendqtoqincludeqaqlotqofqknowledge,qskillq 
development,qandqattitudeqformationqthatqtendqtoqnotqbeqused,qandqtherefore,qtendqtoqbeq

skill,q orq attitude.q Theq rightq contextq willq provideqtheq opportunityq forq thoseq learningq 
outcomesq toq beq retrievedq andq used,q and,q therefore,qtheq perceptionsq ofq qualityq willq beq 
high.qYet,qassumingqeverythingqelseqisqheldqconstant ,qthereqareqnotqasqmanyqchancesqofq 
retrievalqasqinqlongerqandqdeeperqcourses,qand,qso,qshortqcoursesqareqriskier,qinqtermsqofq 
quality,qthanqlongqandqdeepqcourses.q

2.5.3.5.5.2.  Multiple Uses: Spacing Fan and Inhibition Effects 
q
Ifqmultipleq uses qareqconsidered,qthenqtheqlearningqeffect,qobtainedqfromqtheqexperienceqofq 
eachq use,q willq increaseq learning,q andq aq newq stageq ofq knowledgeq willq beq achieved.q 
Wheneverq aq newq useq occurs,q aq retrievalq situationq happens,q theq retentionq intervalq isq 
refreshed,q andq theq probabilityq ofq havingq anotherq retrievalq situationq andq anotherq useq 
increases.qq
q
ZechmeisterqandqShaughnessyq(1980)qstudiedqtheqeffectsqofqtheqtimeqbetweenqeachquse,q 
calledqtheq spacing effect .qTheyqfoundqthatqwidelyRspacedq repetitions q(thatqisqtoqsay,q uses )q 
areqmoreqeffectiveq thanqnarrowlyRspacedq repetitions.q NarrowlyRspacedq repetitionsq giveq 
learnersq greaterq confidenceq butq theyq actuallyq recallq narrowlyRspacedq repetitionsq lessq 
highlyq thanq widelyRspacedq repetitions.q Ifq theirq conclusionsq holdq trueq inq use q andq 
experience q contexts,q then,q immediateqrepetitionsq ofq useqcannotq minimizeq forgettingqasq 
muchqasqwidelyqspacedqrepetitionsqofquse,qwhichqisqcontradictoryqwithqtheqlearningqeffectq 
ofqeachquse.qYet,qifqeachqcontextqofquseqisqdifferentqfromqtheqlearningqcontextqandqtheq 
contextqofqeachqpreviousquse,qthenqtheqabilityqtoqtransferqpreviousqknowledgeqandqadaptq 
itqtoqtheqcurrentqcontextqisqmoreqimportantqthanqtheqvolumeqofqusesqorqtheqspacingqeffect.q 
Moreover,qvitalqimpulsesqandqacquiredqhabitsqoftenqoperateqwithoutqtheqinterventionqofq 
anqendRinRviewqorqaqpurposeq(Dewey,q1939,qp.q39)qandqcanqbecomeqsoqroutinedqthatqnoq 
reflectiveqthoughtqisqmadequponqthem,qwhichqwillqhinderqevenqtheqconsciousnessqofquse.qq
q
Theq fan effect q(J.qR.qAnderson,q1974;qJ.qR.qAndersonq&qReder,q1999)qexplainsqtheqabilityq 
ofqtheqbrainqtoqoptimizeqmemoryqretrievalqbyqkeepingqbetterqaccessqtoqmemoriesqthatqareq 
moreq likelyq toq beq relevant.q Theq fan effect q statesq thatq theq amountq ofq timeq requiredq toq 
retrieveqaqparticularqfactqaboutqaqspecificqconceptqtendsqtoqincreaseqwithqtheqnumberqofq 
factsqthatqareqknownqaboutqthatqconcept.qThisq fan effect qisqusuallyqheldqresponsibleqforq 
theqslowingqdownqofqmemoryqretrievalqwithqage,qasqtheqnumberqofqfactsqthatqareqknownq 
aboutqaqspecificqconceptqtendqtoqbeqhigher.qq
q
Besidesq theq knownq factsq aboutq aq concept,q age q alsoq influencesq memoryq retrieval.q 
Youngerq individualsq haveq aq higherq inhibition effect ,q whichq isq theq abilityq toq suppressq 
relatedqbutqirrelevantqfactsqduringqlongRtermqmemoryqretrieval,qwhereasqolderqonesqhaveq 
smallerq inhibitionq effects,q i.e.q olderq individualsqareq lessq effectiveq atq suppressingq 
irrelevantqinformationq(Hasher,qZacks,q&qMay,q1999;qRadvansky  et al .,q2006).qTheq fan 
effect q andq theq inhibition effect q areq negativelyq correlatedq (Radvansky,q 1999),q asq theq 
formerqtendsqtoqincreaseqwithqageqandqtheqlatterqoneqtendsqdoqdecrease.q

Chapter 3  
Research Objectives and Approach 
 
 
We conducted a case study at EVOLUI.COM, a Portugue se company that provides 
short-term courses in e-learning.  The case study w as based on mixed methods to 
address the main dimensions of quality in e-learnin g courses. In order to 
triangulate and explore different related variables , we collected different but 
complementary data using different approaches.  
 
We initiated our research with a participant observ ation, which was combined 
with interview, to explore the phenomenon of qualit y in e-learning courses. Based 
on the major conclusions of this qualitative study,  we conducted two quantitative 
studies. The first one was used to test the hypothe sis that utility is an important 
dimension of e-learning quality and to determine the influence of several variables 
on perceptions of quality and the major factors  of quality. The second quantitative 
study was used to confirm the hypothesis that, like  perceptions of quality, the 
perceptions of value are also related to utility. T his study was also used to explore 
the motivational profile of the trainees, namely th e relation between financial 
sacrifice and their presence at training events wit h quality and utility. The reason 
for collecting both quantitative and qualitative da ta was to bring together the 
strengths of both forms of research and validate results.

effectsq inq realq contexts,q recognizingq thatq contextqisq aq powerfulq determinantq ofq bothq

inqcaseqstudies.qqq

3.2.3.  EVOLUI.COM as the Case Study 
q
We focused our study on clients of EVOLUI.COM (avai lable at www.evolui.com ),qaq 
Portuguese e-learning service provider.  
 
The choice of this provider rested on several reasons:  
 
R It is one of the oldest and most experienced e-lear ning providers in 
Portugal (it was founded in 1999, after two years of experiments with an e-
learning service provider called DIGITO Formação); 
R No conflicts of interests exist between the author of this thesis proposal 
and the company’s stakeholders;  
R It has a diversified courses portfolio with more th an 160 online courses 
available and more than 50.000 registered users, most of them with several 


PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
115 
purchases, providing a good source of ‘experienced’ clients. 
R Unconditional and free access to the clients’ datab ase was guaranteed as 
well as total freedom to make the studies;  
R Technical resources were available to adapt the cur rent platform to the 
planned research, to provide evidence to document a nd to allow external 
validation and external audits to the study.   
 
Due to ethical concerns, it is worth mentioning that the author of this thesis has full 
management privileges in the company.  
 
As Taylor and Bodgan (1984,qp.q19)qrefer, the ideal research setting is one in which 
the observer obtains easy access, establishes immed iate rapport with informants, 
and gathers data directly related to the research i nterests, but such settings 
seldom exist. They recommendqthatqresearchersqstayqawayqfromqsettingsqinqwhichqtheyq 
haveqaqdirectqpersonalqorqprofessionalqstake.qTheyqreportqthatqnoviceqobserversqtendqtoq 
wantqtoqstudyqfriendsqandqfamiliarqsurroundingsqandqthatqwhenqoneqisqdirectlyqinvolvedq 
inq aq settingq oneq isq likelyq toq seeq thingsq fromq onlyqoneq pointq ofq view.q Yet,q theq 
recommendedqdistanceqisqsometimesqincompatibleqwithqtheqneedqofqaccess.qParticipantq 
observersqusuallyqgainqaccessqtoqorganizationsqbyqrequestingqpermissionqfromqthoseqinq 
charge,qalsoqcalledq gatekeepers q(H.qS.qBecker,q1970,qquotedqinqTaylorq&qBodgan,q1984,q 
p.q 20)q andq theseq oftenq closeq theirq ‘gates’,q especiallyq inq ourq case,q asq theyq perceiveq theq 
researcherqasqaqcompetitor.qThis access and closeness versus  distance question is not 
very clear in the literature. Although researchers are advised to stay away from 
familiar contexts, some authors recommend researche rs to involve themselves 
with the community, hang out, make friends, and dev elop social relations with 
potential respondents q(Taylorq&qBodgan,q1984,qpp.q23R24) .q

3.4.1.  The Subjects of Study: The Respondents 
 
The subjects of our study were not potential traine es but rather actual 
clients/trainees of EVOLUI.COM: they were qparticipantsqinqanqonlineqtrainingqcourseq 
thatqtheyqhadqpaidqfor.  
 
Respondentsq wereq notq invitedq toq participateq inq thisq PhDq research.q They were not 
informed that online discussions would be used for this research, or that the 
surveys they answered were more than ‘reaction surv eys’ or ‘motivational 

PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
117 
surveys’. As we will discuss later, several reasons accounted for this decision:  
 
R EVOLUI.COM’s general service conditions anticipate the usage of every kind 
of data collected during the course for research purposes ;q
R If they had been informed about the research purpos es, that could have 
influenced their behaviour or their opinions and th e way they expressed 
themselves; q
R Theqkindqofqquestionsqtheyqwereqaskedqwasqperfectlyqcontextualizedqandqcouldq 
notq beq consideredq purposelessq inq theq contextq ofq aq trainingq courseq orq inq theq 
contextqofqtheqspecificqtrainingqcourseqthatqtheyqwereqattending.qq
 
In the qualitative study that we carried out initia lly we intended to focus our 
attention on clients that already had purchased and attended several courses in an 
e-learning format, to avoid disturbing factors as n ovelty, technical difficulties, 
loneliness, and unrealistic expectations among othe rs, and because serviceqqualityq 
isqaqlongRtermq attitude q(CroninqJr.q&qTaylor,q1994;qOliver,q1981).qYet,qweqrealizedqthatq 
evenqnovicesqhadqrelevantqcontributionsqtoqgiveqandqthatqevenqthoughqtheyqhadqnoqpriorq 
experience,qtheyqhadq expectations qonqwhatqtheqqualityqofqanqeRlearningqcourseqshouldqbe.q
Evenq so,q inq theq qualitativeq studyq most respondents were training professionals – 
clients who, one way or another, were connected to human resources development 
and training. This included general managers, human  resources managers, talent 
managers, training managers, trainers, and teachers . This was not a selection that 
we have made but we had predicted that this might h appen, as we used 
pedagogical courses to conduct our qualitative research.  
 
We believe that our research was enriched by this f act because we were able to 
interview professionals who have experience in plan ning, organizing, executing 
and auditing training events, and, therefore, are a ware of the training process and 
of small details that can make a difference in term s of quality. Yet, in that context, 
they were still trainees who were attending a cours e, customers who, at that 
specific moment, were looking for additional compet ences, as all the others. The 
fact that most of the respondents were training pro fessionals added some useful 
insights on e-learning quality and provided a more global approach to e-learning 
quality. 
 
Inq theq quantitativeq studies,q respondentsq hadq aq tremendousq varietyq ofq occupationsq andq 
experience,qwhichqisqrepresentativeqofqtheqprofileqofqEVOLUI.COM’sqclients.q

systematically and unobtrusively collected .qTheqdataqobtainedqfromqobservationqconsistsq 
ofqdetailedqdescriptionsqofqtheqpeople’sqactivities,qbehaviours,qactions,qandqtheqfullqrangeq 
ofq interpersonalq interactionsq andq organizationalq processesq thatq areq partq ofq observableq 
humanqexperienceq(Patton,q1990,qp.q4).qq
q
Inq participantq observationalq studies,q theq researcherq staysq withq theq participantsq forq aq 
substantialq periodq ofq timeq andq recordsq whatq isq happening,q whileq takingq aq roleq inq theq 
situation.qByqstayingqinqaqsituationqoverqaqlongqperiod,qtheqresearcherqisqalsoqableqtoqseeq 
howq eventsq evolveq overq time,q catchingq theq dynamicsqofq situations,q theq people,q 
personalities,qcontexts,qresources,qroles,qetc.q(L.qCohenq et al .,q2007,qpp.q404R405).q
q
Inq contrastq toqmostq methodsq inq whichq theq researcher’sq hypothesesq andq proceduresq areq 
determinedq aq priori,q theq researchq designq inq participant observation q remainsq flexible,q
bothq beforeq andq throughoutq theq researchq (Taylorq &q Bodgan,q 1984,q p.q 16).q Taylorq andq 
Bodganqrecognizeqthatqalthoughqparticipantqobserversqhaveqaqmethodologyqtoqfollowqandq 
perhapsqsomeqgeneralqresearchqinterests,qtheqspecificsqofqtheirqapproachqevolveqasqtheyq 
proceed.q Evenq so,q mostq researchersq oftenq haveq someqgeneralq questionsq inq mindq whenq 
theyq enterq theq field,q whichq fallq intoq oneq ofq twoq broadq questions:q substantiveq andq 
theoretical.qTheqformerqincludesqquestionsqrelatedqtoqspecificqissuesqinqaqparticularqtypeq 
ofq settings,q andq theq latterq isq moreq closelyq tiedq toq basicq sociologicalq issuesq suchq asq 
socialization,qdeviance,qandqsocialqcontrolq(Taylorq&qBodgan,q1984,qp.q17).q

4.1.2.2.2.  Degrees of Participation 
q
Thereqareqvariationsqinqobservationalqmethodsq(Figureq21).qq
q
Theqfirstqcharacteristicqthatqdifferentiatesqobservationalqstrategiesqconcernsqtheqextentqtoq 
whichqtheqobserverqwillqbeqaqparticipantqinqtheqsettingqbeingqstudied.qThisqinvolvesqmoreq 
thanq aq simpleq choiceq betweenq participation q andq nonparticipation .q Theq extentq ofq 
participationqisqaqcontinuumqthatqvariesqfromqcompleteqimmersionqinqtheqsettingqasqfullq 
participantq toq completeq separationq fromq theq settingq asq spectator,q withq aq greatq dealq ofq 
variationq alongq theq continuumq betweenq theseq twoq endq points.q Yet,q thisq isq notq justq aq
simpleqmatterqofqdeciding,qatqtheqbeginning,qhowqmuchqtheqobserverqwillqparticipate.qTheq 
extentqofqparticipationqcanqchangeqoverqtime.qTheqresearcherqmayqbeginqtheqstudyqasqanq 
onlookerqandqgraduallyqbecomeqaqparticipantqasqfieldworkqprogressesqandqtheqoppositeq 
canqalsoqoccur.qAnqevaluatorqmightqbeginqasqaqcompleteqparticipant,qtoqexperienceqwhatq 
itq isq likeq toq beq initiallyq immersedq inq theq program,q andq thenq graduallyq withdrawq 
participationqoverqtheqperiodqofqstudy,quntilqfinallyqtakingqtheqroleqofqoccasionalqobserverq 
fromqanqonlookerqstanceq(Patton,q1990,qp.q265).q
q
Theqdegreeqofqparticipationqandqtheqnatureqofqobservationqvaryqalongqaqwideqcontinuumq 
ofq possibilitiesq betweenq theseq twoq ends.q Forq Pattonq (1990,q p.q 267),q theq idealq inq 
evaluationqisqtoqdesignqandqnegotiateqthatqdegreeqofqparticipationqthatqwillqyieldqtheqmostq 
meaningfulq dataq aboutq theq program,q givenq theq characteristicsq ofq theq participants,q theq

4.1.2.4.  Participant Observation and Online Ethnography 
q
Asq ourq observationq takesq placeq inq theq field,q weq canq assumeq itq asq aq naturalistic 
observation q orq ethnographic ,q asq itq isq conductedq inq theq “natural”q setting.q Typically,q 
anthropologicalq fieldworkersq combineq inq theirq fieldq notesq dataq fromq personal,q 
eyewitnessq observationq withq informationq gainedq fromq informalq naturalq interviewsq andq 
informant’sq descriptions.q Thus,q theq participantq observerq employsq multipleq andq 
overlappingq dataq collectionq strategies:qbeingq fullyqengagedq inq experiencingq theqsettingq 
(participation)q whileq atq theq sameq timeq observingq andq talkingq withq otherq participantsq 
aboutq whateverq isq happeningq (Patton,q 1990,q pp.q 265R266).q Ethnographersq haveq 
traditionallyqbeenqusingqtheqmethodsqofqparticipantqobservationqandqintensiveqfieldworkq 
toq studyq everythingq fromq smallq groupsq toq nationRstates.q Yet,q whatq itq meansq toq 
‘participate’q orq beingq inq theq ‘field’q orqevenq beq aq‘group’q hasq changedq withq theq Worldq 
Wideq Webq andq theq emergenceq ofq theq virtual ethnographer ,q whoq studiesq peopleq 
connectedqthroughqdistributedqelectronicqenvironmentsq(Ruhleder,q2000).qThisqcomputerq 
mediationq hasqinfluencedq communicationqhabits,qandqbothq traditionalqassumptionsqandq 
previouslyqtakenqforqgrantedqrubricsqofqsocialqresearchqhaveqtoqbeqrevised,qasqsuggestedq 
byqMarkhamq(2005).qTheqwayqthatqqualitativeqresearchqisqmadeqonqtheqInternetqisqbeingq 
createdq andq transformedq inq waysq thatq areq stillq newqandq experimentalq andq hasq beenq 
gatheringqtheqattentionqofqtheqscientificqcommunityq(forqinstance,qC.qMannq&qStewart,q 
2000).q
qq
Researchersqstudyingqtheseqdistributedqsettingsqareqoftenqfocusedqonqthreeqsetsqofqissuesq 
(Ruhleder,q2000):q
q
- Theyq lookq atq waysq inq whichq new work practices q emergeq toq supportq effectiveq 
participationqinqvirtualqandqparticularlyqhybridqenvironments;q
- Theyqstudyq theq waysq inqwhichqbroaderq technicalqinfrastructures,q organizationalq 
policies,q andq culturalq barriersq andq assumptionsq defineq theq integration of 
technologies qwithinqandqacrossqinstitutions;qandq
- Theyqfurtherqstudyqtheqwaysqinq which people work to integrate qvirtualqandqhybridq 
activitiesq intoq theirq broaderq lifescapes,q oftenq challengingq establishedq 
relationshipsqandqboundariesqinqtheqprocess.q
q
Markhamq (2005)q recallsq thatq theq individual’sq identityq hasq changedq inq theq lastq twoq 
decades.qInqcyberspace,qsheqdefends,qsomeoneqisqonlyqacknowledgedqthroughqsomeqsortq 
ofqresponse.q“Iqamqperceived,qthereforeqIqam”qandq“Iqamqrespondedqto,qthereforeqIqam”q 
seemq toq beq appropriateq identityq signs.q Socialq beingq isq initiatedq throughq aq processq ofq
creatingq andq sendingq aq message,qandq negotiatedq throughq aq processq ofq interaction.q Sheq 
alsoqrecallsqtheqimportanceqofqtextqtoqaqperson’sqconstructionqandqnegotiationqofqidentityq 
inqonlineqtextRbasedqenvironmentsq(forqinstance,qsomequsersquseqcorrectqpunctuationqandq 
striveqtoqmakeqtheqmeaningqasqclearqasqpossible,qwhileqothersqdoqnotqpayqmuchqattentionq 
toq theq textualq andq linguisticq aspectq ofq theq medium).q Althoughq technologiesq facilitateq 
visualq andq audioq communications,q textq remainsq aq primaryq unitq ofq analysisq forq theq 
qualitativeq researcherq (Markham,q 2005).q Yet,q theq tendencyq isq notq toq includeq onlineq 
audioRvisualqcommunicationsqbutqtoqstudyqhybridqenvironments,qwhereqtheqphysicalqandq 
theqvirtualqoverlapqandqinteract.qAsqMarkhamq(2005)qpointsqout,qethnographicqinquiryqisq 
shiftingq fromq theq studyq ofq onlineRonlyq environmentsq andq virtualq identityq toq theq 
intersectionqofqcomputerRmediatedqcommunicationqwithqeverydayqlife.q

4.1.2.4.1.  The Online Ethnography in Our Research 
q
Ourqresearchqincludedqsomeqethnographicalqelements.qq
q
Besidesqpersonalqinformation,qweqgatheredqsomeqelementsqinqorderqtoqgetqaqsenseqofqtheq 
field.q Forq instance,q theq numberq ofq topicsq addressedq byq eachq trainee,q whoq respondsq toq 
whom,qwhenq(inqtime)qdidqtraineesqpost,qwhatqwasqtheqresponseqlag,qtoqwhomqdidqtheyq 
respond,qifqtheyqrespondedqtoqotherqmessagesqbesidesqtheqonesqthatqwereqrelatedqtoqthisq 
research,qandqwhatqwasqourqperceptionqofqwhatqtheirqfeelingsqwereqwhenqtheyqrespondedq 
(didq theyq seemedqangry,q enthusiastic,q careless,q etc.),q theqlengthq ofq theirq posts,qandq theq 
patternsq ofq quotingq earlierq messages,q asq wellq asq theq useq ofq emoticonsq (probablyq toq 
compensateqforq theq absenceqofq nonverbals).q Thisq providedq usq withq someq insights.q Forq 
instance,qtraineesqusuallyqrespondedqtoqourqpostsqbutqrarelyqrespondedqtoqthoseqofqtheirq 
colleagues.q Theyq usuallyq quotedq ourq messagesq (“asq Rosárioq said”q wasq aq frequentq 
expression)qandqusedqaqlotqofqemoticonsqandqexclamations,qwhichqincludedqexpressionsq 
ofqaffectionq(“Iqadmireqyourqwork”,q“lovelyqthought”,q“that’sqanqinterestingqidea”,q“hopeq 
toqseeqyouqsoon”),qasqwellqasqlotsqofq“kissesqandqhugs”.q
q
Thereq areq severalq elementsq thatq weq didq notq gather,qasq theq socialq andq informalq 
relationshipsqthatqtraineesqdevelopedqoutsideqtheqforumq(asqtheyqusuallyqexchangeqmsnq 
andq emailq contacts)q orq afterq theq trainingq hasq ended,q and,q forq instance,q whoq providedq 
email/msnqcontactsqfirstqandqwhoqdidqnotqprovideqtheirqownqtoqtheqcolleagues.qAnotherq 
levelq ofq representationq wouldq alsoq requireq theqincorporationq ofq specificq measurementsq 
suchqasqtheqnumberqofqclicksqinqeachqthreadq(i.e.qtheqnumberqofqtimesqthequserqreadqeachq 
message),qwhereqsheqwentqafterqreadingqeachqmessage,qandqhowqmuchqtimeqdidqsheqtakeq
toqanswerqeachqmessageqorqevenqifqsheqactuallyqansweredqit.qThereqareqthingsqweqareqnotq 
ableqtoqknowqandqwouldqbeqhardqtoqget:qhowqtraineesqorganizedqbothqtheirqprofessionalq 
andqtrainingqtoRdo’s,qinqwhichqsettingsqdidqtheyqaccomplishqtheirqtrainingqtasksq(duringq 
workqhours,qatqtheqoffice,qinqtheqmiddleqofqaqmeeting,qduringqtraffic,qhermeticallyqclosedq 
atq home/officeq withq aq nonq disturbq signq atq theq door,q etc.),q howq theyq dealtq withq theirq 
technicalq andq socialq difficultiesq ofqremoteqparticipation,qandq whatq kindq ofq effortsq theyq 
hadqtoqmakeqinqorderqtoqrespondqtoqaqmessage.qq
q
Weq wereq ableq toq reconstructq theq discussionq atq anyq time,q andq readq eachq messageq 
wheneverqweqneeded,qasqallqofqthemqwereqkeptqafterqeachqcourseqended.qArchivesqallowq 
usqtoqrecaptureqsomeqaspectsqofqtheqvirtualqclassqexperience,qasqeachqforumqwasqsavedq 
andqplacedqintoqanqarchive.qTheseqkindsqofqarchivalqmaterialsqrepresentqaqrichqsourceqofq 
dataq andq weq areq awareq thatq weq onlyq analyzedq aq smallq partq ofq them.q Puttingq thisq inq aq 
positiveq way,q theq dataq isq generousq enoughq toq provideq usq severalq alternativeq researchq 
paths.q Weq decidedq toq supportq ourq conclusionsq onq theq textualq elements,q inq orderq toq 
minimizeqtheqsubjectiveness.qBecauseqofqthis,qtheqethnographicalqsideqofqourqresearchqisq

4.2.1.1.3.  Single-items versus  Multi-items Surveys 
q
Theqliteratureqdistinguishesqbetweenqtwoqtypesqofqmeasures:qsingleRitemqandqmultiRitemq 
measures.qYet,qtheqliteratureqalsoqrevealsqsomeqconfusionqregardingqwhatqareqsingleqandq 
multiRitemq scales.q Simplyq put,q singleRitemq measuresq attemptq toq identifyq anq attitudeq 
(qualityqperception,qforqinstance)qonqaqparticularqdimensionq(i.e.,qobjectivesqfulfilment)q 
withq oneq scaleq item.q Inqcontrast,q multipleRitemq scalesq normallyq useq aq largeq numberqofq 
itemsqtoqmeasureqthatqparticularqdimension.q
q
SingleRitemq measuresq haveq severalq disadvantagesq (Mittal,q Kumar,q &q Tsiros,q 1999;q 
Snijders,q2003):q
q
R Theyq doq notq provideq informationq onq theq componentsq andq doq notq allowq anq 
evaluationqofqeachqdimensionqseparately,qwhichqmeansqthatqtheyqmayqattenuateq 
theqestimatedqrelationshipsqandqtheyqmayqnotqexpressqfullyqtheqcomplexityqofqaq 
construct;q
R Itq isq moreq difficultq toq evaluateq theq internalq consistencyq andq reliabilityq ofq theq 
constructs.q Theq reliabilityq ofq singleRitemq questionq isq lowerq thanq inq multiRitemq 
measuresq becauseq inq singleq questionsq peopleq areq lessq likelyq toq giveq consistentq 
answersqoverqtime:qtheyqmayqchooseqyesqtoqaqquestionqoneqdayqandqsayqnoqtheq 
otherqday,qandqtheyqmayqinterpretqtheqquestionqdifferentlyqoverqtime.qInqmultiR
itemqmeasures,qtheqcompositeqscore,qbasedqonqallqquestions,qisqmoreqconsistentq 
overqtime;q
R Theyqalsoqhaveqlowerqvalidity,qasqmanyqsocialqcharacteristicsqareqbroadqinqscopeq 
andq itq isq difficultq toq assessq themq withq aq singleq question.q MultiRitemq measuresq 
coverqmoreqscopeqofqtheqmeasuredqcharacteristic.qqq
q
Evenqso,qsingleRitemqscalesqhaveqseveralqadvantages.qFirstqofqall,qtheyqprovideqshortqandq 
quickq surveysq andq stimulateq sincereq answers.q Inq addition,q theyq minimizeq theq 
disadvantagesqofqmultiRitemqscales,qwhichqtendqtoqinflateqcorrelationsqbetweenqerrorsqandq

affectq theq reliabilityq ofq theq responses.q Inq fact,q althoughq multiRitemq surveysq areq 
commonlyq used,q theyq haveq severalq problems.q LaBarberaq andq Mazurskyq (1983),q forq 
instance,qpointqoutqthatqinqlongitudinalqsurveysqthequseqofqmultiRitemqscalesqcanqaffectqtheq 
responseq rateq adversely,q dueq toq longerq surveyq length,q andq mayq decrease,q ratherq thanq 
increase,qoverallqreliability.q
q
SingleRitemqscalesqhaveqbeenqemployedqsuccessfullyqinqlargeRscaleqsurveysqdedicatedqtoq 
performanceqandqsatisfactionqstudiesq(forqexample,qMittalq et al .,q1999),qandqperceptionsq 
ofqqualityqandqvalueq(forqexample,qBoltonq&qDrew,q1991b)q.qWeqhaveqconsideredqsingleR
itemqmeasuresqasqadequateqforqthisqstudy.qIfqweqhadqchosenqaqmultiRitemqmeasure,qweq 
wouldq createq threeq orq fourq componentsq forq eachq qualityq antecedent,q runq confirmatoryq 
factorq analysisq toq checkqthem,qand,q mostq probably,qweq wouldq useq structuralqequationsq 
modellingqinqthisqanalysis.qYet,qasqthisqisqanqexploratoryqstudy,qweqcouldqnotqdetermineq 
theqconstructs,qandqtherefore,qitqwasqsenselessqtoqguessqthoseqconstructs.qq

3.8.1.1.1.1.  Satisfaction 
q
Oneq ofq theq variablesq ofq theq surveyq isq global satisfaction .q Asq discussedq previously,q 
serviceqqualityqandqcustomerqsatisfactionqareqdistinctqconstructsq(Bitner,q1990;qBoltonq&q 
Drew,q1991a,q1991b;qCroninqJr.q&qTaylor,q1992;qParasuramanq et al .,q1985,q1988)qbutqtheq 
differenceq betweenq theseq twoq constructsq andq theirq relationshipq isq notq veryq clear.q Theq 
literatureq isq dividedq betweenq authorsq whoq defendq thatq satisfactionq isq aq dimensionq ofq 
qualityq(Bitner,q1990;qBoltonq&qDrew,q1991a,q1991b)qandqothersqwhoqdefendqqualityqasq 
anq antecedentq ofq satisfactionq (Croninq Jr.q &q Taylor,q 1992;q J.q L.q Heskett,q 1987;q 
Parasuramanqetqal.,q1985,q1988).q
q
q
3.8.1.1.1.2.  Fulfilment of Expectations 
q
Often,qresearchersqcannotqidentifyqpurchasersqbeforeqconsumptionqandqareqconstrainedqtoq 
measureqexpectationsqatqtheqsameqtimeqasqtheqlevelqofqsatisfactionqisqassessed.qThereqareq 
severalqreasonsqwhyqtheqresearcherqisqforcedqtoqrelyqonqexpectationsq ex post facto .qOneq 
ofqthemqisqthatqsomeqcompaniesqmayqnotqwishqtoqsuggestqpossibleqserviceqexperienceqtoq 
consumersqbeforequse,qandqanotherqisqthatqmostqcompaniesqdoqnotqhaveqaccessqtoqtheirq 
customersqpriorq toq theq purchaseq ofqtheq service.qExpectationsq arequsuallyq measuredq ex-
post ,q whichq meansq thatq theyq areq notq anticipatoryq expectations,q butq ratherq postRserviceq 
judgmentsqofqpriorqexpectations.qSeveralqproblemsqcanqariseqfromqthisqpractice:qoneqisq 
theq possibilityq ofq individualsq makingq aq biasq judgmentq ofq theirq priorq expectations;q theq 
otherqisqthatqindividualsqmayqalsoqhaveqexperiencedqotherqservicesqandqhaveqotherqpriorq 
experiences,q andq expectationsq retrievalq canq beq confusedq orq biased.q Mostq probably,q 
retrievedqexpectationsqwillqbeqbiasedqandqtendqtoqalignqwithqexperiencedqperformance.q 
Retrospectiveqexpectationsqareqconsideredqvalid,qespeciallyqifqtheqanticipationsqareqclearq 
andqrelatedqtoqtheqparticularqservicequnderqanalysisq(Oliver,q1997,qpp.q87R88).qEvenqso,q 
recalledq expectationsq areq higherq forq dissatisfiedq andq complainingq customersq thanq forq 
satisfiedq andq nonRcomplainingq consumers:q aq negativeq experienceq willq createq higherq 
expectanciesqinqretrospectqtoqjustifyqtheqdissatisfactionq(Halstead,q1993).qOliver’sq(1980,q 
1993)q disconfirmationq paradigmq ofq serviceq qualityq andq SERVQUALq (Parasuraman  et 
al. ,q1985,q1988)qinfluencedqtheqintroductionqofqtheqquestionqrelatedqtoqtheqfulfilmentqofq 
expectationqinqtheqsurvey. q

3.8.1.1.1.3.  Initial and Final Motivation 
q
Motivationq isq consideredq aq relevantq contributorq toqtheq learningq processq (forq example,q 
Holton1996).qMotivationqtoqlearnqhasqaqdirectqimpactqonqlearning.qMotivationalqelementsq 
includeqmotivationqinqdifferentqmomentsqofqtimeqandqdifferentqobjects.qHoltonq(1996,qp.q 
9)q consideredq motivationq toq learn,q motivationq toq transfer,q andq expectedq utilityq asq

3.8.1.1.1.4.  Immediate and Future Utility 
q
Holtonq (1996,q p.q 9)q considersq utilityq asq aq motivationalq element.q Perceptionsq ofq utilityq 
influenceq motivationq toq transfer,q which,q inq turn,q influencesq motivationq toq learn.q 
Learning,qindividualqperformance,qandqorganisationalqresults,qand,qtherefore,qtheqoverallq 
evaluationqmade,qwillqinfluenceqandqbeqinfluencedqbyqtheqperceptionsqofqutility.qOnqoneq 
hand,q utilityq isq relatedq toq changesq inq performance,q whichq areq probablyq theq mostq 
importantq use ofqtrainingqcourses.qOnqtheqotherqhand,qqualityqisqdefinedqbyqJuranq(1951,q 
Sectionq 2R2)q asq fitness for use .q Theq qualitativeq studyq weq haveq previouslyq madeq 
influencedq theq creationq ofq twoq specificq variables:qimmediate utility q andq future utility .q 
Theseqvariablesq wereq introducedq inq theqhappyq sheetqalsoq inqconsonanceqwithq theq fiveR
levelqROIqframeworkq(J.qJ.qPhillips,q1994;qJ.qJ.qPhillipsq&qHolton,q1995),qwhichqdefinesq 
inqitsqfirstqlevelqnotqonlyq reactions qbutqalsoqtheq planned action .qTheq planned action ,qinq 
turn,q includesq aq planq ofq whatq participantsq intendq toq applyq fromq theq course.q Theq twoq 
variablesqwereqalsoqinspiredqinqtheqfifthqlevelqofqtheq carousel of development q(Industrialq 
Society,q2000),qwhichqisqfocusedqonq use qandq reinforce learning .qq

3.8.1.1.1.5.  Quality and Quality-Price Relation 
q
Theqperceptionqofqoverallqqualityqisqourqmainqvariable,qtheqoneqthatqweqwantqtoqrelateqtoq 
allqtheqothers.q Quality-price relation qwasqintroducedqbecauseqtheqconceptqofqqualityqisq 
notq absolute:q Feigenbaumq (1961,q p.q 13)q defendedq thatq qualityq isq theq bestq forq certainq 
customerq conditions,q oneq ofq thoseq beingq theq actualqendq useq andq theq otherq theq price.q
Severalqotherqapproachesqtoqqualityqareqrelatedqtoqtheqpriceqpaid,qsuchqasqBroh’sq(1982,q 
p.q3)qdefinition,qwhichqdefinesqqualityqasqtheqdegreeqofqexcellenceqatqanqacceptableqpriceq 
andq theq controlq ofq variabilityq atq anq acceptableq cost.  Garvin’sq (1983,q 1988,q pp.q 40R46)q
valueRbasedq approachq toq qualityq alsoq definesq qualityq inq termsq ofq costsq andq prices:q “aq 
qualityqproductqisqoneqthatqprovidesqperformanceqatqanqacceptableqprice”.qLeiflerq(1982)q
makesq aq similarq relationq ofq qualityq toq theq priceq paidq whenq heq definesq qualityq asq “theq 
amountsq ofq theq unpricedq attributesq containedq inq eachq unitq ofq theq pricedq attribute”.q 
Finally,q priceq isq aq tangibleq elementq fromq whichq customersq drawq conclusionsq aboutq 
qualityq(Kotlerq et al .,q1996,qp.q589),qand,qtherefore,qtheqquality-price relation qincludesq 
thatqevaluation. q

Weqhaveqbasedqourqdecisionsqregardingqtheqscalesqonqtheqliteratureqaboutqsatisfaction.qq

R UsingqmultipleRindicatorqapproachesq(toqachieveqgreaterqaccuracy);q
R Estimatingqviaq partial least squares q(Wold,q1973).q

thenqrepresentedqinq1qtoq10qLikertq(1932)qscalesqandqtheqmeaningqofqthoseqpositionsqwasq 
communicated:q 1q wasq theq lowestq levelq andq 10q theq highestq one.q Radios q wereq putq

(Figureq24).qTheqvariablesqwereqlaterqcodedqforqstatisticalqanalysisq(Tableq29,qavailableq

4.2.2.3.  Handling Duplicates 
q
Twoqdifferentqsituationsqofqduplicatedqanswersqwereqtreated:q
q
R First,q forq theq sameq course,q theq customerq submittedqtheq surveyq twice.q Inq thisq 
situation,q weq consideredq theq secondq answer,q asq weq believeq itq wasq aq wayq ofq 
correctingqtheqevaluationqmade.qTheqfirstqanswerqwasqdiscarded.q111qcasesqwereq 
inqthisqsituation;q
R Theq secondq typeq ofq duplicateq situationsq wasq notq treatedq theq sameq way:q Asq 
severalqcustomersqtookqseveralqcoursesqduringqtheqperiodqofqanalysis,qtheyqwereq 
ableq toqsubmitq severalq timesqtheirqanswers.q Inq theseqsituations,q weqagreedq thatq 
thoseq customersq hadq theq rightq toq expressq theirq opinionq everyqtimeq theyq tookq aq 
course,qandq thatq theirq qualityq perceptionqcouldq beqquiteq differentqfromq timeq toq 
timeqandqfromqcourseqtoqcourse.qInqtheseqcases,qtheseqduplicateqanswersqwereqnotq 
discardedqandqwereqincludedqinqtheqanalysis.qTherefore,qtheqdataqisqrelatedqnotqtoq 
2630q customersq butq ratherq toq 2630q registrations.q 1085q uniqueq customersq 
participatedq inq ourq study.q Thisq meansq that,q onq average,q eachq oneq hasq attendedq 
2.42q coursesq duringq theq periodq considered.q Thisq isqtheq sameq toq sayq that,q onq 
average,qeachqcustomerqmadeqaqnewqregistrationqeveryq136qdays.qAfterqdealingq 
withq missingq valuesq (below),q weq keptq 2481q cases,q whichq correspondq toq 1041q 
uniqueqcustomers.qq

4.2.2.4.  Missing Value Analysis (MVA) 
q
Inqtheqpreparatoryqanalyses,qweqhaveqidentifiedqtheqexistenceqofqmissingqvaluesq(MV).q
Severalqfactorsqmayqleadqtoqmissingqvalues:q
q
R Misunderstandingqofqtheqquestions:qtheqindividualqdoesqnotqunderstandqwhatqisq 
beingqasked;q
R Unavailabilityq ofq theq inquired:q theq individualq mayqbeq saturatedq ofq answeringq
surveysq(whichqisqbecomingqaqmoreqfrequentqsituation),qbequnderqtimeqpressure,q 
provideqanswersqinqaqfrivolousqway,qandqbequnavailableqtoqreflectqonqwhatqsheqisq 
beingqquestionedqabout;q
R Unawarenessqofqmissingqdata:qtheqindividualqmayqnotqbeqawareqthatqsheqdidqnotq 
provideqanqanswerqtoqallqquestions.qq
q
Thereqisqnoqconsensusqinqtheqliteratureqregardingqtheqbestqwayqofqdealingqwithqmissingq 
values.q Traditionalq approaches,q asq listwise,q pairwise,q andq meanq substitution,q areq 
confrontedq withq alternativesq asq singleq imputation,qmultipleq imputation,q andq fullq 
informationqmaximumqlikelihoodqestimationq(Acock,q2005).qThequseqofqcompleteqcaseq 
methodsqthatqdropqsubjectsqmissingqanyqobservationsqareqcommonlyqseenqinqpractice,qbutq 
isqanqapproachqconsideredqinefficientqasqwellqasqpotentiallyqbiasedq(Hortonq&qKleinman,q 
2007).q Theq oppositeq solutionq alsoq hasq problems:q modelsq thatq incorporateq incompleteq 
dataqmayqleadqtoqaqlargeqnumberqofqobservationsqwithqsomeqmissingqinformation.qAlisonq 
(2002)qandqLittleqandqRubinq(1987)qareqsomeqofqtheqauthorsqwhoqhaveqbeenqprovidingqanq
overviewqofqtheqmethodsqtoquseqinqthisqsituations.qq
q
13.38%qofqourqcasesqhadqatqleastqoneqmissingqvalue.qAsqdroppingqallqtheseqobservationsq 
andq fittingq aq modelq toq onlyq theq completeq casesq wouldq beq “hugelyq inefficientq andq 
potentiallyqbiased”q(Hortonq&qKleinman,q2007),qweqdecidedqtoqsearchqforqotherqcriteriaq 
ofqmissingqdataqhandling,qtoqdecideqwhetherqorqnotqtoqexcludedqcasesqwithqincompleteq 
observations.qToqbetterqdecideqwhichqstrategyqtoqpursue,qweqanalyzedqifqtheqmissingqdataq 
hadq aq randomq distribution,q andq ifq thereq wereq casesqwithq moreq thanq 10%q ofq missingq 
answersq (Allison,q 2002),q as,q beyondq thisq value,q thereq isq moreq probabilityq ofq bias.q 203q 
casesq hadq oneq(6,66%)q missingq value,q whichq representsq 7.8%q ofqtheq totalqsample.qWeq 
identifiedq 149q casesq withq moreq thanq 10%q ofq missingqvaluesq (5.66%q ofq ourq sample)q 
(Tableq 32).q Weq decidedq toq eliminateq theseq 149q casesq fromq ourq sampleq andq onlyq 2481q 
casesqwereqleftq(Tableq33).qq

4.2.2.6.  Runs Tests 
q
Theq runs test qprocedureqtestsqindicateqwhetherqtheqorderqofqoccurrenceqofqtwoqvaluesqofqaq 
variableqisqrandomqandqisqusedqtoqdetermineqwhetherqtheqsampleqwasqdrawnqatqrandom.q 
Aq runs test qisqaqspecialqcaseqofqtheqbinomialqtestqthatqexaminesqnonRrandomnessqwhenq 
thereqisqaqsequenceqofqbinaryqevents,qi.e.qtoqdetermineqifqtheqconsequenceqofqeventsqisq 
random.qThisqtestqisqrelatedqtoqconcernsqofqrandomnessqandqwhetherqtheqseriesqofqeventsq 
isqcomingqfromqaqrandomqsequenceqthatqwouldqproduceqaqbinaryqsequenceqwhereqtheqtwoq 
eventsqareqoccurringqinqaqrandomqsequenceq(Coughlin,q1999,qp.q11).qAq run qisqdefinedqasq 
aqsequenceqofqlikeqitemsqthatqareqfollowedqorqprecededqbyqaqdifferentqitemqorqnoqitemqatq 
all.qIfqthereqisqaqmuchqsmallerqnumberqorqlargerqnumberqofqrunsqthanqoneqwouldqexpect,q 
thenqtheqlikelihoodqisqthatqtheqsequenceqisqnotqrandom,qi.e.qasqaqrunqisqaqsequenceqofqlikeq 
observations,q ifq aq sampleq includesq tooq manyq orq tooqfewq runsq thatq suggestsq thatq theq 
sampleqisqnotqrandom.qForqlargeqsamples,qoneqwouldqexpectq2p*q*nqrunsqwhereqpqisqtheq 
portionqinqoneqofqtheqcategories,qqqisqtheqportionqinqtheqotherq(qq=q1qRqp),qandqnqisqtheq 
numberqofqobservationsq(Coughlin,q1999,qp.q11).qq
q
Theqhypothesesqare:qq
H0:qRq=qR oq
H1:qRq≠qR 0q
whereqRqareqtheqruns.qq
q
Inqourqcase,qtheqsequenceqselectedqisqtheqmomentqofqtimeqwhenqtheqrespondentqsubmittedq

Virtuallyqallqcustomerqsatisfactionqandqqualityqresearchqisqhamperedqbyqhighlyqskewedq 
distributionsq forq theq indicatorsq ofq theq satisfactionq construct.qEvenq inq lessq thanq perfectq 
markets,qasqlongqasqthereqareqavailableqalternativesqand/orqsomeqelasticityqofqdemand,qtheq 
distributionqofqsatisfactionqandqqualityqscoresqshouldqbeqnegativelyqskewedq(illustratedq 
Figureq 26).q Onlyq inq captiveq marketsq mightq repeatq buyersq beq dissatisfiedq inq generalq 
(Fornell,q1992).q
q
Skewnessqisqaqproblem,qbutqitqisqaqstatisticalqone.qHighlyqskewedqvariableqdistributionsq 
doq notq lendq themselvesq toq conventionalq testsq ofq significanceq andq leadq toq downwardq 
biasesq inq theq correlationalq analysis,q lowq reliability,q and,q sometimes,q misleadingq 
arithmeticqmeans.qTheqimplicationsqareqthatqitqisqveryqdifficultqtoqaccountqproperlyqforq 
theqvariationqinqsatisfactionqratingsqbyqthequseqofqotherqvariablesqandqthatqtheqresultsqareq 
unstable.qq

4.2.3.1.  Tests for Normality  
q
Thereqareqseveralqwaysqtoqtestqforqnormality.qq
q
Theqevaluationqofqskewnessqandqkurtosisqcanqhelpqtheqresearcherqdetermineqwhetherqtheq 
dataqreflectqaqnormalqorqnonRnormalqdistributionq(Coughlin,q1999,qp.q7):qq
q
R Skewness qisqaqmeasureqofqasymmetryqofqtheqdistributionqofqnumbers.qAqnormalq 
distributionqisqsymmetrical;q
R Kurtosis qisqaqmeasureqofqtheqpresenceqofqextremeqvaluesqinqtheqdistribution.qIfqtheq 
distributionqisqrelativelyqpeakedqinqtheqmiddle,qkurtosisqwillqbeqgreaterqthanqzero.q 
Ifq theq distributionq isq ratherq flat,q theq kurtosisq willq beq lessq thanq zero.q Normalq 
distributionsqhaveqaqkurtosisqofqzero.qq
q
Toq determineq ifq aq distributionq isq statisticallyq differentq fromq aq normalq distribution,q theq 
skewnessqandqkurtosisqstatisticsqcanqbeqconvertedqtoqZqscoresqbyqdividingqtheqstatisticqbyq 
itsqstandardqerror.qTheqscoresqareqthenqcomparedqtoq1,96q( p-value qofq.05)qandqifqtheqZq 
valueqisqlessqthanqthatqcriticalqvalue,qitqcanqbeqassumedqthatqtheqdistributionqofqtheqsetqofq 
scoresqisqnormallyqdistributedq(Coughlin,q1999,qp.q7).q
q
Theq resultsq ofq Tableq 43q suggestq thatq normalityq shouldq beq rejectedq butq thereq areq threeq 
additionalqmethodsqthatqcanqbequsedqtoqconfirmqthat:qq
q
R Theqstemqandqleafqdistribution:qandqnormalityqisqrejectedqifqtheqdistributionqdoesq 
notqhaveqaqnormalqlooking;qq
R TheqQRQq plot:qifqtheq observationsqareq veryq nearqtheq line,q theyq reflectqaqnormalq 
distribution;q
R Analyticalqtests,qasqtheqKolmogorovRSmirnovqtestqandqtheqShapiroRWilkqtest.qq
q
Inq orderq toq excludeq theq hypothesisq ofq normalityq inqtheq variables,q weq ranq bothq 
KolmogorovRSmirnovq andq ShapiroRWilkq tests,q asq theseq areq theq mostq preciseq methodsq
andqcouldqbeqappliedqtoqallqvariablesqatqtheqsameqtime.qBothqtestsqrejectedqtheqnormalityq 
hypothesisqinqallqvariables,qwithqaq p-value qofq0q(Tableq45).qq

Hadq weqfacedq aq scenarioq ofq highq future utility q withq lowq immediate utility ,q thatq wouldq 
suggestqthatqtheqtypicalqindividualqwasqplanningqtoqmakeqaqcareerqchange,qthatqtheqcourseq 
sheq hadq justq attendedq wasq notq relatedq toq herq currentq job,q thatq sheq wasq tooq optimisticq 
aboutq herq futureq opportunities,q orq thatq sheq believedq thatq sheq wouldq notq beq givenq theq 
opportunityq toq applyq whatq sheq hadq justq learntq inq theq currentq functionq untilq herq teamq 
leaderq wasqreplacedq orq someq workingq conditionsqchanged.q Yet,q thatq isq notq theqcurrentq 
situation,qasqweqfaceqtheqcoexistenceqofqhighq future utility qwithqaqhigh,qalthoughqlower,q
immediate utility .qWeqwouldqexpectqthatqifq immediate utility qwasqperceived,qthenqsomeq 
future utility qshouldqalsoqbeqconsideredq(ifqitqisqusefulqnow,qwhyqnotqbeingqusefulqinqtheq 
future?).q Toq aq lesserq extent,q ifq theq traineeq expectedq future utility ,q eventuallyq someq 
immediate utility qcouldqoccur.qThisqsuggestsqthat,qifq immediate utility qisqperceived,qthen,q
mostqprobably,qfuture utility qwillqalsoqexist.qYet,qtheqperceptionqofq future utility qdoesqnotq 
guaranteeq immediate utility .q Therefore,q weq expectedq theseq twoq variablesq toq beqhighly,q 
butqnotqperfectly,qcorrelated.qq

rangesqfromqR1qandq1qandqtheqclosestqitqisqfromqtheseqextremeqvalues,qtheqhigherqisqtheq

Yet,q weq hadq toq testq bothq utilitiesq toq knowq ifq theyqwereq inq fact,q statisticallyq speaking,q 
differentiated.qForqthatqpurpose,qweqranqaqWilcoxonq(1945)qtestqforqtwoqrelatedq(paired)q 
samplesq (Tableq 51).q Theq Wilcoxonq signedRrankq testq (Wilcoxon,q 1945)q isq aq nonR
parametricq statisticalq hypothesisq testq forq theq caseq ofq twoq relatedq samplesq orq repeatedq 
measurementsqonqaqsingleqsample.qThisqtestqisqanqalternativeqtoqtheqpairedqStudent'sqtRtestq 
whenqtheqpopulationqcannotqbeqassumedqtoqbeqnormallyqdistributed,qasqisqourqcase.qWeq 
couldqhaveq usedq theq signq testqforq thisqpurpose,qbutq theqWilcoxonq signedRrankq testqisqaq 
moreq powerfulq alternativeq toq theq signq test.q Besides,q theq Wilcoxonq testq considers,q notq 
onlyq theq directionq ofq aq difference,q butq alsoq theq magnitudeq ofq theq differenceq betweenq 
pairs,qandqtheseqareqtheqtwoqmainqreasonsqwhyqweqdecidedqtoquseqitqinsteadqofqtheqsignq 
test.qSomeqliteratureq(forqinstance,qMayhall,q2004,qp.q64)qassumesqthatqtheqWilcoxonqcanq 
beq appliedq toq ordinalq orq measurementq data,q withoutqanyq additionalq assumption.q Someq 
authorsq (Coughlin,q 1999,q p.q 15;q Eastonq &q McColl,q 2009,q p.q 476;q Pestanaq &q Gageiro,q 
2005,q p.q 476)q defendq that,q toq applyq thisq test,q weq haveq toq assumeq thatq theq populationq 
probabilityq distributionq isq symmetric.q Thatq isq toq sayq thatq weq haveq toq assumeq thatq theq 
underlyingq populationq fromq whichq theq sampleq isq drawnq isq symmetricalq aboutq theq 
hypothesizedqmedian,qleadingqtoqtheqassumptionqthatqtheqdifferenceqhasqaqsymmetricalq 
distributionqaroundqzero.qThisqisqnotqaqveryqhardqassumptionqtoqmakeqinqourqcase,qasqtheq 
medianq ofq theq differenceq betweenq futureq andq immediate utility q inq theq sampleq isq 0,q theq 
averageq differenceq isq .19.q We,q therefore,q assumeq thatq theq populationq fromq whichq thisq 
sampleqisqdrawnqhasqaqsymmetricalqdistributionqaboutqzero,qregardingqtheqdifferenceqofq 
theqtwoqvariablesqbeingqanalyzed 29 .qWeqalsoqassumeqthisqinqallqtheqotherqsituationsqwhereq 
wequseqthisqtest.qq
q
Ourqhypothesesqwere:qq
q
Ho:q Immediate utility qisqequalqtoq future utility q
H1:q immediate utility qisqdifferentqfromq future utility q
q
WhileqrunningqWilcoxonqtest,qweqexcludedqcasesq test-by-test qbutqtheqconclusionsqwouldq 
holdqtrueqifqweqhadqexcludedqcasesq listwise (Tableq51).qWeqrejectedqtheqhypothesisqofq 
equalityqofqtheqcentralqtendencyqofqtheq immediate qandq future utilities q(Tableq52).qWithq 
theqp-value qobtained,qweqcanqevenqhypothesizeqaqunilateralqtestqandqinqthisqcaseqweqcanq 
conclude,q withq aq 95%q confidence,q thatq future utility q isq perceivedq asq higherq thanq 
immediate utility .qq
q

whereq iq isq theq groupq ofq regularq vocationalqcoursesqq andq jq isq theq groupq ofq coursesq thatq

WeqranqaqtwoRindependentqsampleqnonRparametricqtestqforqthisqpurpose.qq
q
Thereqareqtwoqtypesqofqtestsqthatqcanqbeqappliedqtoqthisqsituationqwhereqtwoqindependentq 
samplesqareqcomparedq(Coughlin,q1999,qpp.q16R21):qq
q
R Theq medianq test,q whichq isq usedq whenq evaluatingq whetherq twoq independentq 
samplesq withq theq sameq distributionq haveq theq sameq median.q Inq thisq test,q theq 
statisticq considersq theq variationq inq bothq samplesq andq determinesq theq likelihoodq 
thatqtheqtwoqsamplesqcomeqfromqtheqsameqdistributionqwithqtheqsameqmedian;q
R TheqMannRWhitneyqtestq(1947),qwhichqisqtheqnonRparametricqtestqthatqisqanalogueq 
toqtheqtwoRsampleqparametricqtRtest.q
q
WeqdecidedqtoquseqtheqMannRWhitneyq(1947)qtestqtoqanalyseqtheqhypotheses.qq

Inqbothqgroups,q future utility qwasqhigherqthanq immediate utility qandqtheqdifferenceqwasq

immediate utility qandqR0.839qinq future utility .qWe,qtherefore,qdoqnotqrejectqtheqhypothesisq 
of,q atq aq significanceq levelq ofq 5%,q theq averagesq ofqbothq utilitiesq beingq equalq betweenq 
regularqvocationalqeRlearningqcoursesqandqcoursesqthatqallowqprofessionalqqualification.q
Evenqso,qweqhaveqtoqbeqcarefulqwithqtheseqresults,qasqthereqmayqbeqaqmisunderstandingqofq

EVOLUI.COM’sqbestRsellersqever,qisqaqcertifiedqcourseqthatqallowsqprofessionalqtrainersq 
toq revalidateq theirq trainer’sq certificate.q Yet,q thisqcourseq isqattendedqalsoqbyq individualsq

4.2.6.  Factor Analysis of Quality Perceptions  
q
4.2.6.1.  Description of Factor Analysis 
q
Factorq analysis,q whichqwasq originallyq developedq byqSpearmanq (1904a),q isq aq statisticalq 
techniqueqwidelyqusedqinqpsychologyqandqtheqsocialqsciences.qItqconsistsqofqaqnumberqofq 
statisticalqtechniques,qtheqaimqofqwhichqisqtoqsimplifyqcomplexqsetsqofqdataq(Kline,q1994,q 
p.q 3),q likeq humanq abilities.q Asq Klineq (1994,q p.q 2)qexemplifies,q withq asq fewq asq fiveq 
variables,qthereqareq25qentriesqinqaqcorrelationqmatrix,qwhichqareqhardqtoqkeepqinqone’sq 
head.q Inq aq studyq withq 100q variables,q thereq areq 10.000q correlations.q Theseq correlationsq 
wouldqbeqincomprehensibleqwithoutqaqsimplifyingqprocedure,qwhichqcanqhelpqdiscoverq 
whatq mightq accountq forq thoseq correlations.q Factorq analysisq aimsq toq simplifyq humanq 
abilitiesqbyqsimplifyingqtheqcorrespondentqcorrelationqmatrix.qFactorqanalysisqisqusedqtoq 
exploreq theq interrelationshipsq amongq variablesq toq discernq whetherq orqnotq theq variablesq 
canq beq groupedq intoq aq smallerq setq ofq underlyingq factors.q Thereq areq threeq primaryq 
applicationsq ofq factorq analysisq (Coughlin,q 1999;q Coughlinq &q Knight,q 2003,q pp.q 180R
181).q Theq firstq isq toq exploreq dataq forq patterns:q exploratory factor analysis q revealsq 
patternsq amongq theq interRrelationshipsq ofq theq items,q andq isq usedq forq thisq purpose.q Theq 
secondqapplicationqisqforqdataqreduction:qa)qfactorqanalysisqcanqbequsedqtoqreduceqaqlargeq 
numberqofqvariablesqintoqaqsmallerqandqmoreqmanageableqnumberqofqfactors;qandqb)qitq 
canqcreateqfactorqscoresqforqeachqsubjectqthatqrepresentsqtheseqhigherqorderqvariables.qTheq 
thirdq andq lastq purposeq isq toq confirmq theq hypothesisq ofq aq preRexistingq factorq structure:q 
whenqaqgivenqfactorqstructureqexists,q confirmatory factor analysis qcanqbeqconductedqtoq 
supportqtheqvalidityqofqthisqfactorqstructureqi.e.,qtoqconfirmqanqexistingqorqhypothesizedq 
factorqstructure.q
q
Traditionally,qfactorqanalysisqhasqbeenqusedqtoq explore qtheqpossiblequnderlyingqstructureq 
inq aq setq ofq interrelatedq variables,q withoutq imposingq anyq preconceivedq structureq onq theq 
outcome.qItqisqrareqtoqfindqinvestigationqprocessesqthatqareqmadeqwithoutqanyqtheoreticalq 
background,q asq defendedq inq grounded theory q (Glaserq &q Strauss,q 1967):q evenq openq 
questionnairesqandqunstructuredqinterviewsqstartqwithqquestionsqthatqhaveqhunchesqbuiltq 
intoq them.q Yet,q inq exploratoryq factorq analysis,q althoughq someq previousq theoreticalq 
influencesqhaveqconditionedqtheqdesignqofqtheqdataqcollectingqinstruments,qthereqisqaqfreeq 
spirit,qtoqwhichqChidq(1970,qp.q6)qcalledqtheq“let’sqseeqwhatqhappensqspirit”.qAtqtheqotherq 
extremeqweqfindqconfirmatoryqanalysis,qtoqwhichqCattellq(Hurleyq&qCattell,q1962,qquotedq 
inq Child,q 1970,q p.q 7)q callsq theq Procrustes technique .q Procrutesq was,q inq theq Greekq 
mythology,q aq banditq whoq tiedq hisq victimsq toq aq bedq andq madeq themq fitq it,q eitherq byq 
stretchingqthemqorqcuttingqoffqtheirqlimbs.qInqconfirmatoryqfactorqanalysis,qtheqProcrutesq 
techniqueq involvesq testingq dataq toq seeq howq closelyqtheyq fitq toq aq hypothesizedq factorq 
structureq (withoutq cuttingq orq stretchingq involved).q Theq objectiveq isq toq confirmq orq testq 
hypotheses,q ratherq thanq createq them.q Confirmatoryq analysisq startsq withq aq hypothesisq 
aboutqtheqpossibleqstructureqofqaqgivenqconcept,qandqonlyqthenqareqtheqvariablesqcarefullyq 
chosenqtoqfitqtheqstructure.qAsqChildq(1970,qp.q7)qputsqit,q“itqisqaqlittleqbitqlikeqcreatingqaq 
mouldqandqtestingqanqobjectqagainstqtheqmouldqtoqseeqhowqwellqitqfits”.q
q
Klineq(1993,qp.q115)qdifferentiatesqexploratoryqandqconfirmatoryqfactorqanalysisqasqthis:qq
q
R Exploratoryqfactorqanalysisqisqusedqtoqsimplifyqaqlargeqsetqofqdata,qandqtoqmapq 
outqtheqmostqimportantqvariables;qq
R Confirmatoryq factorq analysisq isq usedq toq supportq hypothesesq andq toq investigateq

Eachq factorq isq aq dimension q orq construct ,q whichq isq aq condensedq statementq ofq theq 
relationshipsq betweenq aq setq ofq variables.q Aq linearqcombinationq ofq variables,q anyq 
combination,q isq aq factor .q Combinationsq mayq involveq differentialq weightingsqofq eachq

Aq factor q isq aq constructq operationallyq definedq byq itsq factor loadings ,q whichq areq theq 
correlationsq ofq aq variableq withq aq factor q (orq component )q (Royce,q 1963).q Sinceq aq factorq 
scoreqisqaqscoreqonqaqgivenqlinearqcombinationqofqvariablesqforqeachqsubject,qitqisqclearq 
thatq thisq scoreq canq beq correlatedq withq theq scoreq onq eachq variableq inq theq dataq matrix.q 
Theseqcorrelationsqareqtheqfactorqloadings.qTheseqcorrelationsqcanqbeqpositiveqorqnegativeq 
andqofqanyqsizeq(Kline,q1993,qp.q116).qTheqmeaningqofqfactorqloadingsqisqmadeqclearqinq 
theqcomponentqanalysisqthatqweqdiscussqlater.q
q
ItqisqunlikelyqthatqtheqvarianceqinRgroupqofqdataqcanqbeqexplainedqbyqoneqfactor.qAfterqtheq 
firstqfactorqhasqbeenqextracted,qitqisqnecessaryqtoqextractqtheqotherqfactors.qTheqnumberqofq 
factorsqdependsquponqtheqfactorqloadingsqonqtheqfirstqandqsubsequentqfactors.qVeryqhighq 
loadingsq implyq thatq onlyq oneq factorq isq necessary.q Ifq theq firstq factorq hasq virtuallyq zeroq 
loadings,qthatqmeansqthatqthereqisqnoqcommonqfactor.qInqgeneral,qtheqfirstqfactorqusuallyq 
hasqmoderateqloadings,qrangingqaroundq.3qandq.7,qandqtheirqsignqisqirrelevantqtoqtheqsize.q 
Inqthisqcase,qfurtherqfactorsqcanqbeqextractedq(Kline,q1993,qpp.q116R118).qq
q
Theqconceptsqofq factor qandq factor loadings qimplyqthatq(Kline,q1993,qp.q118):qq

R Theqsquaredqfactorqloadingqofqaqvariableqindicatesqhowqmuchqtheqvarianceqofqthatq

meansqthatq64%qofqtheqvarianceqofqthatqvariableqisqexplainedqbyqthatqfactor;q
R Theqaverageqsquaredqloadingsqofqaqfactorqshowqtheqpercentageqofqvarianceqinqtheq 
dataqthatqisqexplainedqbyqtheqfactor;qq

largerq theq communality ,q theq betterq theq factorsq accountq forq theq varianceq ofq theq

Exploratoryqfactorqanalysisqhasqthreeqbasicqdecisionqpoints:qqq

4.2.6.4.1.  The Number of Factors 
q
Theq aimq ofq exploratoryq factorq analysisq isq toq determineq ifq theq itemsq canq beq validlyq 
organizedq intoq aq smallerq setq ofq underlyingq factors.q Whenq determiningq theq appropriateq 
numberqofqfactors,qoneqfactorqisqidentifiedqforqeachqvariableqorqitem.qIfqnoqrelationshipsq 
existqbetweenqtheqvariables,qeachqvariableqwouldqmakeqitsqownquniqueqfactor.qIdeally,qaq 
factorqreductionqwillqoccur.qThereqareqseveralqmethodsqforqfindingqtheqnumberqofqfactorsq 
toq beq extracted,q asq theq eigen-one ,q theq scree q test,q andq parallel analysis .q Theq mostq 
commonq approachq toq decidingq theq numberq ofq factorsq isq toq generateq aq screeq plot.q Theq 
screeqplotqisqaqtwoqdimensionalqgraphqwithqfactorsqonqtheqxRaxisqandqeigenvaluesqonqtheq 
yRaxis.qq
q
Eigenvalues qrepresentqtheq varianceq accountedq forqbyqeachq underlyingq factor.q Theyq areq 
notq representedq byq percentagesq butq scoresq thatq totalq theq numberq ofq items.q Aq 12Ritemq 
scaleqwill,qtheoretically,qhaveq12qpossiblequnderlyingqfactors,qandqeachqfactorqwillqhaveq 
anq eigenvalue qthatqindicatesqtheqamountqofqvariationqinqtheqitemsqaccountedqforqbyqeachq 
factor.qIfqtheqfirstqfactorqhasqanq eigenvalue qofq3.0,qitqaccountsqforq25%qofqtheqvarianceq 
(3/12=.25).q Theq totalq ofq allq theq eigenvalues q willq beq 12q ifq thereq areq 12q items,q soq someq 
factorsqwillqhaveqsmallerqeigenvalues.q Eigenvalues qareqtypicallyqarrangedqinqaqscreeqplotq

(Coughlin,q1999,qp.q189).qFromqtheqscreeqplotq(Figureq37qinqpageq191)qweqcanqseeqthatq

Anotherq approachq isq calledq theq Kaiser-Guttman rule q (Guttman,q 1954;q Kaiser,q 1960),q 
whichq statesq thatq theq numberq ofq factorsq isq equalq toq theq numberq ofq factorsq withq 
eigenvalues qgreaterqthanq1.0:qtheqresearcherqisqinstructedqtoqkeepqonlyqtheqfactorsqwhoseq 
eigenvalues q areq greaterq thanq 1.0q andq discardq theq rest.q Theq rationaleq forq choosingq theq 
valueqofq1.0qisqthatqaqfactorqmustqaccountqforqaqvarianceqatqleastqasqlargeqasqtheqvarianceq 
ofq aq singleq standardizedq variableq (whichq hasq aq meanq ofq zeroq andq aq varianceq ofq 1).q 
Accordingq toq Guttmanq andq Kaiserq (Guttman,q 1954;q Kaiser,q 1960),q whenq aqcorrelationq 
matrixqisqfactorized,qitqmakesqnoqsenseqtoqretainqcomponentsqthatqexplainqlessqvarianceq

R Theq generalizedq leastRsquaresq factorq extractionq method,q whichq minimizesq theq

R Theq maximumRlikelihoodq factorq extractionq methodq providesq parameterq

4.2.6.4.3.  The Rotation Method 
q
Afterqtheqextractionqofqfactors,qitqmightqbeqdifficultqtoqinterpretqandqnameqtheqfactorsqorq 
components,q basedq onq theirq factorq loadings.q Onceq anq initialq solutionq isq obtained,q theq

Usually,qthereqareqthreeqtypesqofqproblemsqwithinqtheqinitialqfactorqstructureq(Coughlin,q 
1999,qpp.q191R193):qq
q
R Theqfirstqfactorqexplainsqtheqmostqamountqofqvarianceqand,qasqaqresult,qmostqofq
theqvariablesqwillqhaveqatqleastqsomeqrelationshipqwithqthisqfirstqfactor.qAsqtheq 
firstq factorq accountsq forq theq maximumq shareq ofq theqvariance,q thisq meansq thatq 
mostqvariablesqwillqhaveqhighqloadingsqonqtheqmostqimportantqfactor,qandqsmallq 
loadingsqonqtheqotherqfactors.qThus,qthisqfirstqfactorqbecomesqveryqgeneralizedq 
andqdifficultqtoqinterpret;qq
R Manyq factorsq areq bipolar.q Aq bipolar factor q isq oneq inq whichq bothq significantq 
positiveq andq negativeq loadingsq exist.q Aq negativeq loadingq isq likeq aq negativeq 
correlationqcoefficient.qBipolarqfactors,qcanqcreateqnegativeqloadingsqthatqcannotq 
beqinterpretedqlogicallyqfromqtheqdata;qq
R Becauseqofqtheqfirstqfactorqbeingqaqgeneralqfactor,qmanyqvariablesqmayqloadqonq 
moreqthanqoneqfactor,qcreatingq double factor qloadings.q
q
Rotationqisqaqwayqofqmaximizingqhighqloadingsqandqminimizingqlowqloadings,qsoqthatqtheq 
simplestqpossibleqstructureqisqachieved.qThereqareqtwoqbasicqtypesqofqrotation:qorthogonalq 
andqoblique:qqq
q
R Orthogonalq meansq thatq theq factorsq areq assumedq toq beq uncorrelatedq withq oneq 
another.qqFactorsqareqrotatedqinqsuchqaqwayqthatqtheyqareqalwaysqatqrightqanglesqtoq 
eachqotherq(cosq90ºq=q0);qThisqisqtheqdefaultqsettingqinqallqstatisticalqpackagesqbutq 
isq rarelyq aq logicalq assumptionq aboutq factorsq inq theq socialq sciences,q albeitq itq isq 
commonlyqusedqasqobliqueqrotationqhasqseriousqproblemsq(Kline,q1994,qpp.q62R
63);qqq
R Obliqueq rotationq derivesq factorq loadingsq basedq onq theq assumptionq thatq theq 
factorsqareqcorrelatedqandqgivesqtheqcorrelationqbetweenqtheqfactorsqinqadditionqtoq 
theqloadingsq(Newsom,q2008).qInqobliqueqrotations,qtheqfactorqaxesqcanqtakequpq 
anyq positionq inq factorq space,q whichq allowsq moreq freedomq inq selectingq theq 
positionqofqeachqfactorqinqtheqfactorqspaceqthanqdoesqorthogonalqrotation,qwhereq 
thereq isq theq constraintq ofq orthogonalityq (Kline,q 1994,q p.q 62).q Theq closerq theq 
rotationqangleqisq toqzero,qtheq higherqtheqcorrelationq betweenqtheqfactors.qIfq theq 
rotationq angleq isq zero,q thisq meansq thatq theq twoq factorsq haveq merged.q Ifq theq 
rotationq angleq approachesq 90º,q theq relationshipq betweenq theq factorsq nearsq zeroq 
andq approximatesq theq orthogonalq rotationq methodq (Coughlin,q 1999,q pp.q 195R
196).qq
q
Withinqeachqrotationqmethodqthereqareqseveralqavailableqalgorithmsq(Kline,q1994,qp.q68;q 
Newsom,q2008):qq
q
R OrthogonalqrotationqincludesqVarimax,qQuartamax,qandqEquamax;q
R Obliqueq rotationq includesq Oblimin,q Quartmin,q Biquartmin,q Oblimax,q 
Covarimin,qBinormamin,qPromax,qandqDirectqQuartmin;q
q
Varimaxq rotationq (Kaiser,q 1958)q aimsq atq simple structure q (Thurstone,q 1947)q whileq 
keepingqtheqfactorqaxesqorthogonal.qThisqmeansqthatqtheqrotatedqfactorsqarequncorrelatedq 
andq theqcommunalitiesq andq theq abilityq toq reproduceqtheqoriginalqcorrelationqmatrixq areq 
identicalqtoqtheqoriginalqfactorqanalysis.qVarimaxqaimsqtoqmaximizeqtheqsumqofq variances q
ofqsquaredqloadingsqinqtheqcolumnsqofqtheqfactorqmatrix.qThisqproducesqinqeachqcolumnq 
(i.e.,qinqeachqfactor)qloadingsqthatqareqeitherqhighqorqnearqzeroq(Kline,q1994,qpp.q67R68).q

WequsedqVarimaxqasqtheqrotationqmethodqbecauseqitqisqconsideredq“anqexcellentqmethodq

q
Thisqsimpleqstructureqsuggestsqthatqeachqitemqshouldqbeqrelatedqtoqonlyqoneqfactor.qq
Evenqso,qsometimesqresearchersqmayqkeepqitemsqwithqdoubleqfactorqloadingsqasqlongqasq 
theqitemsqlogicallyqrelateqtoqbothqfactorsq(Coughlin,q1999,qp.q198).qq
q
q
4.2.6.5.  Application 
q
Weqcarriedqoutqaqfactorqanalysisqinqorderqtoqfindqhigherqcomponentsqthatqcouldqexplainq 
theqcorrelationqmatrixq(Tableq44,qavailableqinqpageq163)qandqdetermineqqualityqfactors.q 
Asq extractionq method,q weq usedq theq principalq componentsq methodq withq eigenvalues q
higherq thanq 1q andq Varimax rotationq withq Kaiser q normalizationq andq choseq toq excludeq 
missingqvaluesq listwise .qq
q
Twoqdistinctqfactorsqwereqfoundq(Figureq37,qTableq71,qandqTableq72).qTheqtwoqfactorsq 
explainq 73%q ofq totalq varianceq (Tableq 73).q Givenq theq extractedq numberq ofq factors,q theq 
eigenvaluesq wereq thenq recalculatedq basedq onq theq extractedq factorsq only.q Theq secondq 
panelq inq Tableq 73q displaysq theseq valuesq andq onlyq theq twoq factors.q Theq KaiserRMeyerR
Olkinq (KMO)q measureq ofq samplingq adequacyq testq (see,q forq instance,q Kaiser,q 1981)q
(Tableq 74)q returnedq aq valueq ofq 0.953,q which,q beingqgreaterq thanq 0.5,q meansq thatq aq 
satisfactoryq factorq analysisq wasq made.q Anotherq indicatorq ofq theq strengthq ofq theq 
relationshipqamongqvariablesqisqBartlett'sq(1937)qtestqofqsphericity,qwhichqisqusedqtoqtestq 
theq nullq hypothesisq thatq theq variablesq inq theq populationq correlationq matrixq areq 
uncorrelated.qTheqobservedqsignificanceqlevelqisq.000,qwhichqisqsmallqenoughqtoq rejectq 
theq hypothesisq andq allowq usq toq concludeq thatq theq strengthq ofq theq relationshipq amongq 
variablesq isq strongq andq theq factorq analysisq madeq isq satisfactoryq (Coughlinq &q Knight,q 
2003)q(Tableq74).q

4.2.6.6.  Limitations 
q
Althoughq weq paidq attentionq toq allq theq considerationsq thatq mustq beq attendedq whenq 
carryingqoutqaqfactorqanalysisq(asqpointedqoutqbyqChild,q1970,qpp.q152R154)qweqhaveqtoq 
assumeqtheqlimitationsqofqthisqprocedure,qtoqwhichqChildq(1970,qp.q8)qalerts:qq
q
R Weq didq notq doubleq orq trebleq checkq theq findingsq byq usingq differentq programsq 
(otherqthanqSPSS);q
R Labellingqfactorsqisqveryqsubjectiveqandqresearchersqtendqtoqseeqwhatqtheyqwishq 
toqsee,qandqmayqbeqtemptedqtoqfitqtheqfactorsqtoqtheirqhypotheses.qqq

4.2.7.  Do Quality Perceptions Depend on Who Pays the Bill? 
q
Weqwantedqtoqknowqifqtheqfactqthatqtheqtrainingqcourseqisqpaidqnotqbyqtheqtraineeqherself,q
butq byq theq companyq sheq worksq for,q madeq anyq difference,q especiallyq inq termsq ofq 
perceptionsq ofq quality.q Weq plottedq (Figureq 42)q global satisfaction ,q initial q andq final 
motivation ,q immediate q and  future utility ,q global quality perception ,q andq quality-price 
relation q forq bothq cases.q Theq simpleq analysisq ofq theq meanq ofq theq 15q variablesq ofq ourq 
surveyqaccordingqtoqwhoqhadqpaidqforqtheqcourseqshowedq(Tableq80)qthatqtheqmeansqofqallq 
variablesqareqalwaysqhigherqinqrespondentsqwhoqpaidqforqtheqcourseqthanqinqthoseqcasesq 
whereqtheqcourseqwasqpaidqbyqtheqcompanyqtheyqworkqfor.qq
q
Theseqtwoqinstrumentsq(Figureq42qandqTableq80)qgavequsqimportantqinsights:qq
q
R Allqvariablesqhaveqhigherqratingsqwhenqtheqcourseqisqpaidqbyqtheqtrainee;qq
R Initial motivation q hasq aq widerq distributionq whenq theq courseq isq paidq byq theq 
companyqtheqtraineeqworksqfor;qandq
R Surprisingly,q inq theqcaseq whereq theq traineesq doqnotq payq anythingq toq attendq theq 
course,q theyq haveq aq lowerq perceptionq onq quality-price relation ,q mostq probablyq 
dueqtoqaqlowerqqualityqperception.q
