4.2.8.  Motivation as a Quality Dimension 
q
4.2.8.1.  Why Look Deeper into Motivation? 
q
Althoughqmotivationqwasqnotqaqcentralqissueqinqourqresearch,qweqdecidedqtoqlookqdeeperq 
intoq it,q forq severalq reasons.q Onq oneq hand,q initial motivation q wasq includedq inq theq finalq 
modelq ofq linearq regressionq (pageq 178);q yet,q final  motivation q wasq leftq apartq fromq theq 
modelqinqtheqtwoqpartialqanalysesqweqmade,qandqwasqonlyqconsideredqinqtheqmodelqwithq 
theqcompleteqsample.qTheqfactorqanalysisqalsoqincludedqinitialqandq final motivation qinqtheq 
factorq relatedq toq attitudesq (pageq 189).q Onq theq otherq hand,q ifq qualityq isq fitness for use 
(Juran,q1951,qSectionq2R2),qthereqisqalwaysqanq end-in-view q(Dewey,q1939,qp.q34)qandqanq 
expectationqofquse,qwhichqexplainsqtheqrelationqofqqualityqwithqutility.qInqthisqscenario,q 
weqcanqhypothesizeqthatqtraineesqwillqbeqmoreqmotivatedqifqanq end-in-view qexists,qevenqifq 
itq isq aq longRtermq end.q Thisq allq suggestedq usq toq lookq deeperq intoq motivationq dataq toq 
understandq betterq theq roleq ofq motivationq inq theq processq ofq formationq ofq qualityq 
perception.q
q
q
4.2.8.2.  Initial and Final Motivation Measured in the End of the 
Course 
q
Inq theq satisfactionq surveyq thatq isq givenq toq traineesq atq theq endq ofq theq course,q weq askedq 
themqtoqrateqtheirqperceptionqofqtheirqmotivationqatqtheqbeginningqandqatqtheqendqofqtheq 
course.qThatqisqtoqsay,qtheyqwereqasked,qatqtheqendqofqtheqcourse,qnotqonlyqtoqrateqtheirq 
currentqmotivation,qbutqalsoqtheirqcurrentqperceptionqofqwhatqhadqbeenqtheirqmotivationqatq 
theqbeginningqofqtheqcourse.qWeqrealizeqthatqweqcouldqhaveqaskedqthemqatqtheqbeginningq 
ofqtheqcourseqtoqrateqtheirqmotivation,qandqthenqaskqthemqagainqatqtheqendqofqtheqcourse,q 
butq weq choseq notq toq doq itq thatq way.q Thisq way,q theq individualq wasq ableq toq rankq themq 
comparatively.qInqTableq83qweqcompareqtheqtwoqoptionsqweqhad.qWeqdecidedqtoquseqtheq 
secondqhypothesis.qThisqmeansqthatqtheqcollectionqofqdataqrelatingqtoq initial motivation q
wasq madeq retrospectively.q Thisq ex post fact q researchq methodologyq isq commonq inq 
situationsq whereq experimentsq areq notq possible,q areqethicallyq inappropriate,q orq involveq 
risksq ofq influencingq theq responses.q Manyq importantqinvestigationsq inq educationq areq ex 
post facto q designsq (L.q Cohenq et al .,q 2007,q p.q 267).q Medicalq cohortq studiesq andq 
sociologicalqstudiesqusuallyqareqalsoq ex post facto qstudies:qforqexample,qdoctorsqwillqnotq 
askqaqgroupqofqpatientsqtoqsmokeqmoreqjustqtoqtestqtheqimpactqofqmarginalqcigarsqinqtheq 
probabilityqofqcancer;qlikewise,qdriversqwillqnotqbeqaskedqtoqdrinkqanqextraqglassqofqwineq 
toqtestqifqtheyqhaveqmoreqcarqaccidents.qq
q
Ourqdecisionqtoquseqaqretrospectiveqmeasurementqofqinitial motivation qwasqbasedqonqtwoq 
motives:qq
q
R Weqwantedqtoqminimizeqtheqriskqofqinfluencingqtheqresponses:qifqweqhadqaskedq 
theqtraineeqaboutqherqmotivationqatqtheqbeginningqofqtheqcourse,qsheqwouldqhaveq 
toqrecallqthatqatqtheqendqofqtheqcourse,qwhenqsheqwouldqbeqfacedqwithqthisqsurvey.q 
Sheqwouldqbeqworriedqtoqrecallqwhatqhadqbeenqherqfirstqanswerqandqthatqwouldq 
influenceq herq finalq answer.q Weq cannotq beq sureq thatqtheq processq ofq retrievalq 
wouldq notq beq biasedq andq theq riskq ofq notq rememberingq theq initialq ratingq wasq aq 
strongqinfluenceqinqourqdecision;qq
R Askingq themq toq rateq bothq motivationsq atq theq sameq timeq allowsq respondentsq toq 
makeq aq comparativeq judgment:q ifq sheq ratesq final motivation q lowerq thanq initial

Ourqsampleqincludesqsurveysqthatqwereqansweredqbyqcustomersqwhoqhadqbeenqattendingq

professionalqtrainers.qThisqcourseqisqusuallyqmadeqinqaq100%qfaceRtoRface,qthreeqmonthsq 
durationqformat,qandqitqusuallyqtakesqatqleastq90qhoursqtoqbeqcompleted.qq
q
EVOLUI.COMq offersq thisq courseq inq aq bRlearning,q sevenq weeksq andq 114q hoursq formatq
thatq includesq onlyq sixq faceRtoRfaceq sessionsq thatq takeq placeq exclusivelyq onq Saturdays.q 
TheseqsessionsqarequsuallyqheldqatqFigueiraqdaqFozqorqLisbonq(althoughqEVOLUI.COMq 
hasqalreadyqheldqthemqinqotherqcitiesqlikeqAveiro,qÁgueda,qandqAlbergaria),qand,qinqotherq
cases,qatqtheqclient’sqofficesq(mostlyqinqLisbon).qq
q
Thisq courseq hasq aq moreq limitedq geographicalq potentialq whenq comparedq toq eRlearningq 
coursesq(asqtheqeRlearningqcoursesqatqEVOLUI.COMqhaveqregularqsalesqinq28qcountries),q

4.2.11.  Final Reflections 
q
Weq conductedq anq onlineq surveyq toq betterq understandqtheq perceptionsq onq qualityq inq eR
learningq courses.q Aq quantitativeq analysisq wasq carriedq outq onq 2630q answersq thatq wereq 
considered.qAllqtheqvariablesqunderqstudyqhadqaqnegativeqskewness,qasqexpected,qandqforq 
whichq Petersonq andq Wilsonq (1992,q quotedq inq Danaherq&q Haddrell,q 1996)q provideq 
reasonableqexplanationsq(pageq161).qImmediate qandq future utilities qareqhighlyqcorrelated,q
butq weq provedq theyq areq statisticallyq different,q andq thatq future utility q perceptionsq areq 
higherqthanq immediate utility .qThisqsuggestsqthatqtraineesqvalueqtheqcourseqnotqonlyqforq 
theq contributionq itq canq bringq toq theirq currentq jobqperformance,q butq alsoq forq theq 
hypotheticalq uses q theyq couldq haveq inq theq futureq forq havingq attendedqtheq course.q Bothq 
immediate qandq future utilities qareqhigherqinqfemaleqtraineesqthanqinqmales.qWomenqalsoq 
haveqhigherqperceptionsqofqquality,qmayqbeqbecauseqtheyqperceiveqhigherqutilityqinqtheq 
courses.qq
q
Accordingq toq theq regressionq analysis,q global satisfaction q andq future utility q areq theq 
variablesqthatqexplainqmostqofqquality.q Immediate utility qisqaqpoorqcontributorqtoqquality.q 
Thisq providesq evidenceq thatq qualityq isq aq moreq longRtermq attitudeq thanq aq shortRtermq 
attitudeq(CroninqJr.q&qTaylor,q1994;qOliver,q1981).qq
q
Theq techniqueq usedq forq dataq reductionq providedq threeq factorsq thatq explainq quality:q theq 
training process ,qtheq training attitudes ,qandqperceptionsqofq training utility .qThisqfactorq 
structureq wasq crossedq withq theq mostq usedq modelsq ofqtrainingq evaluation,q namelyq 
Kirkpatrick’sq (2006)q andq Holton  (1996;q Holtonq III,q Coco,q Lowe,q &q Dutsch,q 2006).q 
Theseq twoq modelsq areq focusedq inq theq evaluationq ofq trainingq coursesq fromq anq 
organizationalqpointqofqview:qtheyqemphasizeqtheqchangesqinqperformanceqandqtheqeffectsq 
ofq thatq changeq onq theq organizationalq results.q Fromqtheq trainee’sq pointq ofq view,q theseq 
modelsq mayq notq beq theq bestq fittingq conceptualq representations.q Ourq factorq structure,q 
whichqwasqdrawnqfromqaqsignificantqsampleqofqmainlyqresidentialqtrainees,qidentifiesqtheq 
mostq crucialq qualityq dimensionsq perceivedq byq theq traineeq –q andq notq byq herq company.q 
Traineesq mayq notq beq interestedq inq theq organizationalq impactq ofq theq coursesq theyq haveq 
attended,qbutqtheyqcertainlyqareqinterestedqinqtheqfuture utility qofqthatqcourse.qWeqbelieveq 
thatq thisq threeRfactorq structureq ofq qualityq dimensionsq shouldq beq furtherq investigated,q 
especiallyqifqtheqorganizationsqcontinueqtoqdelegateqtoqtheqtraineesqtheqresponsibilityqforq
choosingqtheirqprofessionalqdevelopmentqandqtraining.qqq
q
Evenq thoughq inq periodsq ofq economicalq andq politicalqinstabilityq companiesq tendq toq 
decreaseq evenq moreq theirq investmentsq inq training,q weq mustq acknowledgeq thatq theq 
delegationq onq theq traineeq ofq thatq responsibilityq isq moreq orq lessq independentq ofq theq 
economicalq cycleq andq ofq theq financialq situationq ofqtheq company.q Thatq delegationq isq 
consistentq withq theq currentq approachesq toq theq psychological contracts q (forq example,q 
Lesterq &q Kickul,q 2001),q whichq ruleq theq beliefsq concerningq theq obligationsq thatq existq 
betweenq theq employeeq andq theq organization,q asq weq discussq inq theq nextq section.q Thatq 
delegationqhasqanqimpactqonqqualityqperceptionsqandqoverallqtrainingqevaluation:q global 
satisfaction ,q initial q andq final motivation ,q future q andq immediate utility ,q quality 
perception ,qandq quality-price relation qareqstatisticallyqhigherqwhenqtheqcourseqisqpaidqbyq 
theq trainee.q Thisq suggestsq thatq theq psychologicalq contractq shouldq alsoq includeq theq 
delegationq ofq theq trainingq responsibility,q evenq thoughq itq isq notq clearq if,q fromq theq 
organization’sq pointq ofq view,q thatq wouldq beq better.q Inq otherq words,q whenq theq traineeq 
assumesqtheqpaymentqofqtheqcourse,qtheqcourseqreceivesqhigherqqualityqratings,qwhichqisq 
theqbestqscenarioqforqtheqtrainingqcompany,qbutqnotqnecessarilyqtheqbestqforqtheqcompanyq 
theqtraineeqworksqfor,qsinceqitqdoesqnotqguaranteeqtheqmaximizationqofqperformanceqandq

4.3.5.2.  Restoration and Enhancement (question 1) 
 
Withinq operant conditioning ,q theq twoq typesq ofq operantq conditioningq –qrestoration q andq 
enhancement qwereqstudied.q73,51%qofqtheqrespondentsqdecidedqtoqattendqtheqcourseqtoq 
increase their skills ,qratherqthanqtoq suppress any current need ,qwhichqmeansqthatqthereq 
wasqnoqspecificqcurrent,qorqurgent,qtrainingqneed.qOnlyq26,49%qmentionedqthatqtheyqhadq 
decidedqtoqattendqtheqcourseqtoqcopeqwithqcurrentqdifficulties,qtoqfindqanotherqjob,qorqtoq 
getq solutionsq toq aq specificq problem.q Thisq suggestsqthatq thereq mayq beq noq concreteq andq 
immediate utility qbut,qrather,qaqsearchqforqnewqskills,qaqdesireqtoqknowqmoreqorqperformq 
better,qwhich,qinqturn,qmayqbequsefulqinqtheqfutureq(Tableq127qandqFigureq55).q
q q
Thisq leadsq usq toq concludeq thatq positive reinforcement ,q whichq isq aq moreq longRtermq
strategyq thatq theqrestorative q tactics,q isq theq mainq objectiveq ofq theq trainees.q Trainingq isq 
moreq relatedq toq futureq possibleq utilityq (as,q forq instance,q theq needq toq copeq withq aq moreq 
defyingq job),q thanq toq immediateq useq inq theq currentqprofessionalq contextq andq currentq 
specificqperformanceqproblems.qThisqmotivationalqprofileqsuggestsqthatqfuturequseqwasqaq 
determinantq buyingq factor,q whichq isq closeq toq theq supremacyq ofq futureq utilityq overq 
immediatequtility,qasqseenqpreviouslyqinqtheqotherqstudy.q

Figureq56quntilqFigureq59).qThisqlongRtermqperspectiveqconflictsqwithqsomeqtendenciesqofq 
theqlabourqmarket,qsuchqasqprecariousqcontracts.qOneqmightqaskqwhyqbotherqtoqinvestqinq 
theqfutureqskillsqofqanqemployeeqifqsheqprobablyqwillqnotqbeqworkingqforqtheqcompany.qq
Thisq apparentq conflictq mayq reflectq theq recentq ideasq ofq psychological contracts q (forq 
example,qLesterq&qKickul,q2001),whichqruleqtheqbeliefsqconcerningqtheqobligationsqthatq 
existqbetweenqtheqemployeeqandqtheqorganization.qq
q
Inq theq past,q theq relationq employerRemployeeq wasq aq longRtermq contract.q Currently,q 
employmentqisqdominatedqbyqshortRtermqcontractsqforqhighlyRskilledqprofessionals,qwhoq
areq dismissedq whenq theirq specificq skillsq areq noq longerq requiredq byq theq organizationq 
(Dharmawardena,q 2009).q Inq thisq newq psychologicalq contract,q noq promisesq ofq futureq 
careerqandqcorporateqcareqforqtheqfutureqofqtheqemployeeqareqcompensatedqbyqshortRtermq 
benefits,qnamelyqtrainingqcoursesqthatqareqnotqofqparticularqinterestqtoqtheqcompanyqbutq 
usefulq forq theq futureq careerq ofq theq employee,q probablyq withinq anotherq company.q 
Preparingqtheqemployeeqtoqaqcareerqsheqmayqhaveqwhenqsheqleavesqtheqcompanyqisqaqwayq 
ofq relievingq theq pressureq whenq theq timeq comesq toq askq herq toq leave.q Yet,q twoq 
interpretationsq canq beq made:q theq firstq isq thatq eRlearningq coursesq promotedq orq paidq byq 
companiesqareqnotqrelatedqtoqimmediateqperformanceqneeds,qasqweqhaveqjustqdiscussed.q 
Theqsecond,qisqthatqtraineesqperceiveqthatqtheyqdoqnotqhaveqperformanceqhandicapsqandq

careqandqinterest.qqq

4.3.8.  Final Reflections 
q
Oneq ofq theq mostq permanentq questionsq weq hadq alongq ourq workq wasq aboutq theq kindq ofq 
relationq thatq existsq betweenq qualityq andq valueq perceptions.q Previously,q weq hadq relatedq 
qualityqtoqthreeqfactors:qtheqtrainee'sqattitudes,qtheqtrainingqprocess,qandqtrainingqutility,q 
whichq includedq immediateq andq future utility q perceptions,q butq theq relationq betweenq 
qualityqandqvalueqperceptionqwasqnotqclear.qq
q
Thisqsurveyqhelpsqusqdiscardqsomeqapproachesqtoqtheqvalueqofqaqtrainingqcourse,qnamelyq 
thoseqthatqrelateqvalueqwithqtheqpriceqpaidqandqsomeqtypesqofqvalueqthatqareqcommonlyq 
consideredq byq theq literature.q Valueq perceptionsq areq mainlyq self-oriented ,q active ,q andq 
extrinsic (Holbrook,q 1999c,q p.q 12).q Theq perceptionq ofq valueq inq eRlearningq coursesq isq
relatedqtoqthequtilityqofqtheqcourse,qespeciallyqinqtheqcasesqwhereqtheqregistrationqisqpaidq 
byq theq company.q Theq perceptionsq ofq utilityq areq alsoq presentq inq theq trainee'sq attitudes,q 
bothqwhenqtheqcompanyqprovidesqthemqtrainingqprogramsqandqwhenqitqdoesqnot:q
q
R Immediate utility ,qonqoneqhand,qisqaqmotivatingqfactorqwhenqtheqtraineeqreceivesq 
training;qq
R Future utility ,qonqtheqotherqhand,qisqconsideredqanqimportantq discomfort factor qinq 
situationsqofqabsenceqofqtraining.q
q
Whatq motivatesq traineesq toq theq courseq isq theq anticipation of some consequences ,q anq 
operantqconditioningqreaction,qwhichqsuggestsqthatqanqendRinRviewq(Dewey,q1939,qp.q39)q
isqpresent.qThoseqconsequencesqareqnotqrelatedqtoqtheq restoration qofqlostqskills,qbutqratherq 
toqimprovement and enhancement qofqhighlyqrankedqskills.qThisqsuggestsqthatqtheqcoursesq 
areq carefullyq planned,q havingq inq mindq strategicq andq longRtermq objectives,q ratherq thanq 
beingq shortRtermq responsesq toq currentq problemsq orq difficulties.q Future,q ratherq thanq 
immediate,qutilityqis,qtherefore,qmoreqemphasized.qThisqisqalsoqtrueqinqsituationsqwhereq 
theq courseq wasq paidq forq byq theq company,q andq weq believeq thisq isq relatedq toq currentq 
tendenciesq ofq theq psychologicalq contracts,q whereq companiesq discardq longRtermq

q
243 
obligationsq towardsq employeesq byq compensatingq themqwithq longRtermq skillsq thatq theyq 
canquseqelsewhere.qInqthisqsense,qtheqvalueqofqaqcourseqcouldqbeqregardedqasqtheqpromise q
(Levitt,q1981,qp.q94)qofqaqfutureqcareer,qinqexchangeqforqaqshortRtermqlabourqrelation.qq
q
Evenq so,q weq mustq recognizeq theq limitationsq ofq thisqstudy.q Traineesq suggestq thatq theyq 
attendedqtheqcoursesqtoqimproveqtheirqskills,qratherqthanqtoqsuppressqcurrentqperformanceq 
problems.qYet,qthisqcouldqnotqbeqconfirmed.qTraineesqcanqperceiveqthatqtheyqdoqnotqhaveq 
performanceqhandicapsqwhileqtheirqsupervisorsqmayqthinkqotherwise.qMoreover,qtraineesq 
mayqbelieveqthatqtheyqareqbeingqofferedqtheqcourseqbecauseqtheqcompanyqcaresqforqthem,q 
which,qinqturn,qmayqlookqlikeqtheqcompanyqwishesqtoqkeepqthemqindefinitely.qAnotherq 
limitationqofqourqanalysisqisqthatqweqareqnotqlookingqtoqwhoqisqonqtheqotherqsideqofqtheq 
barrierqRqtheqcompany,qandqtheqrealqmotivesqwhyqtheqcompanyqprovidesqtrainingqcoursesq 
toq theseq trainees.q Weq believeq thatq theq consequencesq ofq theq psychological contract q inq

perceptionsq areq moreq relatedq toq immediate utility q or,q rather,q toq future utility .q Jobq 
opportunities,qforqinstance,qcanqbeqconsideredqasqmuchqinqtheqshortqasqinqtheqlongRterm.qq

Chapter 5  
Conclusions 
q
Ourq empiricalq researchq aimedq atq discoveringq whatq traineesq thinkq theq qualityq ofq eR
learningq isq andq whatq theq primaryqdimensionsq ofqqualityq ofqeRlearningq coursesq are.qWeq 
startedqwithqanqexploratoryqqualitativeqstudyqofqmessagesqpostedqinqforumsqofqeRlearningq 
coursesq ofq EVOLUI.COM,q aq Portugueseq providerq ofq asynchronousq eRlearningq forq 
professionalqtraining.qMostqreferencesqmadeqtoqtheqqualityqofqeRlearningqwereqrelatedqtoq 
theqtrainingqprocess,qnamelyqtheqtrainingqcontents,qtheqtrainers,qtheqsupportingqstaff,qandq 
theq colleagues.q Weq alsoq foundq referencesq toq attitudesq suchq asq expectations,q trainingq 
needs,q andq objectives,q asq wellq asq referencesq toq trainingq results.q Regardingq trainingq 
results,q theq traineesq referredq toq severalq relatedq ideas,q suchq asq theq changesq orq 
transformationsqthatqtheqcourseqenabled.qThequsesqandqtheqapplicabilityqofqtheqcourse,qasq 
wellqasqitsqutility,qwereqsoqexpressiveqthatqutilityqwasqconsideredqaqrelevantqconceptqtoqbeq 
furtherqexplored.qInqtheqfollowingqstudy,qwequsedqanqonlineqsurveyqwithq15Ritemsqinqaq1R
10qLikertqscaleqthatqwasqcarriedqoutqatqtheqendqofqtheqcoursesqandqreceivedq2630qanswers.q 
Thisqsurveyqwasqintendedqtoqidentifyqtheqvariablesqthatqexplainedqtheqvariabilityqofqtheq 
perceptions of quality q andq theq mostq significantq factors of quality .q Itq wasq alsoq usedq toq 
identifyqdifferencesqinqtermsqofq perceptions of qutility qandqtheqinfluenceqofqtheqdurationq 
andqtheqtypeqofqtheqcourseqinqtheq perception of quality .qInqtheqrangeqofqcoursesqofferedqbyq 
EVOLUI.COMqandqforqtheqsampleqanalyzed,qalthoughq immediate qandq future utilityqwereq 
highlyqratedqandqcorrelated,qtheqperceptionqofq future utility qwasqstatisticallyqhigherqthanq 
theqperceptionqofq immediate utility .qThisqsuggestedqthatqtheqcoursesqareqvaluedqnotqonlyq 
forqtheqcontributionqtheyqcanqbringqtoqimmediateqperformanceqorqimmediateqobjectives,q 
butqalso,qandqmainly,qforq future uses qthatqtheyqmightqenableqinqtheqfuture.qTheqregressionq 
thatqwasqadjustedqhasqshownqthatq global satisfaction andq future utility wereqtheqvariablesq 
thatq explainedq mostq ofq theq perception of quality ,q whileq immediate utility q wasq aq poorq 
contributorq toq quality .q Thisq confirmsqthatq quality q isq aq longRtermqattitude,qasqitqasq beenq 
claimedqbyqCroninqandqTaylorq(1994)qandqOliverq(1981),qratherqthanqaqshortRtermqone.qq
q
Usingq factorq analysis,q weq extractedq threeq factorsq thatq explainq quality:q theq training 
process ,qtheq training attitudes ,qandqtheqperceptionsqofq training utility .qThisqsuggestsqthatq 
allqtheqconceptsqthatqareqassociatedqtoqqualityqcanqbeqreducedqandqclassifiedqintoqoneqofq 
theseqthreeqfactorsqofqquality.qThisqisqaqcomplexqvariableqthatqneedsqtoqbeqsimplifiedqtoq 
beqbetterqunderstood.qTheqresultsqofqtheqfactorqanalysisqareqconsistentqwithqtheqqualitativeq 
studyqthatqweqhadqdoneqpreviously.qYet,qtheqfactorqanalysisqemphasizesqtheqimportanceq 
ofq theq training attitudes q inq theq perception of quality ,q namelyqglobal satisfaction ,q 
motivation ,qandqtheqperceptionqofq fulfilment of expectations qandq of training objectives .q 
Besidesqsatisfaction,qt raining attitudes qareqnotqusuallyqincludedqinqtheqmodelsqofqqualityq
ofq eRlearningq orq inq theq modelsq ofq trainingq evaluation.q Yet,q ourq studyq revealedq thatq 
motivationqisqaqrelevantqvariableqthatqmustqbeqtakenqintoqconsiderationqwhenqevaluatingq 
theq perceptions of quality .q Specifically,q final motivation ,q whichq isq aq variableq thatq isq 
closerqtoqbehaviouralqchanges,qisqanqimportantqvariableqthatqexplainsq global satisfaction ,q 
whichqinqturn,qisqtheqmostqrelevantqvariableqtoqexplainq quality .qTheqthreeRfactorqstructureq 
wasqcrossedqwithqtheqmostqusedqmodelsqofqtrainingqevaluationqwhereqtheqattitudesqofqtheq 
trainees,qbesidesqsatisfaction,qareqnotqincluded.qTheseqmodelsqfollowqtheqpointqofqviewqofq 
theq organizationq theq traineeq worksq for,q andq mayq notq beq theq mostq adequateq forq theq 
evaluationq ofq qualityq fromq theq pointq ofq viewq ofq theq trainees.q Theqtraineesq mayq notq beq 
interestedq inq someq traditionalq levelsq ofq trainingq evaluation,q suchq asq organizationalq

AmongqtheqtraineesqofqEVOLUI.COMqthatqwereqinquired,qweqfoundqthatqwheneverqtheq

thatqweqhadqfoundqpreviously.qYet,qtheqdecisionqtoqattendqaqcourseqtoqsuppressqcurrentq 
needsq orq solveq aq currentq problemq isq moreq commonq inqscenariosq ofq selfRinitiativeq andq 
personalqfinancialqsacrifice,qi.e.,qtheqtraineeqhadqtheqideaqtoqattendqtheqcourseqandqpaidqforq 
it.qOnqoneqhand,qtheqfinancialqsacrificeqmadeqbyqtheqtraineeqisqeasilyqacceptedqwhenqsheq 
perceivesqurgentqtrainingqneeds,qasqtheqbenefitsqareqperceivedqasqimmediate.qOnqtheqotherq

theqfuture,qas,qmostqprobably,qtheqtraineesqwillqnotqworkqforqthatqcompanyqinqtheqlongR
run.qYet,qthisqisqconsistentqwithqtheq psychological contract q(D.qM.qRousseau,q1989).qInq

betweenq quality qandq value .qq
q
Basedqonqaqlargeqsampleqandqonqmultipleqandqrelatedqinstrumentsqandqresearchqdesigns,q 
ourqstudyqprovidesqtheqinitialqcontributionqtoqaqfutureqmodelqofqqualityqinqeRlearningqinq 
theq residentialq marketq andq aq simplifiedq structureq ofq factorsq ofq aq complexq constructq –q
quality .qItqalsoqrevealedqtheqroleqofq utility qasqaqrelevantqdimensionqofq quality qandqasqtheq 
commonqlinkqbetweenq quality qandq value qofqanqeRlearningqcourse.qqq
q

PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
q
q
248 
Yet,qitqhasqsomeqlimitationsqthatqweqmustqacknowledge.qTheqfirstqisqtheqnatureqofqaqcaseq 
study,qwhichqdoesqnotqletqusqmakeqanyqgeneralizationsqofqtheqfindings.qOurqconclusionsq 
holdq justq forq theq caseq ofq EVOLUI.COMq andq forq theq concreteq setq ofq dataq thatq weq 
analyzed,q andq mayq evenq notq holdq trueq forq aq differentq sampleq withinq EVOLUI.COM.q
Therefore,qgeneralizedqconclusionsqcannotqbeqmade.qSecond,qqualitativeqstudiesqhave,qinq 
general,q samplingq issuesq andq includeq aq significantqdegreeq ofq participationq ofq theq 
researcherqwho,qdespiteqherqbestqintentions,qmayqconductqaqbiasedqcollectionqofqdataqandq 
influenceqtheqresponses.qMoreover,qourqfirstqquantitativeqstudy,qwhichqwasqbasedqonqtheq 
majorqconclusionsqofqtheqpreviousqqualitativeqstudy,qwasqaqsingleRitemqsurvey,qandqweq 
acknowledgeqthatqmultipleRitemqsurveysqareqmoreqreliableqandqprovideqhigherqvalidity.q 
Inqaddition,qseveralqtraineesqansweredqtheqthreeqstudiesqweqhaveqmade,qwhichqsuggestsq 
thatqsomeqsaturationqmayqhaveqoccurred.qThird,qthereqareqsomeqconclusionsqtoqwhichqweq 
cannotq provideq reasonedq orq dataRsupportedq explanations,q butq justq formulateq logicalq 
hypotheses.qForqinstance,qweqconcludedqthatqperceptionsqofq immediate qandq future utility ,q 
asqwellqasqtheqoverallq perception of quality ,qareqhigherqinqfemaleqtraineesqthanqinqmales,q 
althoughqtheyqhaveqaqperceptionqofq quality-price relation qsimilarqtoqmaleqtrainees,qbutq 
weqhadqnoqmeansqtoqfindqoutqwhyqthisqgenderqdifferenceqexists.qTheqcaseqofqtheqtrainer’sq 
initialq pedagogicalqcertificationq courseq isq anotherq example,q sinceq weq cannotq tellq ifq theq 
differencesq thatq weq foundq areq dueq toq theq professionalq certificationq thatq itq providesq orq 
becauseqitqisqdoneqinqaqbRlearningqformat.qTheqlastqlimitationqisqrelatedqtoqtheqsubjectsq 
thatq weq inquired:q theq trainees.q Traineesq suggestq thatq theyq doq notq haveq currentq 
performanceqproblemsqandq thatq theyqattendedq theqcoursesq toq improveq theirq skills.qYet,q 
thisq informationq wasq notq crossedq withq theq opinionq ofq theirq hierarchicalq superiorsq orq 
supervisors,q whoq mayq haveq aq differentq opinion.q Moreover,q traineesq mayq beq tooq 
optimisticqregardingqtheirqabilityqtoqretrieve,qinqtheqfuture,qwhatqtheyqhaveqlearntqinqtheq 
course.qAlsoqtheyqmayqhaveqprovidedqaqtooqoptimisticqevaluationqofq future utility ,qandq 
therefore,qofq quality .q
q
Weq suggestq thatq trainingq companiesq shouldq includeq inq theirq reactionq surveysq otherq 
variables,q suchq asq final motivation q andq perceptionsq ofq immediate andq future utility .q 
Theseqvariablesqexpressqexpectations,qratherqthanqjustqaffectiveqreactions,qandqareqmoreq 
behaviourRorientedqthanqsatisfaction.qTheyqcanqalsoqbequsedqtoqmeasureqtheqexpectedquseq
and,qtherefore,qcanqbequsedqtoqevaluateqtheqfitness for use q(Juran,q1951,qsectionq2R2),qi.e.,q
theq perceived quality .qWeqalsoqsuggestqthatqtheqmodelsqofqtrainingqevaluationqshouldqbeq 
adaptedqtoqtheqpointqofqviewqofqtheqtrainee,qratherqthanqincludeqthoseqofqtheqcompany.q 
Thisq wouldq allowq trainingq companiesq thatq workq withqtheq residentialq marketq toq haveq aq 
betterqframeworkqtoqevaluateqtheqcoursesqtheyqofferqandqtheirqquality.qq
q
Basedqonqourqconclusions,qthereqareqseveralqfutureqworksqthatqcanqbeqdone.qTheqthreeR
factorqstructureqofqqualityqfactorsqthatqwasqfoundqshouldqbeqfurtherqinvestigated,qinqorderq 
toqprovideqmoreqadequateqmodelsqofqtrainingqandqqualityqevaluationqtoqthoseqcompaniesq 
thatq offerq eRlearningq coursesq toq theq residentialq market.q Thoseq modelsq wouldq alsoq beq 
usefulq toq companiesq thatq useq eRlearningq coursesq asqaq benefitq includedq inq theq 
psychological contracts.q Anotherq suggestionq isq relatedq toq theq transformationq ofq 
expectationsqofqutilityqintoqeffectivequse:qfirst,qtheqdeadlineqofqanqimmediatequseq–qtheq 
momentqinqtimeqwhenqitqbecomesqaqfuturequse,qshouldqbeqdefined,qasqwellqasqtheqmomentq 
inqtimeqwhenqtheqperceivedqutilityqbecomesqeffectivequse,qandqtheqpossibleqbarriersqtoqtheq 
retrievalq processq orq effectiveq use,q shouldq beq identified.q Regardingq theq trainer’sq initialq 
pedagogicalqcertificationq course,qasq weq wereq notq ableqtoqfindq whatqjustifiesq theq higherq 
utility qandq perception of quality ,qweqbelieveqthatqcomparativeqstudiesqthatqincludedqotherq 
trainingq formatsq (namelyq faceRtoRface,q insteadq ofq theq bRlearningq solution)q andq traineesq 

PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
249 
withqotherqattitudinalqprofilesq(forqexample,qtraineesqofqfundedqcourses)qcouldqbeqhelpfulq 
andqprovideqrelevantqinsightsqtoqtheqstudyqofqoneqofqtheqmostqpopularqtrainingqcoursesqinq 
Portugal.qTheqrelationqandqtheqdifferencesqbetweenqquality qandq value qcouldqalsoqbeqtheq 
objectq ofq futureq work.q Namely,q severalq questionsq shouldq beq addressed:q Isq valueq aq 
shorterRtermqattitude?qIsqvalueqmoreqthanqaqconviction,qratherqthanqanqexperienceRbasedq 
attitude?q Areq traineesq moreq interestedq inq theq value q ofq aq courseq andq companiesq moreq 
interestedq inq theq quality q ofq theq course?q q Doesq qualityq includeq riskq andq uncertaintyq asq 
valueqdoes?qFinally,qtheqinfluenceqandqtheqconsequencesqofqtheq psychological contract qinq 
theqtrainingqdecisionsqshouldqbeqfurtherqanalysed.qq

Appendix 2: Characteristics of Services  
 
1.  Defining Services 
q
WeqcannotqstudyqdeeplyqtheqqualityqofqeRlearningqservicesqwithoutqlookingqatqwhatqtheq 
literatureqmeansqbyqserviceqandqwhatqareqtheqcharacteristicsqofqservicesqandqtheirqimpactq 
onqquality.qTheqmainqreasonqtoqdoqthisqisqthatqservicesq“areqRqinqtheqextremeq–qdifferentq 
fromqgoods”q(Schneiderq&qWhite,q2004,qp.q4).qAlthoughqserviceqcompanies,qinqgeneral,q 
areqcloserqtoqcustomersqthanqproductqcompanies,qandqhaveqanqeasierqjobqassessingq fitness 
for use ,q whichq mayq helpq themq deliverq qualityq (Juran,q 1951,q p.q 473),q theq qualityq ofq 
servicesq isq moreq difficultq forq theq consumerq toq evaluateq thanq theq qualityq ofq goods.q Inq 
addition,qqualityqevaluationsqareqnotqtoqbeqfoundqsolelyqonqtheq outcome qofqaqserviceqbutq 
alsoqinvolveqevaluationsqofqtheq process qofqserviceq delivery  (Grönroos,q1990a) .qq
q
Servicesqarequsuallyqdefinedqinqanqambiguousqandqvagueqway:qq
q
R Aqserviceqisq“workqperformedqforqsomeoneqelse”qandqaqserviceqcompanyqisq“anq 
organizedq systemq ofqspecialq skillsqandq facilities”qthatq sellsq theqbenefitsqofq thisq 
systemqtoqitsqclientsq(Juranq&qBinghamqJr.,q1951,qp.q472);q
R Aqserviceqisq“anyqactivityqorqbenefitqthatqoneqpartyqcanqofferqtoqanotherqwhichqisq 
essentiallyqintangibleqandqdoesqnotqresultqinqtheqownershipqofqanything”q(Kotlerq 
et al. ,q1996,qpp.q588,q935);q
R “Servicesqareqperformancesqratherqthanqobjects”q(Parasuramanq et al .,q1985);qq
R “Servicesqareqdeeds,qprocesses,qandqperformances”q(Zeithamlq et al .,q2006,qp.q4).qqqqq
q
2.  Services Characteristics 
q
Servicesqareqdistributedqinqaqhierarchicalqnetworkqandqnotqrandomlyqdistributedqwithinq 
theq spatialReconomicq landscape.q Lamprechtq (1994,q pp.q 61R62)q gatheredq severalq spatialq 
studiesqandqidentifiedqthreeqbasicqconcepts:q threshold ,q range ,qandq order :qq
q
R Threshold q isq theq minimumq amountq ofq salesq neededq perq timeq periodq toq bringq aq 
firmq intoq existenceq andq keepq itq inq business;q itq isqtheq minimumq marketq thatq isq 
neededqtoqbringqtheqcompanyqintoqexistenceqandqtoqkeepqitqgoing;qq
R Theq range q isq theq averageq maximumq distanceq peopleq willq goq toqpurchaseq it.q 
Lamprechtq exemplifiesq theq rangeq characteristicq quotingq Abler,q Adams,q andq 
Gouldq(1972,qpp.q364R365)qwhoqclaimqthatqtheqrangeqforqaqloafqofqbreadqisqshorterq 
thanqthatqforqaqgoldqbracelet;q
R Theq order q isq aq directq functionq ofq itsq threshold.q Expensiveq andq infrequentlyq 
purchasedqgoodsqorqservicesq(cars,qjewellery,qorqopenRheartqsurgery)qoftenqhaveq 
highqthresholdqandqareqconsideredqhighRorderqgoods.qq
q
Servicesq canq alsoq beq analyzedq inq termsq ofq theirq search ,q experience,q orq credence 
propertiesq(Bloomq&qPailin,q1995;qDarbyq&qKarni,q1973;qNelson,q1974).qTheyqcanqholdq 
search properties q (attributesq whichq consumersq canq determineq priorq toq purchasingq aq 
product),q experience properties q(attributesqthatqcanqonlyqbeqdiscernedqafterqpurchaseqorq 
duringq consumption)q andq credence q propertiesq (attributesq thatq theq consumersq mayq findq 
impossibleq toq evaluateq evenq afterq purchaseq andq consumption,q asq appendectomiesq orq 
brakeqreliningsqonqautomobiles).qMostqservicesqcontainqfewq search qproperties,qwhichqareq

easierqtoqevaluate,qandqareqhighqinq experience qandq credence qproperties,qwhich,qinqturn,q
makesqtheirqqualityqassessmentqmoreqdifficultqtoqevaluateqtheqqualityqofqgoodsq(Zeithaml,q 
1981).q Consumersq typicallyq relyq onq experience properties q whenq evaluatingq serviceq

2.2.   Service Inseparability and Perishability 
q
Serviceq inseparabilityq meansq thatq servicesq cannotq beq separatedq fromq theirq providers.q 
Thatq isq toq sayq thatq theyq cannotq beq produced,q thenq stored,q laterq sold,q andq stillq laterq 
consumed.qServicesqareqfirstqsold,qthenqproducedqandqconsumedqatqtheqsameqtime,qandqinq 
theqsameqplaceq(Kotlerq et al .,q1996,qp.q589).qTheqfactqthatqproductionqandqconsumptionq 
cannotqbeqseparatedqandqareqsimultaneousqposesqadditionalqproblems:qfirst,qnoqqualityR
controlqchecksqcanqbeqdoneqbetweenqproductionqandqconsumption,qtherefore,qnoqsecondq 
changesqareqgivenqtoqreRdoneqtheqserviceqafterqcheckingqforqdefects.qSecond,qcompaniesq 
mustq striveq toq ensureq that,q whenq theq serviceq isq produced,q theq maximumq numberq ofq 
peopleqareqavailableqtoqconsumeqitq(Schneiderq&qWhite,q2004,qp.q7),qsinceqitqcannotqbeq 
inventoriedqforqlaterquse.qForqexample,qaq“seat”qnotqsoldqforqaqspecificqeditionqofqanqeR
learningq courseq willq neverq beq ableq toq beq soldq again.q Usingq totalq productionq capacity,q 
althoughqitqmaximizesqprofitability,qmayqinjureqdedicationqtoqcustomers,qpersonalization,q 
specialq attention,qandqevenq customerq comfortq (forq instance,q regardingq airlineq seats,qallq 
customersqwouldqpreferqtoqhaveqtheqseatqnextqtoqthemqavailableqandqnotqtaken).qAtqlast,q 
anqadditionalqdifficultyqisqdueqtoqtheqfactqthat,qwhenqdemandqrises,qincreasedqplanningq 
andqimprovementsqinqproductivityqareqrequiredqasqdemandqpeaksqcanqleadqtoqunfulfilledq 
supplyqandqunhappyqcustomers.qq
q
Serviceq perishabilityq meansq thatq servicesq cannotq beq storedq forq laterq saleq orq useq andq 
cannotqbeqreturnedqandqresoldq(forqexample,qaqbadqhaircutqcannotqbeqreturnedqandqresoldq 
toq anotherq customer).q Thisq perishabilityq isq notq aq problemq whenq demandq isq steady.q 
Severalqstrategies,qasqpriceqdifferentiation,qcomplementaryqservicesqofferedqduringqpeakq 
times,q andq reservationq systems,q onq theq sideq ofq demand,q andq partRtimeq employees,q 
reschedulingqnonRessentialqtaskqforqpeakqperiods,qandqevenqshiftingqtasksqtoqconsumersq 
(forq example,q theq registrationq application),q onq theq supplyq side,q mustq beq consideredq toq 
dealqwithqvariableqdemandq(Kotlerq et al. ,q1996,qpp.q591R592).q
q
q
2.3.   Variability/Heterogeneity 
q
Serviceqvariabilityqmeansqthatqtheqqualityqofqservicesqdependsqonqwhoqprovidesqthem,qasq 
wellqasqwhen,qwhere,qandqhowqtheyqareqprovidedq(Kotlerq et al. ,q1996,qp.q590).qServicesq 
areq heterogeneousq becauseq theirq performanceq oftenq variesq fromq producerq toq producer,q 
fromq customerq toq customer,q andq fromq dayq toq dayq (Parasuraman  et al. ,q 1985).q
Consistencyqofqpersonnelqbehaviourqandquniformqqualityqisqdifficultqtoqobtainq(Boomsq&q 
Bitner,q1981)qandqensuringqconsistencyqofqserviceqisqchallengingq(Zeithaml  et al. ,q2006,q 
p.q23).qDifferentqserviceqpersonnelqmayqperformqtheqserviceqinqdifferentqways.qTheqsameq 
personq canq haveq externalq factorsq thatq influenceq theq wayq thatq sheq performancesq theq 
service.q Moreover,q theq sameq customerq mayq presentq differentq setsq ofq demands,q 
expectations,q andq desiresq toq whichq theq serviceq personnelq mustq adaptq (Schneiderq &q 
White,q2004,qp.q8).qAsqoneqpersonqcanqgoqtoqaqrestaurantqtoqenjoyqaqloudqbirthdayqpartyq 
andq alsoq goq toq theq sameq restaurantq inq searchq forq aqquietq evening,q sheq canq enrolq inq aq 
learningq programq forq differentq reasonsq andq motivationsq (Boekaerts,q 2002;q Russellq 
Associates,q2006).q
q
Serviceq productq andq deliveryq frequentlyq involvesq theq interactionq ofq bothq serviceq 
personnelq andqcustomers,q andq bothq affectq theq serviceq outcome.q Theq presenceq ofq otherq 
customersq andq theirq behaviourq canq determineq theq serviceq deliveredq (forq example,q aq 
crowdqinqaqrestaurant).qControlqoverqtheqserviceqisqalsoqlowqwhenqconsumerqparticipationq

1.  Conceptualizing and Measuring Expectations 
 
Customers’qexpectationsqplayqaqvitalqroleqinqqualityqassessments.qCustomers’qassessmentq 
ofq serviceq qualityq isq madeq byq comparingq whatq theyq wantq orq expect withq whatq theyq 
perceiveq theyq areq getting .q Inq otherq words,q inq evaluatingq theq qualityq ofq theqservice,q 
consumersqcompareqtheqserviceqtheyqexpectqwithqperceptionsqofqtheqserviceqtheyqreceiveq 
(Parasuramanq et al .,q 1985).q Qualityq perceptionsq involveq aq comparisonqofqexpectationsq 
withq performance,q andq qualityq evaluationq isq aq measureq ofq howq wellq theq serviceq levelq 
deliveredq matchesq customerq expectations.q Thisq suggestsq that,q toq earnq aq reputationq forq 
qualityq service,q companiesq mustq consistentlyq performq atq levelsq customersq perceiveq asq 
meetingqorqsurpassingqtheirqexpectationsq(Berryq&qParasuraman,q1991,qp.q57).q
q
Theq termq expectations, asq aq comparisonq standard,q isq commonlyq usedq inq twoq differentq 
waysq(Berryq&qParasuraman,q1991,qp.q57):q
q
R Whatqtheqcustomersqbelieveq will occur qinqaqserviceqencounterq(predictions);q
R Andqwhatqcustomersq want to occur q(desires).qq
q
Serviceqquality,qasqperceivedqbyqconsumers,qstemsqfromqaqcomparisonqofqwhatqtheyqfeelq 
serviceq companiesq shouldq offerq Rq theirq expectationsq Rq withq theirq perceptionsq ofq theq 
performanceq ofq companiesq providingq theq service.q Expectedq serviceq (Figureq 68)q isq aq 
criticalq componentq ofq perceivedq serviceq qualityq andq isq theq resultq ofq wordRofq mouth,q 
personalq needs,q pastq experiences,q andq externalq communicationsq (Parasuraman  et al. ,q 
1985)q(Figureq68).qq
q
Companiesqfaceqtheqchallengeqofqattemptingqtoqsatisfyqtheirqcustomerqrequirementsqevenq 
whenqoftenqmostqcustomersqarequnableqtoqclearlyqexplainqtheqnatureqofqtheirqneedsqandq 
statingq themq (Sittig,q 1963,q 1964).q Someq needsq areq disguised,q orq evenq unknownq toq theq 
customerq atq theq timeq ofq purchase,q andq theseq needsq oftenq leadq theq customerq toq useq theq 
productqinqaqmannerqdifferentqfromqthatqintendedqbyqtheqsupplierq(Juranq&qGryna,q1993,q 
p.q243).q
q
Thereqareqfourq typesq ofqexpectationsq (Schneiderq &q White,q 2004,q pp.q 41R42),qeachq oneq 
withqaqdifferentqmeaningqandqobjectqofqattention:qq
q
R Predictive :q Howq anq organizationq will q performq orq whatq customersq believeq 
(predict)qwillqactuallyqhappenqinqtheirqencounter;qq
R Normative :q Whatq peopleq believeq should q happenq inq anq organizationq whetherq orq 
notqtheyqbelieveqthatqitqactuallyqwill;qq
R Excellence :q Howq anq excellentq serviceq organizationq shouldq perform.q Theq

realq organization.q Respondentsq canq useq theirq imaginationsq toq createq anq 
organisationqonqwhichqtoqbaseqtheirqexpectationsqofqexcellenceq(Parasuramanq et 
al. ,q1993);q
R Adequate :q Expectationsq forq theq minimumq levelq ofq performanceq theyq wouldq beq 
willingqtoqaccept.qq

Someqliteratureq(Liljanderq&qStrandvik,q1993;qNadiriq&qHussain,q2005;qParasuramanqetq 
al.,q1993;q Parasuramanqetq al.,q1994a;q Teasq&qDeCarlo,q2004)q hasq beenq suggestingq theq 
existenceqofqaq zone of tolerance qforqserviceqquality,qasqtheqdifferenceqbetweenqsomeone’sq 
viewqofqhowqanqexcellentqorganizationqshouldqperform,qandqtheqminimumqsheqisqwillingq 
toqaccept.qTheqconceptqofq zone of tolerance qsuggestedqbyqBerryq&qParasuramanq(1991)q
assumesq thatq customersq doq notq haveq expectationsq ofqaq serviceq attributeq onq oneq givenq 
level,q butq ratherq theyq canq tolerateq aq variationq andq stillq considerq themq acceptable,q
accordingqtoqtheirqexpectations.qq
q
Thisq conceptq alsoq impliesq thatq customers’q expectationsq existq onq twoq levels:q aq desired 
level q (thatq reflectsq onq whatq levelq theq serviceq should q be)q andq anq adequate level q (thatq 
reflectsqwhatqcustomersqbelieveqitq could qbe).qTheqadequateqlevelqisqtheqleastqacceptableq 
levelq ofq theq serviceq experience.q Theseq twoq levelsq ofq expectationsq formq theq bordersq ofq 
customers’q zone of tolerance ,q i.e.,q theq zoneq ofq toleranceq separatesq theq desiredq andq 
adequateqserviceqlevelsq(Figureq69).qIfqtheqrealqexperienceqofqaqcustomerqfallsqinqbetweenq 
theseqborders,q itq isq toleratedqandq theq perceivedq qualityq isqgood.q Theq zoneq ofqtoleranceq 
endsqupqactingqasqaqmediatorqtoqserviceqquality.qq
q
Aq zone of tolerance q is,q therefore,q aq rangeq ofq serviceq performanceq thatq aq customerq 
considersqsatisfactory:qaqperformanceqbelowqtheqtoleranceqzoneqwillqengenderqcustomerq 
frustration,qandqwillqdecreaseqcustomerqloyalty.qAqperformanceqlevelqaboveqtheqtoleranceq 
levelq willq pleasantlyq surpriseq customersq andq strengthenq theirq loyaltyq (Berryq &q 
Parasuraman,q1991).qq

q
3.1.   Insights From Service Recovery Literature 
 
Mistakesq areq aq criticalq partq ofq everyq service,q andqnoq matterq howq hardq theq serviceq 
providersq try,q evenq theq bestq willq makeq mistakesq (Hart,q Heskett,q &q Sasserq Jr.,q 1990).q
Service recovery qrelatesqtoqtheqabilityqofqtheqserviceqproviderqtoqdealqwithqincidentsqwhenq 
theq serviceq hasq failedq (forq example,q aq cancelledq airlineq flight,q aq cancelledq event,q orq aq 
differentqthanqannouncedqcreditqcardqdebt).qService recovery qhasqbeenqstudiedqnotqonlyq 
byq Grönroosq (1990b)q butq alsoq byq severalq othersqauthorsq (Andreassen,q 1999;qBitner,q et 
al. ,q1989,q1990;qFornellq&qWernerfelt,q1984,q1987,q1988;qGilly,q1987)qwhoqfocusqtheirq 
attentionqonqhowqtheqserviceqproviderqrespondsqtoqcustomerqproblemsqandqcomplaints,q 
andqhowqtheyqrespondqtoqservicesqfailures.qq
q
BerryqandqParasuramanq(1991,qp.q34)qdefendqthatq service recovery qisqasqcriticalqasqtheq 
pursuitq ofq errorRfreeq serviceq inq buildingq aq qualityRbasedq foundationq forq marketingq 
services.q Inq otherq words,q errorsq inq serviceq deliveryq areq inevitable,q andq thatq insteadq ofq 
pursuingq aq zeroRdefectq serviceq strategy,q serviceq providersq mustq pursueq excellencyq inq 
serviceqrecovery.qThisqmeansqthatqalthoughqaq“strongqrecoveryqeffortqisqnotqanqeffectiveq
cureq forq chronicq unreliability”q (Berryq &q Parasuraman,q 1991,q p.q 41),q strongq recoveryq 
effortsqcanqimproveqcustomers’qconfidenceqinqtheqcompany’sqserviceqquality.qq
q

• Theqmarginalqbenefitsqofqaqstrong,qoverqaqweakqrecoveryqeffort,qincreaseqasqtheq

Whenqaq serviceq problemq isq followedq byq aq weakq recoveryq effort,q whatq Bitner,q Booms,q

3.2.   Moments of Truth and The Critical Incidents Approach to 
Measure Service Quality 
q
Moments of truth qandq critical incidents qareqtwoqapproachesqthatqcanqbequsedqtoqstudyqtheq 
qualityqofqeRlearning.qAlthoughqtheyqareqquiteqdifferentq(moments of truth qisqtheqresultqofq 
Carlzon’sq (1987)q experienceq asq aq manager,q whileq critical incidents q isq aq researchq 
techniqueqoriginallyqcreatedqbyqFlanaganq(1954)),qtheyqsuggestqthatqqualityqcanqbeqmadeq 
ofqsmallqdetails,qspecificqmomentsqorqincidents.qq
q
Janq Carlzonq(1987)qcreatedq theq conceptq ofq moments of truth q toq illustrateqtheq timeq andq 
placeq whenq andq whereq theq serviceq providerq hasq theq opportunityq toq demonstrateq toq theq 
customerqtheqqualityqofqitsqservices.qTheqcustomerqwillqexperienceqaqseriesqofq moments of 
truth qwhileqinteractingqwithqtheqserviceqprovider.q Moments of truth qareqalsoqmomentsqofq 
opportunity,q windowsq ofq opportunitiesq thatq areq openq andq willq beq lostq whenq customersq 
willqhaveqgone.qAsqpresidentqofqScandinavianqAirlines,qCarlzonqwasqableqtoqrealizeqthatq 
businessesq faceq moments of truth q andq areq judgedq wheneverq theyq interactq withq theirq 
customers.qHowqtheqphoneqisqanswered,qwhatqtheqinvoicesqlookqlike,qandqtheqfriendlinessq 
ofqanqemployee,qareqallq moments of truth .q
q
Mostq ofq theq methodsq toq measureq qualityq areq basedq onq attributesq andq onq quantitativeq 
measurementq ofq thoseq attributes.q Theq critical incident method q (CIT)q isq anq alternativeq 


PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
q
q
306 
wayq ofq creatingq anq understandingq ofq howq customersq perceiveq theq qualityq ofq aq givenq 
service.q Itq isq basedq onq qualitativeq approaches,q itqisq aq veryq flexibleq technique,q andq canq 
evenq useq quantitativeq methodsq toq analyzeq data.q Theqcriticalq incidentq techniqueq wasq 
originallyq developedq byq Flanaganq (1954)q anq isq essentiallyq aq setq ofq operationsq forq 
collectingqdirectqobservationsqofqhumanqbehaviourqinqdefinedqsituationsqinqsuchqaqwayqasq 
toq useq theq informationq toq solveq practicalq problems,q as,q forq example,q assessingq 
educationalqgaps,qobtainingqinformationqtoqimproveqservices,qorqreducingqcompetitors’q 
competitiveq advantage.q CITq isq widelyq usedq forq researchq inq education,q engineering,q 
marketing,qpsychology,qandqmedicine.qAnq incident qisqanyqobservableqhumanqactivityqthatq 
isqsufficientlyqcompleteqtoqallowqinferencesqandqpredictionsqtoqbeqmadeqaboutqtheqpersonq 
performingqtheqact.qInqorderqforqtheqincidentqtoqbeqconsideredq critical ,qitqmustqoccurqinqaq 
situationqwhereqtheqpurposeqorqintentqofqtheqactqseemsqfairlyqclearqtoqtheqobserverqandq 
whereq itsq consequencesq areq sufficientlyq definiteq toq leaveq littleq doubtq concerningq itsq 
effectsq(Flanagan,q1954).qThisqmeansqthatqanqincidentqisq"critical"qwhenqtheqactionqtakenq 
contributedqtoqanqeffectiveqoutcomeq(forqinstance,qitqhelpedqtoqsolveqaqproblemqorqresolveq 
aqsituation).qButqanqincidentqmayqalsoqbeqconsideredq"critical"qwhenqtheqactionqresultedq 
inqanqineffectiveqoutcomeq(forqinstance,qitqpartiallyqresolvedqaqproblem,qbutqcreatedqnewq 
problemsqorqaqneedqforqfurtherqaction)q(Fivarsq&qFitzpatrick,q2003).q
q
CITq emergedq fromq theq assumptionq thatq itq canq facilitateq theq observationq andq 
categorizationqofqhumanqbehaviours.qItqisqfrequentlyqconfusedqwithqphenomenologyqandq 
someq literatureq justifiesq thisq withq theq misinterpretationq ofq Flanagan’sq definitionq ofq 
critical incidentq–qanqincidentqinqwhichqtheqpurposeqorqintentqofqtheqactqisqclearqtoqtheq 
observerq andq theq consequencesqareq definiteq (Byrne,q2001).q CITq isq veryq practicalq asq inq 
reportsq ofq criticalq incidentsq areq describedq situationsq orq actionsq thatq areq significantq Rq
critical qRqinqdeterminingqtheqeffectivenessqorqineffectivenessqofqtheqoutcome.qItqisqusefulq 
inq emphasizingq theq featuresq thatq willq makeq aq systemq particularlyq vulnerableq andq isq 
appropriateqforqtheqidentificationqofqunusualqevents,qwhichqmayqnotqbeqpickedqupqinqotherq 
techniques.qCITqisqconsideredqtoqbeqaqgoodqmethodq(Bitnerq et al. ,1989,q1990)qnamelyqinq 
serviceq industriesq (Gremler,q 2004),q aq goodq providerq ofq richq materialq indicatingq 
problematicqareasqandqstrengths,qandqaqgoodqwayqtoqfindqaqbasisqforqfurtherqresearchqonq 
actionsqnecessaryqtoqimproveqserviceqquality,qasqitqcanqgiveqdirectqindicationsqaboutqtheq 
actionsq neededqtoq beq takenq(Grönroos,q 2007).qYet,q CITq alsoq hasq someq limitationsq andq 
disadvantages:qitqreliesqonqeventsqbeingqrememberedqbyqusersqandqrequiresqtheqaccurateq 
andqtruthfulqreportqofqthem.qThereqisqalsoqaqproblemqofqreliabilityqinqtermsqofqmemory,qasq 
manyqcriticalqincidentsqmayqbeqforgottenqorqdistorted,qand,qfinally,qCITqcanqemphasizeq 
onlyqrareqeventsqandqmissqcommonplaceqeventsq(Infopolisq2qProject,q2000).q
q
CITqinvolvesqfiveqstepsq(Flanagan,q1954):qq
q
• Theqfirstqisqdeterminingqtheqgeneralqaimqofqtheqstudyqi.e.,qaqbriefqstatementqofqtheq 
topicqunderqstudy;q
• Theq secondq isq toq planq andq specifyq howq factualq incidentsq regardingq theq generalq 
aimqofqtheqstudyqwillqbeqcollected;q
• Theqthirdqisqtoqcollectqtheqdataqandqthisqmayqoccurqviaqinterviewqorqmayqconsistq

1.  The Paradoxes of Technology 
q
Theq moreq technologyRorientedq theq firmq is,q theq biggerq isq theq riskq toq defineq qualityq tooq 
narrowly,qandqtoqconsiderqtheqtechnicalqspecificationsqofqtheqserviceqtheqonlyqorqtheqmostq 
importantq featureq ofq perceivedq qualityq (Grönroos,q 2007,q p.q 73).q However,q eRlearningq 
servicesqareqbasedqinqtechnologicalqinfrastructures,qtherefore,qadditionalqconsiderationsq 
haveqtoqbeqmade,qtoqincludeqthisqtechnologicalqsideqofqeRlearning,qnamelyqtheqfactqthatqitq 
dependsq onq physicalq infrastructuresq andq applicationsq orq software.q Asq theq serviceq isq 
deliveredqthroughqtechnologyq–qinqtheqcaseqofqeRlearning,qtheqserviceqisqdeliveredqonlineq 
–qmeansqthatqseveralqidiosyncraticqsituations,qcalledqtheq paradoxes of technology q(Mickq 
&q Fournier,q 1998,q quotedq inq Zeithamlq et al. ,q 2006,q p.q 21)q willq beq present.q Theseq 
paradoxesqholdqbothqpositiveqandqnegativeqsides,qwhichqmeansqthatqtechnologyqcanqhelpq 
orqinjureqtheqcustomer’sqperceptionqofqtheqqualityqofqtheqserviceq(Tableq146).q

2.2.  Quality-Based Approaches to Software Development 
q
Softwareqdevelopment,qwhichqwasqaqpureqtechnologicalqarea,qandqinformationqsystems,q 
areqcurrentlyqveryqsensitiveqtoqcustomers’qbehaviourqandqperceptionsqofqquality,qandqitq 
hasq beenq receivingq influencesq fromq psychoRsociologicalq areasq (Wadeq &q Schneberger,q 
2007),qsuchqasqtheq theory of reasoned action q(Ajzenq&qFishbein,q1973,q1980;qFishbein,q 
1967;q Fishbeinq &q Ajzen,q 1975)q andq theory of planned behaviour q (Ajzen,q 1985,q 
1991).Theq technology acceptance model q (Davis,q 1986,q 1989;q Davis,q Bagozzi,q &q 
Warshaw,q1989),qwhichqisqtheqtheoryqofqreasonedqactionqappliedqtoqinformationqsystems,q 
andqtheq unified theory of acceptance and use of technology q(Venkatesh,qMorris,qDavis,q 
&qDavis,q2003)qareqsomeqexamplesqofqthatqinfluence.qq
q
Extremeq Programmingq (XP)q (2007),q isq currentlyq theq mostq usedq approachq toq ensureq 
qualityqinqsoftwareqdevelopment.qItqisqbasedqonqcustomerqsatisfaction,qandqpresentsqanq 
alternativeqtoqtheqtraditionalq waterfall model qofqsoftwareqdevelopment:qwhileqtraditionalq
softwareqdevelopmentqmethodsqareqsequentialq(theqsoftwareqdevelopmentqflowsqthroughq 
theq phasesq ofq requirementsq analysis,q design,q implementation,q testing,q integration,q andq 
maintenance),q XPq isq designedq toq deliverq softwareq capableq ofq respondingq toq changingq 
customerqrequirements,qatqanyqmoment,qevenqlateqinqtheqlifeqcycle,qasqitqworksqwithqsmallq 
releasesqcyclesqandqsystematicqcodeqtestsq(Figureq73),qwhichqturnsqitqintoqaq“qlightweight,q 
lowRrisk,qflexible,qpredictable,qscientificqandqfunqwayqofqdevelopqsoftware”q(Beck,q2000,q 
p.q xvii).q XPq addressesq commonq softwareq problems,q asq scheduleq slips,q projectq 
cancellation,qhighqdefectqrates,qbusinessqmisunderstandings,qandqchangesq(Beck,q2000,qp.q 
4)qusingqaqsimpleqmodelqbasedqonqprinciplesqasqrapidqfeedback,qsimplicityqassumption,q 
incrementalq change,q changeq embracement,q andq qualityq workq (Beck,q 2000,q pp.q 37R38).q 
Thisqisqmadeqpossibleqthroughqtwoqprinciples:qq
q
R Qualityqcontrolqtestsqareqcreatedqevenqbeforeqtheqcodeqisqwritten,qwhichqmeansq 
thatqasqbugsq areqfound,qnewq testsq areq addedq andq aq safetyq netq ofqtightq meshqisq 
createdqthatqpreventsqbugsqtoqhappenqtwice;qq
R Thereq isq anq openq attitudeq towardsq changingq requirements:q XPq getsq customerq 
feedbackqearly,qwhileqthereqisqstillqtimeqtoqchangeqfunctionalityqorqimprovequserq 
acceptance.qq

q

managementqapproachesqinqinformationqsystemsqhaveqbeenqdevelopedqtoqovercomeqtheq 
limitationsq ofq theq traditionalq systemsq developmentqprocessq inq ensuringq highq qualityq 
systems.qMoreover,qqualityqconcernsqhaveqbeenqexpressedqnotqonlyqinqtheqISOqstandardsq

Fitzpatrick,q1996;qFitzpatrickq&qHiggins,q2000;qFoxq&qFrakes,q1997;qPearson,qCrosby,q 
&qOrwig,q1996R97;qPressmanq&qInce,q2000,qpp.q494R499;qRavichandranq&qRai,q1999;q

2007).qqqqq
q
McCall’sq (1994)q modelq ofq ISq qualityq includesq severalq dimensionsq ofq quality,q asq 
correctness, reliability, efficiency, integrity, usability, maintainability, testability, 
flexibility, portability, reusability and  interoperability. q Otherq authorsq haveq beenq 
proposingq newq instrumentsq ofq measurementq ofq theq qualityq ofq theq informationq systemsq 
(Pitt,qWatson,q &q Kavan,q 1995;q Ravichandranq &qRai,q 1999),q whileq othersq asq Kettingerq 
andq Leeq (1997a,q 1997b)q discussq theq applicationsq ofqSERVQUALq inq informationq 
systems.q
q
Stylianouq andq Kumarq (2000),q forq instance,q identifiedq sixq topRlevelq dimensionsq ofq ISq 
quality:q
q
R Infrastructure quality :qtheqqualityqofqtheqinfrastructureq(hardwareqandqenablingq 
software)qthatqisqfieldedqandqmaintainedqbyqIS,qwhichqincludes,qforqexample,qtheq 
qualityqofqtheqnetworks,qandqsystemsqsoftware;q
R Software quality : theqqualityqofqtheqapplicationsqsoftwareqbuilt,qorqmaintained,q 
orqsupportedqbyqIS;q
R Data quality : theqqualityqofqtheqdataqenteringqtheqvariousqinformationqsystems;q
R Information quality:  theq qualityq ofq theq outputq resultingq fromq theq informationq

4.  Web-Based Service Quality Approaches 
q
WebRbasedqservicesqhaveqbeenqfacingqbothqincreasingqsalesqandqincreasingqcompetitiveq 
pressure.q Buyingq patronsq areq nowq includingq onlineq shoppingq asq anq alternativeq toq 
conventionalqretailingqchannelsqlikeqstreetqshops,qmailqandqphoneqorders,qcatalogues,qandq 
directqsalesqforce,qandqareqexpendingqmoreqmoneyqonqwebRbasedqservices,qandqgainingq 
moreqexperienceqinqonlineqservices.qq
q
Severalqfactorsqhaveqbeenqpointedqoutqasqcontributorsqtoqincreasingqonlineqspending.qTheq 
mainqfactorqisqrelatedqtoqaq“wiredqlifestyle”:qaqpositiveqtechnologyqattitude,qtechnologicalq 
skillsqandqexperience,qaqlotqofqtimeqspentqonline,qaqhigherqdegreeqofqInternetqusageqforq 
searchq toq productq information,q strongq readiness,q technologyq optimismq andq perceivedq 
onlineqskill,qandqanqaccumulatedqonlineqexperience,qbutqalsoqaqcareerRorientedqlifestyle,qaq 
convenienceqorientation,qtimeqstarvation,qandqevenqpreviousquseqofqcatalogueqshoppingq 
(Wolfinbargerq&qGilly,q2002,qp.q4).qSinceqtheqwebqisqtheqdeliveryqchannelqofqeRlearningq 
services,qitqisqimportantqtoqstudyqtheqqualityqofqtheqeRlearningqwebsite,qasqitqmayqbeqasq 
importantqtoqtheqoverallqperceivedqqualityqasqtheqeducationalqcomponent,qasqwellqasqtoq 
theqserviceqcompetitiveness,qsurvivalqandqsuccess.qq
q
Theq instrumentsq ofq perceivedq qualityq ofq webRbasedq servicesq areq eitherq targetingq 
informativeqorqpureqpromotionalqsites,qorqInternetqshoppingqsites,qi.e.,qwebqretailqsitesqinq 
whichqcustomersqcanqbrowse,qevaluate,qorder,qandqpurchaseqaqproductqorqserviceq(Yooq&q 
Donthu,q2001),qandqmostqofqtheqtimes,qtheqlatterqareqfocusedqonqtransactionsqissuesqsuchq 
asq ordering,q pricing,q financialq security,q andq paymentq methods.q Mostq ofq theq literatureq

Renderq&qO'Connor,q1976),qwhich,qinqturn,qrelatesqtheqperceptionsqofqqualityqofqtheqstoreq 
asq aq vitalq extrinsicq cueq aboutq theq qualityq ofq theq productsq ofq theq store.q Yet,q althoughq 
traditionalq dimensionsq ofq serviceq quality,q suchq asqcompetence, courtesy, cleanliness,

Perceptual attributes qareq moreq readilyq assessableq byq allqcustomers.qMoreover,q

Appendix 5: Accreditation and Standards  
 
1.  Accreditation 
q
Accreditationq isq aq processq thatq providesq publicq recognitionq toq institutionsq orq studyq 
programsqthatqmeetqcertainqstandards.qItqensuresqthatqtheqinstitutionqhasqqualifiedqstaff,q 
adequateq facilities,q andq equipment,q operatesq onq aq soundq financialq basis,q andq offersq anq 
approvedq studyq program.q Accreditationq isq givenq toq institutions,q ratherq thanq toq 
educationalq productsq orq approaches.q Aq successfulq accreditationq mayq asq wellq beq 
interpretedq asq aq promiseq toq provideq theq qualityq ofqeducationq beingq claimedq byq theq 
institutionq(Flasdickq&qMichel,q2006,qp.q52).qAccreditationqisqconsideredqtoqbeqtheqbasisq 
ofq qualityq assuranceqinqhigherq educationq(ENQA,q 2005)q andq itqprovidesq confidenceq toq 
potentialq andq currentq students,q asq wellq asq toq potentialq employersq (Flasdickq &q Michel,q 
2006,q p.q 52).q Althoughq internalq qualityq evaluationsq areq gainingq moreq importanceq 
(Lagrosenq et al .,q 2004),q externalq qualityq evaluationsq andq accreditations,q madeq byq anq 
externalq andq independentq evaluationq body,q getq aq broaderq acceptanceq (forq instance,q 
Dickeson,qn.d.;qVanqDamme,q2000).q
q
2.  Quality Marks  
q
Quality marks qareqinstrumentsqthatqintendqtoqassureqqualityqbyqaqcertificationqgivenqbyqaq 
wellRacceptedq certificationq body.q Inq general,q quality marks q coverq aq varietyq ofq 
approaches:q someq qualityq marksq certifyq theq qualityqofq organizationsq andq someq areq 
limitedqtoqtheqcertificationqofqproducts,qsuchqasqcoursesq(Lodzinskiq&qPawlowski,q2006,q 
p.q110).qq
q
Thereqareqseveralqqualityqmarks,qeachqoneqwithqaqdifferentqfocusq(quotedqinqLodzinskiq&q 
Pawlowski,q2006,qpp.q111R112):q
q
- TheqEFMDqcertificationqforqeRlearningq(2004),qwhichqisqaqqualityqmarkqfocusedqinq 
higherqeducation;q
- Theq Gütesiegel q(sealqofqquality)qeRlearningq(Bruder,qOffenbartl,qOsswald,q&qSauer,q 
2004),qwhichqisqfocusedqonqproducts,qsuchqasqcoursesqandqmodels,qandqprovidesqaq 
listqofqcriteriaqforqassessingqquality;q
- Qualitätssiegel e-learning (QSEL),qwhichqintendsqtoqprovideqaqholisticqqualityqmarkq 
andq wasq basedq onq aq surveyq ofq theq Europeanq Qualityq Observatoryq (Ehlersq et al .,q 
2005)qtoqdetermineqwhichqqualityqapproachesqwereqtheqmostqusedqinqEurope;qq
- TheqqualityqmarkqofqArtSetqLQWq(Zech,q2003,q2007),qwhichqprovidesqaqframeworkq 
basedqonqselfRassessmentqandqexternalqauditsqofqeRlearningqinstitutions;qq
- TheqcriteriaqofqWebKollegqNRWq(2006),qwhichqareqapplicableqtoqeRlearningqandqbR
learningqcourses’qmaterials.qq
q
3.  Standards 
q
Standardization  isqtheqprocessqofqestablishingqaqtechnicalqstandardqwithqtheqinclusionqofq 
relatedq nationalq andq internationalq bodies,q whoq areqwillingq andq assignedq toq attendq thisq 
processq (Heddergott,q 2006,q p.q 187).q Pawlowskiq (2006,q p.q 67)q definesq standardsq asq aq 

PERCEPTIONS OF QUALITY IN E-LEARNING: A CASE STUDY  
q
q
q
322 
“qualityqstandardqthatqsupportsqqualityqdevelopmentqinqorganizationsqaccordingqtoqtheirq 
specificqneedsqandqrequirements”.qStandardsqarequsedqbyqinstitutionsqandqgovernmentsqtoq 
ensureqthatqlearningqisqpredicable,qfair,qconsistent,qandqeconomic,qandqachievesqatqleastqaq 
minimumqlevelqofqqualityqacceptableqtoqsocietyq(Holmes,q2006,qp.q24).qHolmesq(2006,qp.q 
24)q suggestsq aq separationq betweenq education standards q andq technical standards :q 
educationq standardsq areq beingq discussedq forq decadesq andq everyq effortq madeq towardsq 
standardizationqhaveqbeenqhardqtoqget;qtechnicalqstandardsqhaveqaqdifferentqsituation,qasq 
thereq isqmoreqconsensusqregardingq theq needq ofq havingqthem,qandq itq hasq beenqeasierq toq 
makeqthemqglobalqstandards,qratherqthanqmakingqthemqonlyqEuropean.q
q
q
3.1.  Purposes and Limitations 
q
StandardsqintendqtoqprovideqtheqeRlearningqmarketqwithqinteroperableqproductsqthatqcanq 
bequsedqinqdifferentqcompaniesqwithqdifferentqtechnologicalqsolutionqi.e.,qtheyqintendqtoq 
allowqtheqtransferqofqlearningqcontentqfromqoneqlearningqenvironmentqtoqanother,qandqtoq 
provideq customersq withq instrumentsq forq aq betterq transparencyq inq theq evaluationq ofq eRqqqqqqqqq 
Rlearningqproducts.qq
qq
Heddergottq(2006,qp.q188)qidentifiesqseveralqpurposesqofqstandards,qasqthequnificationqofq 
relevantq terms,q theq applicationq ofq definedq procedures,q theq managementq ofq qualityq 
assuranceqinqtheqproduction,qandqthequseqofqeRlearning.qHeddergottq(2006,qpp.q190R191)q
identifiesq advantagesq forq bothq vendorsq ofq eRlearningq (namelyq economiesq ofq scale,q 
internationalizationqpotential,qandqthequseqofqeRlearningqstandardsqasqaqmarketingqflag),q 
andq customersq (theq reusabilityq ofq eRlearningq content,q increaseq ofq efficiency,q costq 
reduction,q andq aq greaterq flexibilityq whenq itq comesqtoq chooseq productsq orq suppliersq 
withoutq havingq theq necessityq toq changeq previouslyq usedq eRlearningq components).q Yet,q 
standardsqusuallyqareqnotqrecognizedqatqfirstqsightqfromqlearnersqandqcustomers,qandqmostq 
ofqtheqtimesqcustomersqdoqnotqperceiveqtheirqvalue.qGenerally,q“mostqstandardsqareqforq 
developersq only”q (Heddergott,q 2006,q p.q 186).q Heddergottq (2006)q recognizesq thatq 
standardsqdoqnotqhaveqtheqcapabilityqtoqevaluateqtheqqualityqofqeRlearningqcontentqitselfq 
(p.188),q andq thatq theyq areq instrumentsq toq specifyq eRlearningq products,q ratherq thanq 
evaluatingqlearningqqualityq(p.191).qHeddergottq(2006,qp.197)qrecognizesqthatqthereqareq 
twoq perspectivesq onq theq meaningq andq useq ofq eRlearningq standards:q theq viewq ofq theq 
producers,qandqtheqviewqofqthequsersqandqcustomersqofqeRlearningqproductsqandqconcepts.qq
q
q
3.2.  Standards versus Criteria 
q
FlasdickqandqMichelq(2006,qp.q58)qbelieveqthatq criteria qandq standards qshouldqbeqtheqcoreq 
ofqanyqkindqofqqualityqassessment.qBecauseqtheqdistinctionqbetweenqtheqtermq criteria qandq 
standard qisqblurred,qENQAq(2003,qp.q34;q2008,qp.q8)qprovidedqaqdistinctionqbetweenqtwo:q
qq
- Standards q areq theq expectedq outcomesq ofq theq educationalq trainingq andq areq usedq 
moreqinqconnectionqwithqaccreditation.qStandardsqarequsedqasqthresholdsqvalues,q 
oftenqformulatedqbyqgovernmentqorqotherqeducationalqauthorities;qq
- Criteria qareqcheckpointsqandqbenchmarksqforqassessingqtheqqualityqofqtheqinputq 
andq theq process,q andq areq usedq moreq oftenq linkedq toqevaluation.q Theyq areq notq 
fixed,q butq serveq asq suggestionsq orq recommendedq pointsq ofq referenceq forq goodq 
quality,q againstq whichq theq subject,q theq programme,qandq theq institutionq areq 
evaluated.qq

q
- Standards q areq normative,q qualitative,q and/orq quantitativeq specificationq withq

3.3.  Standards: Types, Levels, and States 
q
Pawlowskiq (2006,q p.q 66)q differentiatesq standards ,q quasi-standards, q andq related 
standards qandqclassifiesqthemqintoqthreeqtypes:qq
q
R Generic quality standards ,q whichq provideq conceptsq forq qualityq managementq ofq
qualityq assurance,q independentq ofq theq domainq ofq usage,q suchqasq ISOq 9000q familyq 
thatq isq usedq inq differentq sectors.q EFQMq (2003c),q forq instance,q isq aq genericq quasiR
standardq alsoq widelyq used,q althoughq notq agreedq onq byq aq formalq standardizationq 
agency;qq
R Specific quality standards ,qwhichqprovideqqualityqmanagementqorqqualityqassuranceq 
conceptsq forq theq fieldq ofq learning,q education,q andqtraining,q andq areq focusedq onq 
specificqrequirementsqconcerningqeducationalqprocessesqorqproducts;qq
R Related standards ,qwhichqarequsedqtoqmanageqorqassureqspecificqaspectsqofqquality.q 
Learningq technologyq standards,q whichq assureq interoperability,q areq anq exampleq ofq 
these.qq
q
Linderq (2006,q p.q 196)q differentiatesq interoperability standards q (thatq heq definesq asq aq 
revisableq wayq ofq implementingq orq combiningq systemsqorq products,q inq orderq toq assureq 
technicalq orq semanticq interoperability),q conceptual standards q (thatq specifyq aq revisableq 
wayq ofq conceivingq servicesq orq practicesq inq orderq toq assureq conceptualq comparabilityq 
amongqtheqservicesqorqpractices)qandq level standards q(thatqspecifyqaqrevisableqlevelqofq 
‘quality’qforqsystems,qproducts,qservices,qorqpractices).qThereqareqalsoqdifferentqlevelsqofq 
standards:q pre-standards ,q whichq representq anq agreementq ofq aq selectedq community;  
national standards ,qasqPASq(PubliclyqAvailableqSpecification);q European standards qandq 
international standards qasqISOq(Heddergott,q2006,qp.q187).qq
q
Linderq (2006,q p.q 196)q distinguishesq formal standards q (thatq areq createdq byq standardsq 
bodiesq asq ANSI,q DIN,q ISO),q community standards q (thatq areq adoptedq byq certainq

3.5.  Architectures and Frameworks 
q
Architectures q areq focusedq onq theq particularityq ofq aggregatingq components,q whileq 
frameworks qareqconcernedqwithqtheqtypologyqofqtheqcomponentsq(Lindner,q2006,qp.q195).q
Fourq approachesq areq worthq mentioningq regardingq architectures:q IEEEq LTSAq (IEEE,q 
2003),q IMSq Abstractq Frameworkq (IMS,q 2003a),q JISCq serviceq orientedq eRlearningq 
frameworkq(2004,q 2007),q andq theqERILEqproposalq(Lindner,q 2006).q Theseqapproachesq 
areqnotqalternativeqorqexchangeable,qbutqratherqcomplementaryqviewsqandqorientations.qq
q
a)  IEEEqLTSAq
q
TheqfiveqdifferentqlevelsqofqtheqarchitectureqIEEEqLTSAqrepresentqtheqdifferentqpointsqofq 
viewqofqaqlearningqprocessq(fromqtheqmostqabstractqtoqtheqleast)  (Corbièreq&qChoquet,q 
2004):q
q
- Level 1 q Rq LearnerRenvironmentq interactions:q thisq levelq isqtheq mostq abstractq andq 
definesqtheqtasksqofqacquisition,qtransfer,qexchange,qandqdiscoveryqforqtheqlearner,q 
asq aq resultq ofq theq interactionsq withq herq environment.q Theseq environmentq andq 
learnerqentitiesqareqseenqasqtwoqsystemsqexchangingqinformation;qq
- Level 2 qRqLearnerRrelatedqdesignqfeatures:qthisqlayerqdefinesqtheqlearner’sqreactionq 
toqtheqenvironment;qqq
- Level 3 - Systemqcomponents:qaqcomponentqsystem,qnormalizedqbyqIEEE,qdefinesq 
anqorganizationqofqaqlearningqprocess,qseenqfromqtheqdataqandqcontrolqflowqpointsq 
ofqview;qq
- Level 4 qRqStakeholderqperspectivesqandqpriorities:qthisqlevelqexploitsqtheqcomponentq 
systemq directly,q inq orderq toq formalizeq theq technologicalq designq constraints.q Itq 
allowsqtheqidentificationqofqtheqsystem’sqactivitiesqduringqtheqlearningqprocess;qq
- Level 5 qRqCodings,qAPIs,qandqprotocols:qthisqlevelqdefinesqtheqabstractqphasesqofq 

theqsoftw areqdevelopmentqbasedqonqtheqcomponentqapproach. 
q
Theqroleqandqtheqbehaviourqofqtheseqdifferentqcomponentsqareqdescribedqusingqaqlearnerq 
scenario,qwhichqisqdividedqintoqeightqstepsq 
q

3.6.  Management Standards 
 
Management standards q (Heddergott,q 2006,q pp.q 188R189)q handleq theq processq ofq 
transferringq eRlearningq contentq intoq otherq environments,q likeq learningq managementq 
platformsq orq toolsetsq forq theq productionq ofq eRlearning.q Theyq areq focusedq onq theqq
interoperabilityqofqlearningqscenarios.qTheqtermq management standards qisqmisleadingqasq 
theseq standardsq areq focused,q notq onq managementq issues,q butq inq theq technicalq 
interoperabilityq ofq suchq packages ,q namelyq toq enableq learnersq toq retrieveq contentq 
packagesqandqreuseqthemqinqdifferentqtools.qThose  eRlearningqcontentqpackages  includeq 
allqfilesqforqaqspecificqeRlearningqofferqbundledqinqoneqcompressedqfile,qwhichqincludesq 
allqHTMLqdocuments,qmediaqfiles,qstyleqsheets,qandqscriptingqcomponentsqusedqwithinq 
theqcontentq(Prpitschq&qVeith,q2006,qp.q209).q
q
Amongqmanagementqstandards,qSCORM,qLOM,qIMSqContentqPackaging,qandqAICCqareq 
worthqofqdetailedqattention:q
q
- IEEEq LOMq (Learningq Objectq Metadata)q (2002a)q specifiesq aq conceptualq dataq 
schemeq andq theq correspondingq XMLRbinding.q Itq consistsq ofq nineq categories:q 
general,q lifecycle,q metaRmetadata,q technical,q educational,q rights,q relation,q 
annotation,qandqclassification;qq
- IMSq CPq (Contentq Packaging)q (IMS,q 2004a,q 2004b)q setsq aq standardizedq setq ofq 
structuresqthatqcanqbequsedqtoqexchangeqcontentqandqconsistsqofqtwoqcomponents:q 
theq information model q (IMS,q 2004a)q andq itsq correspondingq bindingq (IMS,q 
2004b).qIMCqCPqincludesqfourqcategories:qmetadata,qorganization,qresources,qandq 
subRmanifest;q
- SCORMq (Sharableq Contentq Objectq Referenceq Model)q (ADL2004)  providesq aq 
technicalq standardq forq interoperabilityq ofq eRlearningq contentq packagesq betweenq 
LMSq andq eRlearningq contentq authoringq tools.q SCORMq packagesq areq createdq 
accordingqtoqIMSqCP;q
- TheqAICCqguidelinesqandqrecommendationsq(2008),qalsoqknownqasqAGR's,qareq 
focusedq onq theq interoperabilityq betweenq webRbasedq coursewareq andq LMS's.q 
ThereqareqnineqdifferentqAGR'sqbutqtheqAICCqoffersqcertificationqtestingqforqonlyq 
twoq AGR'sq (AGRq 006q Rqcomputer managed instruction q andq AGRq 010q Rqweb-
based computer managed instruction ).qTheqotherqsevenqAICCqguidelinesqthatqareq 
notqformallyqtestedqbyqAICCqare:qAGRq002q( courseware delivery stations ),qAGRq 
003q( digital audition ),qAGRq004q( operating/windowing system ),qAGRq005q(CBT 
peripheral devices ),q AGRq 007q ( courseware interchange ),q AGRq 008q ( digital 
video ),qandqAGRq009q( icon standards: user interface ).qq

3.7.  Content Standards 
q
Contentq standardsq areqfocusedqonq theq ideaqofq buildingq genericqeRlearningq systemsqthatq 
wouldqallowqtheqreuseqofqexistingqlearningqresourcesqinqdifferentqaccessibilityqsettings.q 
Theyq representq aq setq ofq commonlyq agreedq accessibilityq metadataq toq facilitateq theq 
descriptionqofqlearningqresourcesqusingqtheqsameqmetadataqsets,qand,qtherefore,qsupportq 
sharingq ofq accessibleq resourcesq (Karampiperisq &q Sampson,q 2006).q Amongq theseq 
standards,qweqemphasize:qq
q
- W3CqWebqContentqAccessibilityqGuidelinesq(1999);q
- CENqaccessibilityqpropertiesqforqlearningqresourcesq(CEN/ISSS,q2004a);q

- IMSqAccessForAllqmetadataq(IMS,q2003b);qq
- AndqIMSqforqLIPqInformationqmodelqspecificationq(IMS,q2003c).qq
q
IMSq forq LIPq informationq modelq specificationq (IMS,q 2003c),q forq instance,q includesq 
metadataqrequirementsqconcerningqtheqcolourqavoidance,qcolourqdifference,qandqcolourq 
brightness,qandqmetadataqrequirementsqforqlearnerqscaffoldqtools.qContentqstandardsqareq

accessibilityq concernsq withinq it:q itsq technicalq categoryq describesq theq technologyq 
(hardware,q network,q andq software)q thatq isq requiredqforq usingq aq learningq objectq andq

difficultyqofqaqlearningqobject,qtheqtimeqthatqaqtypicalquserqtakesqtoqworkqwithqit,qamongq 
others.qq

3.8.  Didactical Standards 
q
Educational interoperability standards,qalsoqknownqasqEducationalqModellingqLanguageq 
(EML)q (Klebl,q 2006,q p.q 227),q proposeq specificq frameworksq forq aq comprehensiveq 
descriptionq ofq theq teachingRlearningq processq (Klebl,q 2006,q p.q 225).q Theseq standardsq 
provideqelementsqtoqdescribeqbothqcontentqandqoutlineqforqaqunitqofqlearning.qqq
q
Thereq areq twoq alternativeq educationalq interoperabilityq standards : theq IMSq Learningq 
Designq (LD)q (2003e)q andq DINq Didacticalq Objectq Modelq (DINRDOM)q (2004).q Theseq 
educationalq interoperabilityq standardsq representq aqparadigmaticq shiftq awayq fromq aq 
contentRbasedq knowledgeq deliveryq (whichq isq theq baseq ofq metadataq standards,q suchq asq 
IEEEqLOM,qIMSqCP,qandqSCORM,qandqofqcontentqpackagingqprinciples)qtoqaqsocialqandq 
learnerRcentredqparadigm.qIMSqLDqspecifies,qasqSCORMqdoes,qaqpackageqandqaqruntimeq 
environmentqandqusesqIMSqCPqtoqstructureqitsqcontent.qItqprovidesqallqfunctionalitiesqofq 
SCOMq and,q additionally,q providesq aq representationq ofq theq usedq didacticq conception.q 
Kleblq (2006,q pp.q 229,q 237R242)q summarizesq theq basicq conceptsq ofq IMSq LDq (Koper,q 
Olivier,q&qAnderson,q2003a,q2003b,q2003c)qandqDINRDOMq(2004):qq
q
- Bothq describeq theq processq ofq teachingq andq learningqratherq thanq theq learningq 
content;qq
- Theyq areq aq formq ofq standardizedq notationq forq unitsqofq learningq usedq byq 
instructionalq designersq toq layq downq theirq comprehensiveq planq forq aq learningq 
scenario;q
- Bothquseq‘unitqofqlearning’qasqaqstartingqconceptqthatqrefersqtheqcourse,qmodule,q 
lesson,q unitq ofq study,q orq learningq experience,q andqbothq baseq theirq informationq 
modelqonq activities q(describedqasqsomethingqtoqbeqdoneqbyqsomeoneqinqorderqtoq 
achieveqaqpurpose,qandqdirectedqtowardsqlearningqobjectives).qTheyqbothqincludeq 
basicqprinciplesqofqaggregationqofqactivitiesq(ratherqthanqaggregationqofqcontents).qq
q
Kleblq (2006,q p.q 235)q recallsq thatq educational interoperability standards  mustq notq beq 
mistakenqwithq educational qstandardsqthemselves,qasqtheqlatterqareqaqnormativeqconstruct,q 
whileq educational interoperability qstandards areqaqtechnicalqconstructqthatqcanqenhanceq 
qualityqinqteachingRlearningqprocess,qbutqneverqguaranteesqit.qEvenqso,qKleblqidentifiesq 
severalq elementsq inq theseq standardsq thatq provideq anq indirectq relationshipq withq quality,q

3.9.  Learner Model Standards 
q
Someqstandardsqhaveqbeenqdevelopedqfocusedqonqtheqlearnerqprofiles.qTheseqstandardsq 
assumeq thatq theq competitivenessq ofq learnersq dependsq onq theq abilityq toq dealq withq theq 
diversityq ofq naturalq andq technologicalq resourcesq currentlyq availableq (Sgouropoulou,q 
2006,qp.q251).qInqthisqperspective,qstandardsqareqseenqasqtheqkeyqtoqtheqformationqofqaq 
commonq marketplaceq andq theq broadeningq ofq borderlessq learningq pathways.q Forq thatq 
purposes,qlearnerqprofilesqareqseenqasq1)qaqtoolqtoqpersonalizationqofqlearningqresourcesq 
acquisition,q 2)q aq facilitatorq ofq lifelongq learnerq mobilityq withinq andq betweenq higherq 
education,q vocationalq education,q andq trainingq sectors,q andq 3)q aq supportq forq theq 
communicationq ofq competenciesq andq qualificationsq forq employmentq purposesq orq forq 
admissionqtoqlearningqschemesq(Sgouropoulou,q2006,qp.q252).q
q
WithinqEurope,qandqinqtheqcontextqofqtheqLisbonqmeeting,qitqisqclaimedqthatqtheqboostqofq 
competitivenessq willq requireq aq transformationq ofq educationq andq training,q whichq willq 
involveq theq developmentq ofq theq higherq educationq areaq (theq Bolognaq process),q theq 
enhancementq ofq theq Europeanq coRoperationq inq vocationalq educationq andq trainingq (theq 
Copenhagenq process),q theq designq ofq nationalq frameworksq ofq qualifications,q andq anq 
Europeanq Qualificationq Frameworkq (EQF)q forq lifelongq learning.q Theq qualificationq 
frameworkq isq supportedq byq twoq instruments:q theq Europeanq Creditq Transferq Systemq 
(ECTS)qandqtheqSingleqCommunityqFrameworkqforqtheqTransparencyqofqQualificationsq 
andq Competencesq (Europeanq Parlament,q 2004),q alsoq knownq asq Europass.q Europassq 
involvesq theq creationq ofq aq personalq portfolioq ofq documentsq thatq aimq aq betterq 
communicationq andq presentationq ofq qualificationsq andq competences,q andq involvesq 
Europass-CV q (aq curriculum vitae q structureq forq theq presentationq ofq individualq 
qualificationsq andq competences),q Europass-Mobility q (aq recordq ofq periodsq ofq learningq 
attendedq inq otherq countries),q Europass-Diploma Supplement q (aq recordq ofq educationalq 
achievementsq atq higherq educationq level),q Europass-Language Portfolio q (aq recordq ofq 
languageq skills)q andq Europass-Certificate Supplement q (aq recordq ofq competencesq andq 
qualificationsqcorrespondingqtoqaqvocationalqtrainingqcertificate).qq
q
Theq mostq dominantq specificationsq relatedq toq theq learnerq profileq domainq areq theq IMSq 
Leanerq Informationq Packageq (LIP)q (IMS,q 2003d),q theqIEEEq Publicq andq Privateq 
Informationq (PAPI)q (Farance,q 2000;q IEEE,q 2002)q andqCENq agreementsq 15455q andq 
14927qforqlearnerqcompetenciesq(CEN/ISSS,q2004b,q2005).qTheqIMSqLIPq(IMS,q2003d)q
isq aq structuredq informationq modelq thatq includesq educationalq records,q trainingq logs,q 
professionalq developmentq history,q C.V.q withq relevantq workq experience,q andq lifelongq 
learningq record.q IEEq PAPIq (Farance,q 2000;q IEEE,q 2002)q dividesq userq recordsq intoq 
personalq informationq andq performanceq informationq andq separatesq securityq informationq 
fromq otherq typeq ofq learnerq information.q Itq splitsq theq learnerq informationq intoq severalq 
areas:q personalq information,q informationq aboutq relations,q security,q performance,q andq 
portfolio.qThereqisqalsoqaqcommonqneedqtoqhaveqaqreferenceqforqeRportfolioqformats,qandq 
someq technicalq specificationsq haveq beenq madeq forq softwareq developersq toq designq eR
portfolioqtoolsq(Arnaud,q2006,qpp.q263,q270):qq
q

3.10.  Interface Standards 
q
Thereq areq severalq relevantq standardsq inq theq areaq ofq businessq informationq systemq 
integration qthatqinfluenceqtheqstandardizationqofqeRlearningqservices,qnamelyqISOq7498q 
(standardqforqOpenqSystemqIntegrationRqOSI),qXMLq(ExtensibleqMarkupqLanguage),qandq 
infrastructure standards q likeq OMAq (Openq Managementq Architecture).q Bickq &q 
Pawlowskiq(2006,qp.q277)qmakeqaqdistinctionqbetweenq integration qandq interoperability :q 
integration qmainlyqfocusesqapplicationsqandqprocesses,qwhileq interoperability qdescribesq 
theqabilityqofqaqsystemqtoquseqfunctionalitiesqofqanotherq(remote)qsystem.qRegardingqdataq 
exchangeq standards,q theseq authorsq emphasizeq CVS,q EDI,q XML,q ISOq 10303,q ISOq TCq 
184/SC4,qandqtheqIMSqenterpriseqserviceqspecificationq(IMS,q2005a),qwhichqfocusesqonq 
integrationqbetweenqbusinessqinformationqsystemsqandqlearningqmanagementqsystems.qInq 
whatq infrastructureq standardsq areq concerned,q theyq emphasizeq ISOq 7498q (informationq 
processingqsystems),qISO/OSIqRqOpenqSystemqIntegration,qISOq15414q(openqdistributedq 
processingq referenceq model),q andq middlewareq standardsq likeq RPC,q CORBA,q SOAP,q 
WSDL,qandqUDDI.q

q

whoq wantq toq design,q delivery,q evaluateq andq purchaseq qualityq eRlearningq productsq andq

Guidelines,qalsoqknownqasqCanREGs,q(FuturEdq&qCACE2002a),qwhichqareqconsumerR
basedqqualityq standards q(asqEIfELqcallsqit)qforqeRlearningqproductsqandqservices.qeQLsq 
reflectqbestqpracticesqinqeRlearningqandqitsqpurposeqisqtoqprovideqconsumerqconfidenceqinq 
theq eRlearningq enterpriseq andq consumerq protectionq forq theq investmentq madeq (Barker,q 
2007).qq
q
Weq considerq thatq consumerq standardsq areq differentq fromq learnerq standardsq (pageq 334)q

UnderqtheqeRlearningqinitiative,qlaunchedqbyqtheqEuropeanqCommission,qfourqproposalsq 
emerged:qEQOq(EuropeanqQualityqObservatory),qQUALRERLEARNINGq(QualityqinqER
Learning),q SEELq (Supportingq Excellenceq inq ERLearning),q andq SEEQUELq (Sustainableq 
EnvironmentqforqtheqEvaluationqofqQualityqinqERLearning).qLater,qinq2005,qtheseqprojectsq 
jointq theirq effortsq underq aq newq projectq calledq TRIANGLE,q whichq establishedq theq 
EFQUELq(EuropeanqFoundationqforqQualityqinqERLearning).qq
q
1.  EQO (European Quality Observatory) 
q
Theq Europeanq Qualityq Observatoryq (EQO)q (2004b;q Pawlowski,q 2003)q developedq aq 
reference model (EQO2004a) , i.e.,qaqframeworkqthatqdefinesqconcreteqstepsqandqcriteriaq 
asq anq exemplary template q (Hildebrandtq &q Teschler,q 2006,q p.q 172)q forq analyzingq andq 
describingq qualityq approachesq forq theq fieldq ofq Europeanq eRlearning.q Itq isq aq metadataq 
schemeqforqtheqanalysis,qdescription,qand,qtherefore,qcomparisonqofqqualityqapproachesq 
applicableq forq Europeanq eRlearning.q Itq providesq aq classification scheme q forq theq 
discussionqaboutqqualityqinqeRlearningqandqaqdecisionRsupportqcycleq(Figureq79)qtoqguideq 
usersqthroughqtheqprocessqofqhowqtoqfindqandqtoqadaptqtheqrightqqualityqapproachqtoqherq 
contextqofquse.qTheqEQOqmodelq(2004a)qisqdividedqintoqtwoqparts:qInqtheqfirst,qqualityq 
approachesq areq analyzedq onq aq theoreticalq basisq byq qualityq expertsq usingq theq officialq 
documentationqandqpublicationsqaboutqtheqdifferentqapproaches.qThisqtheoreticalqanalysisq 
ofq approachesq coversq threeq categories:q generalq information,q contextq ofq usage,q andq 
methodq ofq qualityq approach.q Inq theq secondq part,q implementationq orq actualq useq 
experiencesq inq implementingq qualityq approachesq areqcategorizedq andq analyzed.q Theq
EQOq decisionq cycleq isq basedq onq theq EQOq metadataq model.q Itq involvesq fourq steps:q 1)q 
analysisqofqqualityqneeds,q2)qanalysisqandqcomparisonqofqqualityqapproaches,q3)qdecisionq 
support,qandq4)qadaptationqandqimplementationqofqrecommendations.qq

11.  EFQM (European Foundation for Quality Management) Framework 
q
TheqEFQMqExcellenceqModelq(2003b,q2003b)qisqaqnonRprescriptiveqframeworkqbasedqonq 
nineq criteria.q Fiveq ofq theseq areq enablers q andq theq otherq fourq areq results .q Theq enabler q
criteriaq coverq whatq anq organizationq does,q whileq theq results q criteriaq coverq whatq anq 
organizationq achieves.q Enablers q causeq r esults ,q andq enablers q areq improvedq usingq 
feedbackq fromq results .q Theq EFQMq Modelq isq presentedq inq Figureq 82.q Theq arrowsq 
emphasiseqtheqdynamicqnatureqofqtheqmodelqandqshowqthatqinnovationqandqlearningqhelpq 
toqimproveqenablers,qwhich,qinqturn,qleadqtoqimprovedqresults.qTheqbasisqofqtheqEFQMq 
Excellenceq Modelq areq theq eightq fundamental concepts of excellence ofq theq EFQMq 
(2003c),qwhichqare:qq
q
- Resultsq orientation:q excellenceq isq achievingq resultsq thatq delightq allq theq 
organisation’sqstakeholders;qq
- Customerqfocus:qexcellenceqisqcreatingqsustainableqcustomerqvalue;qq
- Leadershipqandqconstancyqofqpurpose:qexcellenceqisqvisionaryqandqinspirationalq 
leadership,qcoupledqwithqconstancyqofqpurpose;qq
- Managementq byq processesq andq facts:q excellenceq isq managingq theq organizationq 
throughqaqsetqofqinterdependentqandqinterrelatedqsystems,qprocesses,qandqfacts;qq
- Peopleqdevelopmentqandqinvolvement:qexcellenceqisqmaximizingqtheqcontributionq 
ofqemployeesqthroughqtheirqdevelopmentqandqinvolvement;qq
- Continuousq learning,q innovation,q andq improvement:q excellenceq isq challengingq 
theq status quo andqpromotingqchangeqbyqutilizingqlearningqtoqcreateqinnovationq 
andqimprovementqopportunities;qq
- Partnershipq development:q excellenceq isq developingq andq maintainingq valueR
addingqpartnerships;qq
- Corporateqsocialqresponsibility:qexcellenceqisqexceedingqtheqminimumqregulatoryq 
frameworkqandqtoqstriveqtoqunderstandqandqrespondqtoqtheqexpectationsqofqtheirq 
stakeholdersqinqsociety.q
