12.  QCC-eL - Quality Criteria for E-learning Products 
q
Bergerq (2006)q proposedq aq catalogueq ofq qualityq criteriaq forq eRlearningq productsq calledq 
QCCReL,q alsoq knownq asq theq product criteria catalogue q andq itq isq partq ofq theq Germanq 
PublicqAvailableqSpecificationq(PAS)q1032R1qandqpartqofqISOq19796R1.qTheqcatalogueqofq 
QCCReLqhasq682qcriteriaqandqisqdividedqintoqcategoriesq(Tableq157).qQCCReLqisqusedqtoq 
describeq orq verifyq theq pedagogicalq andq didacticq productq characteristics,q theq featuresq 
havingq anq effectq onq learningq andq motivation,q asq wellq asq theq functionalq productq 
characteristics.qTheqcriteriaqareqbasedqon:qq
q
- Relevantq ISORstandardsq forq usabilityq ofq softwareq andq multimediaq interfacesq 
(ISO/EN/DINq 9241,q 14915).q QCCReLq tookq intoq considerationq ISOq 9241,q whichq 
describesq theq ergonomicq criteria/principlesq forq softwareq productsq andq ISOq 14915,q 
whichqestablishesqtheq designq principlesqforq multimediaq userq interfaces.q Theseqtwoq 
ISOqstandardsqareqnotqregulatedqstandards,qandqQCCReLqspecifiesqtheqmethodsqthatq 
canq beq usedqtoq determineqwhetherq standardsq areq beingq met,q i.e.,q itq operationalizesq 
theqstandards.qForqinstance,qISOq14915R3q(5.6.)qrefersq“supportingquserqpreferences”q 
andqQCCReLqoperationalizesqasq“asqlongqasqitqisqappropriateqforqtheqtask,qalternativeq 
formsqofqmediaqshouldqbeqavailableqtoqusers,qfromqwhichqtheyqcanqselectqaqpreferredq 
mediumqorqdeactivateqspecificqmedia”q(Berger,q2006,qp.q145);q
- Relevantq EUq andq Germanq lawsq andq regulations,q namelyq dataq protectionq lawsq andq 
consumerqprotectionqlaws;q
- Consolidatedq empiricalq findingsq takenq fromq theq relevantq scientificq areas.q Thisq 
includesq findingsq fromq theq areasq ofq learningq andq motivationalq psychology,q mediaq 
psychology,qpedagogic,qandqdidacticqfindingsqfromqtheqscientificqsector.qqq

Appendix 7: Theories of Motivation 
qq
1.  Murray’s Psychogenic Needs 
q
Murrayq (1938)q developedq aq theoryq ofq personalityq basedq uponq needsq andq motivesq 
suggestingqthatqaqperson’sqpersonalityqisqaqreflectionqofqbehavioursqcontrolledqbyqneeds.q 
Heq createdq aq listq ofq potentiallyq motivatingq psychogenicq (causedq byq psychologicalq 
factors,q ratherq thanq physicalq dysfunction)q needsq (Tableq 158).q Accordingq toq him,q theseq 
psychogenicqneedsqfunctionqmostlyqonqthequnconsciousqlevel,qbutqplayqaqmajorqroleqinq 
one’sqpersonality.qAccordingqtoqMurray,qeveryoneqhasqtheseqneeds,qbutqeachqindividualq 
tendsq toq haveq aqcertainq levelq ofq eachq need.q Forq instance,q peopleq withq aq highq needq forq 
achievementqtendqtoqselectqmoreqchallengingqtasks.qPeopleqwhoqrateqhighqonqaffiliationq 
needsqtendqtoqhaveqlargerqsocialqgroups,qspendqmoreqtimeqinqsocialqinteraction,qandqareq 
moreq likelyq toq sufferq lonelinessq whenq facedq withq littleq socialq contact.q Althoughq eachq 
needqisqimportantqbyqitself,qtheqneedsqcanqbeqinterrelated:qtheyqcanqsupportqotherqneedsqorq 
conflictqwithqotherqneeds.qForqexample,qtheqneedqforqdominanceqmayqconflictqwithqtheq 
needqforqaffiliation.q

2.  Horney’s Neurotic Needs  
q

appearanceqofqneeds.qBasicqanxietyq(and,qtherefore,qneurosis)qcouldqresultqfromqaqvarietyq

hostileqatmosphere,qandqsoqonqandqsoqon"qq(K.qV.qWagner,q2008,qquotingqHorney,q1945).qq

3.  Maslow’s Hierarchical Needs Theory 
q
Maslow’sq theoryq (1943,q 1954,q 1968)q isq basedq onq theqassumptionq thatq motivationq isq 
drivenqbyqtheqexistenceqofqunsatisfiedqneeds.qHeqdevelopedqaqmodelqinqwhichqbasic,qlowR
levelq needs,q suchq asq physiologicalq requirementsq andq safety,q mustq beq satisfiedq beforeq 
higherRlevelq needs,q suchq asq selfRfulfilment,q areq pursued.q Maslow’sq pyramidq ofq 
hierarchicalq needsq includesq theq sixq levelsq detailedq inq Tableq 160.q Inq thisq hierarchical 
model :q
q
• Ifqoneqlevelqofqneedsqisqnotqsatisfied,qthenqone'sqmotivationqwillqariseqfromqtheq 
questqtoqsatisfyqthem;qq
• Higherqorderqneedsqwillqnotqariseqandqwillqnotqbeqfeltquntilqoneqhasqmetqtheqlowerq 
levelqneeds;q
• Whenqaqneedqisqmostlyqsatisfied,qitqnoqlongerqmotivatesqandqtheqnextqhigherqneedq 
takesqitsqplace.q
q
IfqMaslow’sqtheoryqholds,qthereqareqsomeqimportantqimplicationsqforqtrainingqproviders.q 
Asq notq allq individualsqareq drivenq byq theqsameq needs,qitqisq importantq toq understandqtheq 
needsq beingq pursuedq byq eachq trainee.q Furthermore,q trainingq providersq haveq theq 
opportunityqtoqmotivateqtraineesqinqeachqlevelqofqneed:qq
q
• Physiologicalq needs:q providingq coffeeq breaks,q restqbreaks,q financialq incentivesq 
forqtrainingqextraRhoursqandqmaterials;qq
• Safetyqneeds:qprovidingqaqsafeqtrainingqenvironmentqandqaqgoodqcustomerqserviceq 
(namelyqtechnical)qhelp;qq
• Socialqneeds:qcreatingqaqsenseqofqcommunityqthroughqteamRbasedqprojects,qsocialq 
eventsq(asqclassqdinnerqorqaqhangingRoutqprogram),qorqsocialqforums;qq
• Esteemq needs:q organizingq trainingq eventsq inq smallq learningq objects,q creatingq 
learningqmilestones,qorqrecognizingqachievements;q
• SelfRactualization:q workingq withq currentq orq potentialq employersq toq provideq 
traineesqaqchallengeqandqtheqopportunityqtoqreachqtheirqfullqcareerqpotential.qq

6.  Herzberg’s Two Factors Theory 
q
UnlikeqMaslow,qwhoqintendedqtoqcreateqaqgeneralqtheoryqofqhumanq(need)qmotivation,q 
Herzberg’sqtheoryq(1966,q1968;qHerzbergq et al .,q1959)qisqveryqworkRorientedqandqrelatedq 
toqjobqsatisfactionqandqisqcloseqtoqtheqpositive/negativeqreinforcementqconceptualqmodel.q
Usingq theq criticalRincidentq technique,q whereq employeesq wereq askedq whatq pleasedq andq 
displeasedqthemqaboutqtheirqwork,qHerzbergq et al. q(1959)qfoundqtwoqsetsqofqfactorsqinqjobq 
satisfaction:qoneqpredominantqinqtheqincidentsqofqsatisfactionqandqtheqotherqpredominantq 
inqtheqincidentsqofqdissatisfaction.qTheyqargueqthatqthereqareqtwoqdistinctqhumanqneedsq 
portrayedqinqthisqframework:qfirst,qthereqareq physiological needs qthatqcanqbeqfulfilledqbyq 
money,q forq example,q toq purchaseq foodq andq shelter;q andq second,q thereq isq theq 
psychological need toq achieveq andq grow,q andq thisq needq isq fulfilledq byqactivitiesq thatq 
causeqoneq toq grow.q Herzbergqandqhisqcolleaguesq(1959)q foundqthatq theqfactorsqcausingq 
jobqsatisfactionq(and,qpresumably,qmotivation)qwereqdifferentqfromqthoseqthatqcauseqjobq 
dissatisfaction.qForqthatqreason,qtheqtwoqfeelingsqcannotqsimplyqbeqtreatedqasqoppositesqofq 
oneqanother:qtheqoppositeqofqsatisfactionqisqnotqdissatisfaction,qbutqrather,qnoqsatisfaction;q 
similarly,qtheqoppositeqofqdissatisfactionqisqnoqdissatisfaction.qThisqmeansqthatqthereqisq 
notqaqsingleqcontinuumqthatqrangesqfromqjobqdissatisfactionqatqoneqendqofqtheqcontinuum,q 
toqjobq satisfactionq atq theq otherqend,q butq ratherq thereqareqtwoq separateqcontinuums:q oneq 
rangingqfromqjobqsatisfactionqtoqnoqjobqsatisfactionq(motivation)qandqtheqotherqrangingq 
fromqjobqdissatisfactionqtoqnoqjobqdissatisfactionq(hygiene).q
q
Moreover,q theq factorsq thatq determineq whetherq thereqisq dissatisfactionq orq noq 
dissatisfactionqareqnotqpartqofqtheqworkqitself,qbutqratherqexternalqfactorsq(Tableq163).qTheq 
dissatisfiersq consistedq primaryq ofq job context q factorsq suchq asq workingq conditions,q 
companyqpolicy,qandqhierarchicalqrelationships.qTheqsatisfiersqconsistedqprimaryqofq job 
content q factorsq suchq asq theq workq itself,q achievement,q power,q andq responsibility.q 
Herzbergqcalledq motivators qtoqtheqsatisfiersqandq hygiene factors qtoqtheqdissatisfying.qq

punishmentq toq causeq someoneq toq doq something.q Hygiene factors q canq onlyq causeq

Criticsq ofq Herzberg'sq theoryq argueq thatq theq twoRfactorq resultq isq observedq becauseq itq isq

q
Extrinsicqmotivationq(Petri,q1991)qexistsqwhenqaqpersonqisqmotivatedqbyqexternalqfactors,q 
asq opposedq toq theq internalq driversq ofq intrinsicq motivation.q Extrinsicq motivationq drivesq 
peopleq toq doq thingsq forq tangibleq rewardsq orq pressures,q ratherq thanq forq theq funq ofq it.q
Supermarkets’q loyaltyq andq discountsq cards,q airq miles,q corporateq bonuses,q andq salesq 
commissionsqareqexamplesqofqextrinsicqmotivators.qPriceqdiscountsqinqtrainingqeventsqareq 
alsoq extrinsicq motivators.q Traditionalq (faceq toq face)q trainingq companies,q forq instance,q 
usuallyq offerq offRpeakq periodq discountq pricesq orq earlyRenrolmentq discounts.q Extrinsicq 
motivationq canq beq measuredq byq priceq sensitivityq andq isq closelyq relatedq toq theq over 
justification effect (Deci,q Koestner,q&qRyan,q 2001;qLepper,q Greene,q &q Nisbett,q 1973),q 
whichqoccursqwhenqanqexternalqincentive,qsuchqasqmoneyqorqaqprize,qdecreasesqaqperson’sq

13.1.  Cognitive Dissonance 
q
Festingerq (1957;q Festingerq &q Carlsmith,q 1959)q createdq theq expressionq cognitive 
dissonance q toq defineq theq feelingq ofq uncomfortableq tensionq thatq oneq personq has,q whichq 
comesqfromqholdingqtwoqconflictingqthoughtsqinqtheqmindqatqtheqsameqtime.qq
q
Dissonanceqincreasesqwith:q
q
• Theqimportanceqofqtheqsubjectqtoqtheqperson;qq
• Howqstronglyqtheqdissonantqthoughtsqconflict;qq
• Theqperson’sqinabilityqtoqrationalizeqandqexplainqawayqtheqconflict;qq
• Behavioursqthatqtheqpersonqmakesqthatqareqagainstqtoqwhatqsheqbelievesqin;q
• Theq importanceq andq impactq ofq theq decision,q alongq withq theq difficultyq ofq 
reversingqit.qForqinstance,qdiscomfortqaboutqmakingqtheqwrongqchoiceqofqcarq 
isqbiggerqthanqwhenqchoosingqaqmealqorqaqlamp.q
q
Cognitiveq dissonanceq isq aq tensionq betweenq theq twoq opposingq thoughts.q Toq releaseq theq 
tension,qoneqofqthreeqactionsqcanqbeqtaken:q
q
• Changeqbehaviour;q
• Justifyqbehaviourqbyqchangingqtheqconflictingqcognition;qq
• Justifyqbehaviourqbyqaddingqnewqcognitions.q
q
Cognitiveq dissonanceq isq aq veryq powerfulq motivatorq thatq willq oftenq leadq theq personq toq 
changeqoneqorqotherqofqtheqconflictingqbeliefqorqbehaviour.qAsqsmokersqfindqallqkindsqofq 
reasonsq toq explainq awayq theirq unhealthyq habit,q highlyq selfRconfidentq personsq withq 
trainingqneedsqwillqargueqtheyqareqattendingqaqtrainingqcourseqnotqbecauseqtheyqneedqandq 
lackqsomeqcompetences,qbutqratherqbecauseqtheyqwantqtoqknowqaqlittleqbitqofqeverythingq 
andq theyq enjoyq beingq updated.q Likewise,q aq personq thatq believesq inq lifelongq continualq 
trainingqhasqaqcognitiveqdissonanceqifqsheqdoesqnotqattendqanyqtrainingqcourseqforqseveralq 
yearsqandqwillqenrolqinqtrainingqcoursesqtoqdealqwithqit,qevenqifqsheqdoesqnotqhaveqanyq 
specificqtrainingqneedqatqtheqmoment.qq

13.3.  Attribution Theory 
q
Attributionqtheoryq(Heider,q1958;qE.qE.qJonesq&qDavis,q1965;qKammer,q1982;qKelley,q 
1967;q Roeschq &q Amirkham,q 1997)qarguesqthatq individualsqhaveq aq needqtoq explainq theq 
world,q attributingq causesq andq explainingq behaviour.q Whenq aq personq makesq aq mistake,q 
sheqtendsqtoquseqexternalqattribution,qimputingqtheqerrorqtoqsituationalqfactors,qratherqthanq 
blamingqherself.qRegardingqtheqerrorsqofqanotherqperson,qsheqwillquseqinternalqattribution,q 
defendingq thatq itq wasq dueq toq internalq personalityq factors.q Inq successq situations,q sheq 
attributesqherqownqsuccessqtoqinternalqfactorsqandqtheqothers’qsuccessqtoqexternalqfactors,q
suchq asq pureq luck.q Thisq explains,q forq instance,q why,q inq theq endq ofq aq footballq game,q 
supportersqtendqtoqsayq“weqwon’,qifqtheirqteamqhasqwon,qbutqsayq‘theyqlost”qifqtheirqteamq 
didqnotqwonqtheqgame.qSo,qpeopleqtendqtoqblameqothersqandqavoidqselfRrecrimination,qandq 
theseq attributionsq areq theq resultq ofq personalq emotionalq andq motivationalq drivers.q 
Attributionq isq aq twoRstepq processq thatq startsq withqanq automaticq internalq attribution,q 
followedq byq aq slowerq considerationq ofq whetherq anq externalq attributionq isq moreq 
appropriate,qalthoughqthisqlastqstepqisqnotqalwaysqpresent.qq
q
Inq theq trainingq context,q thisq couldq meanq thatq ifq theq learningq processq isq effective,q theq 
traineeqwillqattributeqthatqtoqherqpreviousqknowledgeqandqexperienceqandqtoqherqabilityqtoq 
adaptqtoqdifferentqtrainingqenvironmentsqandqintellectualqskills.qIfqsomeqproblemsqoccurq 
duringqtheqtrainingqevent,qsuchqasqherqinadaptationqtoqtheqeRlearningqwayqofqlearning,qsheq 
willqtendqtoqblameqtheqplatform,qtheqtutor,qorqtheqsupportingqstaff.qq

q
McGregorq(1960)qproposedqtwoqtheoriesqtoqapproachqemployee’sqmotivation,qtoqwhichq

implicitq threats,q closeq supervision,q andq tightq controls,q or,q inq aq softerq style,q onq beingq 
permissiveq andq seekq harmonyq withqtheq hopeq that,q inqreturn,qemployeesq willq cooperateq

assumptionsq ofq theory X q areq notq correctq andq proposedq anq alternative,q whichq heq calledq 
TheoryqY,qwhichqhasqtheqfollowingqassumptions:qq

• Workqcanqbeqasqnaturalqasqplayqandqrest;q
• PeopleqwillqbeqselfRdirectedqtoqmeetqtheirqworkqobjectivesqifqtheyqareqcommittedqtoq 
them;qq
• Peopleqwillqbeqcommittedqtoqtheirqobjectivesqifqrewardsqaddressqhigherqneeds,qsuchq

13.5.  Side Bet Theory  
 
Sideq betq theoryq (H.q Becker,q 1960)q isq oftenq usedq toqtestq modelsq ofq organizationalq 
commitment,q whichq usuallyq includeq sideRbetq indexesqsuchq asq age,q tenure,q education,q 
marriage,q gender,q salary,q andq position.q Sideq betsq refersq toq theq accumulationq ofq 
investmentsqvaluedqbyqtheqindividualqthatqwouldqbeqlostqorqdeemedqworthlessqifqsheqwereq 
toq leaveq theq organization.q Theq individualq isq boundqtoq theq organizationq byq extraneousq 
factors,q suchq asq incomeq andq hierarchicalq position,qandq intraneous q factors,q suchq asq theq 
factqthatqhequsedqtoqtheqcompanyqandqtheqwayqthingsqareqdoneqinqtheir,qandqinterpersonalq 
relationships.q Theq lossq ofq friendshipsq andq seniorityq rightsq canq alsoq beq aq factorq whenq 
changingq employersq (Gattiker,q 1992).q Individualsq makeq choicesq thatq includeq sideq betsq 
thatqareqbasedqonqaqmainqbetqorqactivityqsucceeding.qIfqtheqmainqbetqfails,qthenqsheqwillq 
alsoq looseq theq sideq bet.q Thisq meansq thatq theqsideq betsq increaseq theq commitmentq toq theq 
mainqbet.qAsqBeckerq(1960)qputsqit,q"commitmentsqcomeqintoqbeingqwhenqaqperson,qbyq 
makingqaqsideRbet,qlinksqextraneousqinterestsqwithqaqconsistentqlineqofqactivity".qSideqbetq 
theoryqhelpsqtoqexplainqwhyqaqpersonqmayqrefuseqaqhigherqpaidqjob:qsheqcanqperceiveqitqasq 
riskierqinqtermsqofqpotentialqfailureqwhileqsheqhasqaqsideqbet,qwhichqisqtheqacquisitionqofqaq 
newqhouse,qwhichqwillqrequireqaqstableqincome.qTheqreverseqsituationqcanqalsoqoccur:qifqaq 
personqmakesqaqsideqbetqonqwhichqsheqwinqifqtheqmainqbetqfails,qthenqherqcommitmentqtoq 
theqmainqbetqfails.qq
q
Inqaqtrainingqcontext,qthisqmayqsuggestqthatqaqpersonqmayqbeqattendingqaqcourseq(theqsideq 
bet)qjustqinqcaseqherqcurrentqjobqfailsq(mainqbet)qandqsheqneedsqtoqreinventqherqcareer.qInq

1.  A Theory of Value 
q
Frondiziq(1971,qp.q3)qclaimsqthatqtheqvalueqtheoryqdidqnotqexistquntilqtheqendqofqtheq19 th q
century.qYet,qmodernqaxiology,qrelatedqtoqtheqdesired,qtheqpreferred,qandqtheqgood,qwasq 
raisedqinqPlato’sq theory of forms or ideas ,qinqhisq ideaq ofq theq Good,qandqdevelopedqbyq 
Aristotle’sqrelationqofqhigherqvalueqwithqfinalqcauseqinqGod,qandqinqKant’sqrelationshipqofq 
knowledgeq withq moral,q aesthetic,q andq religiousq values.q Theq meaningq ofq value,q asq itq isq 
seenqtoday,qwasqstudiedqduringqthatqperiodqbyqseveralqphilosophers,qunderqtheqinfluenceq 
ofq neoRKantiansq asq Lotze,q Ritschl,q Meinong,qandq vonq Ehrenfels.q Theseq firstq essaysq inq 
axiologyqwereqdirectedqtoqseparateqvalueqfromq facts q(Frondizi,q1971,qp.q3).qqYet,qtheqmostq 
importantq contributionsq wereq givenq yearsq later,q inqtheq beginningq ofq theq 20 th q century,q 
throughq theq workq ofq Urbanq (1909),q vonq Hartmann’sq o utline of axiology q (1908),q 
Münsterberg’sq(1909)qeternal values ,qNietzsche’sq(1910,q1914)qtheory of transvaluation 
of all values ,qlaterqthroughq Perry’sq(1926)qgeneral theory of value ,qDewey’sq theory of 
valuation (1939),q and,q moreq recently,q throughq Frondizi’sq (1971)q question:q what is 
value? 
 
2.  Value and Values 
q
Aqpertinentqquestionqmayqariseqregardingqwhetherqorqnotqthereqisqaqdifferenceqbetweenq 
value q(singular)qandq values q(plural).qItqisqgenerallyqacceptedqthatqvalueq(singular)qisqusedq 
toq designateq the outcome of an evaluative judgment q (thatq isq theq summary valuation ),q 
whereasqvaluesq(plural)qrefersqtoqstandards,qrules,qcriteria,qnorms,qgoals,qorqidealsqonqtheq 
basisq ofq whichq evaluativeq judgmentsq getq madeq (thatqis,q theq underlyingq evaluative 
criteria )q (Holbrook,q 1999c,q p.q 8).q Values q standq forq enduringq beliefsq orq forq whatq isq 
ultimatelyqgoodqandqdesirableqinqlifeq(Rokeach,q1973,qquotedqinqBoztepe,q2007)qwhileq 
value qareqtemporaryqjudgments.qAsqaqtemporaryqjudgment,qvalueqcanqeasilyqchangeqoverq 
time,qandqchangesqinqvalueqperceptionsqareqeasierqtoqmakeqandqacceptqthanqchangesqinq 
values.qq
q
3.   Value and Valuation 
3.1.   Is Value Ejaculatory or the Result of a Valuation Process? 
q
Valuationsq areq constantqphenomenaq ofq humanq behaviour.qEmotionsq andq desiresqframeq 
meansq andq ends,q andq havingq endsRinRview,q henceq formulatingq aq valuation,q isq whatq 
distinctqhumanqfromqnonhumanqbehaviour.qHumanqbeingsqareqcontinuouslyqengagedqinq 
valuationsq(Dewey,q1939,qpp.q57R58,q66),qbutqthisqdoesqnotqmeanqthatqhumanqbeingsqareq 
permanentlyqableqtoqformulateqvaluationRpropositions.qqq
q
Johnq Deweyq (1939,q p.q 1)q alertsq thatq valuesq canq beq viewed,q atq oneq extreme,q asq theq

4.3.  The Criterion of Value 
q
Theq criterion of value qisqrelatedqtoqtheqstandardqforqtestingqvaluesqandqisqinfluencedqbyq

Accordingq toq Runesq (1942),q theseq criteriaq rangeq fromq preference,q normsq orq ideals,q 
wholenessq andq coherence,q inclusivenessq orq adjustment.q Accordingq toq Perryq (1926,q p.q 
599)qitqisqtheq interest thatqconfersq value qonqtheqobject,qandqso,qitqmustqalsoqbeqinterestq 
whichqconfersqtheq amount qofqvalue.qThisqphilosopherqproposedqthreeqcriteriaqtoqdefineq 
thatqamountqofqvalueqandqtheqhierarchyqofqvalues,qwhichqheqcallsqtheq commensurability 
of values q(Perry,q1926,qpp.q600,q626)qandqsuggestsqthatqallqvaluesqcanqbeqarrangedqinqaq 
single,q allRcomprehensive,q andq systematicq hierarchy.q Perryq (1926,q pp.q 615R616)q
proposesq threeq criteriaq toq defineq theq hierarchyq ofqvalues:q intensity ,q preference ,q andq 
inclusiveness .qAnqobject,qasqwine,qforqinstance,qisqbetterqthanqanotherqobject,qwater:q(1)qifq 
theqinterestqinqtheqwineqisqmoreqintenseqthanqtheqinterestqinqtheqwater,q(2)qifqtheqwineqisq

interestqinqtheqwater.qq
q
Preferenceqisqexpressedqinqtheqformq“thisqisqmoreqtoqmyqtasteqthanqthat”,qratherqthanqinq

ofqintensity,qitqdoesqnotqriseqinqtheqorderqofqpreference,qandqtakesqtheqplaceqofqcoldqwaterq

4.4.  The Metaphysical Status of Value: Objectivism vs.  Subjectivism 
q
Theq metaphysical status of value qexploresqtheqrelationqofqvaluesqtoqtheqfactsqinvestigatedq 
byq naturalq science,q ofq humanq experienceq ofq valueq toq realityq independentq man.q Thisq 
metaphysicalqissueqtriesqtoqdiscoverqwhatqtheqsourceqofqvalueqis,qandqitsqmainqdiscussionq 
isq betweenq objectivistsq andq subjectivists.q Specifically,qoneq ofqtheq majorq disagreementsq 
amongqdifferentqtheoriesqisqwhetherqvalueqisqsomethingqsubjectivelyqassignedqbyqthequserq 
andqindependentqofqtheqproduct’sqphysicalqqualities,qorqsomethingqthatqisqembeddedqinq 
theqobject,qandqrecognizedqbyqthequser.qAsqHolbrookq(1994,qpp.q29R31)qargues,qaxiologyq 
hasq beenq debatingq differentq polaritiesq inq theq meaningq ofq valueq characterizedq asq

naturalistic,qmonisticq versus qpluralistic,qorqintensiveq versus extensive,qbutqthisqobjectivistq 
versus qsubjectivistqdiscussionqisqconsideredqtheqmostqimportant.qq
q
Theqdiscussionqbetweenqobjectivistqandqsubjectivistqisqcloselyqrelatedqwithqtheqdistinctionq 
madeqbetweenqinstrumentalqandqintrinsicqvalueq–qbetweenqwhatqisqgoodqasqaqmean,qandq 
whatq isq goodq asq anq end.q Theq coreq problemq betweenq objectivistsq andq subjectivistsq isq 
whetherqthingsqareqvaluableqbecauseqweqdesireqthem,qorqweqdesireqthemqbecauseqtheyqareq 
valuable.qAsqFrondiziq(1971,qp.q19)qputsqit,q“doesqdesire,qpleasure,qorqinterestqgiveqvalueq

valueqisq objective qifqitsqexistenceqandqnatureqisqindependentqofqaqsubject,qandqisq subjective q
ifq itq owesq itsq existence,q itsq sense,q orq itsq validity,q toq theq feelings,q orq attitudesq ofq theq 
subject.qq

experience.q Asq Holbrookq (1994,q p.q 30)q recalls,q subjectivistsq defendq thatq valueq isq 
somethingq subjectively qassignedqbyqthequserqandqindependentqofqtheqproduct’sqphysicalq 
qualities,qand,qinqtheseqsituations,qvalueqisqentirelyqdependentqonqandqrelativeqtoqhumanq 
experienceqofqit.qHowever,qasqtheqobjectivistsqwouldqsay,qtheq“desirable”qisqrelatedqtoqtheq

differentqdegreesqofqsubjectivismqcanqbeqfoundqinqtheqliterature:qTheq extreme subjectivist q
positionqholdsqthatq“valueqisqentirelyqdependentqonqandqrelativeqtoqhumanqexperienceqofq

Anq intermediate position ,qcalledqtheq interactionist qview q(Holbrook,q1994,qp.q33)qholdsq 
thatqvalueqentailsqaq“dyadicqorqrelational”qnexusqbetweenqsubjectqandqobjectq(Osborne,q

Aq Gestalt qisqmoreqthanqtheqaggregateqofqitsqconstituentqparts,qandqisqaqnewqquality,qwhichq

Aq Gestalt qqualityqhasqtheqfollowingqcharacteristicsq(Frondizi,q1971,qpp.q163R164):qq
q

Appendix 9: The Economic Approach to Utility 
 
1.  Cardinal and Ordinal Utility 
q
Economicsqdistinguishesqbetweenqcardinalqutilityqandqordinalqutility.qWhenqrepresentingq 
consumerqpreferences,qeconomistsqassumeqthatqpeopleqareqableqtoqrankqeachqbundleqinq 
orderq ofq preference.q Thisq isq theq ordinal utility approach q toq consumerq budgetingq 
problem.q Inq thisq approach,q itq isq notq requiredq thatqpeopleq beq ableq toq makeq quantitativeq 
statementsqaboutqhowqmuchqtheyqlikeqvariousqbundles.qThus,qitqassumesqthatqaqconsumerq 
willqalwaysqbeqableqtoqsayqwhetherqsheqprefersqAqtoqB,qbutqthatqsheqmayqnotqbeqableqtoq 
makeq muchq statementsq asq Aq isq 6,43q timesq asq goodq asqB.q Inq theq nineteenthq century,q 
economistsqcommonlyqassumedqthatqpeopleqcouldqmakeqsuchqstatements.qThatqisqcalledq 
theq cardinal utility approach toqtheqconsumerqchoiceqproblem.qWithqaqtwoRgoodsqcase,q 
inq thisq approach,q itq isq assumedq thatq theq satisfactionq providedq byq anyq bundleq canq beq 
assignedqaqnumericalqorqcardinalqvalueqbyqaqutilityqfunctionq(Frank,q1991,qp.q88).q
Whenqonlyqordinalqapproachesqareqassumed,qsomeqquantitativeqcomparisonsqinqtermsqofq 
utilityqbetweenqgoodsqareqpossible,qasq“theqAqgoodqisqbetterqthanqBqgoodqbyqtheqexactq 
amountqbyqwhichqtheqBqgoodqisqbetterqthanqCqgood”.qYet,qstatementsqsuchqasq“Aqgoodqisq 
twiceqasqgoodqasqBqgood”qareqsubstitutedqbyqqualitativeqstatementsqsuchqasq“Aqgoodqisq 
preferredqtoqtheqCqgood”.q
q
2.  Indifference Curves and Economic Equilibrium 
q
Evenq whenq onlyq ordinalq preferencesq areq considered,qconsumerq preferencesq areq stillq 
representedqwithqaqcardinalqutilityqindexqandqplottedqinqquantitativeqaxes.qUtilityqisqbuiltq 
uponq indifference curves ,q whichq plotq theq combinationq ofq goodsq thatq theq individualq 
requiresqtoq maintainqaqgivenq levelq ofq satisfaction.q Microeconomicq modelsq areqbuiltqonq 
theseqindifferenceqcurveqmaps,qwhichqareqbasedqonqthequtilityqthatqconsumersqperceiveqtoq 
differentq setsq ofq packsq ofq goods.q Andq itq isq fromq indifferenceq curvesq thatq economistsq 
derivateq anq ordinaryq demandq curveq (see,q forq instance,q Friedman,q 1986,q forq 
demonstration).q Asq linesqjoiningq combinationsq thatqgiveq aq personq theq sameq amountqofq 
utility,q indifferenceq curvesq doq notq meetq orq intersect,q andq areq convexq toq theq originq 
(Douglas,q 1992b,q p.q 40).q Thisq meansq thatq productsq orq servicesq areq notq perfectlyq 
substitutesqnorqperfectqcomplementsq(see,qforqexample,qFrank,q1991,qp.q270).qThisqalsoq 
meansqthatqthereqisqaqdiminishingq marginal rate of substitution q(MRS),qwhichqisqtoqsayq 
that,qalongqanyqindifferenceqcurve,qtheqmoreqaqconsumerqhasqofqoneqgood,qtheqmoreqsheq 
mustqbeqgivenqofqthatqfoodqbeforeqsheqwillqbeqwillingqtoqgivequpqaqunitqofqtheqotherqgood.q 
Statedq differently,q MRSq declinesq asq weq moveq downwardq toq theq rightq alongq anq 
indifferenceq curve.q Aq preferenceq orderingq withq diminishingq MRSq will,q thus,q generateq 
indifferenceqcurvesqthatqareqconvexq–qorqbowedqoutward,qwhenqviewedqfromqtheqoriginq 
(Frank,q1991,qp.q73).qq
q
Eachqindifferenceqcurveqrepresentsqallqcombinationsqofqtwoqproductsqthatqyieldqtheqsameq 
levelq ofq utility.q Severalq combinationsq ofq goodsq canq provideq theq sameq levelq ofq 
satisfaction,q whichq makesq theq individualq toq goq upq orq downq inq theq sameq indifferenceq 
curveq(Frank,q1991,qpp.q69R70,q90).qThisqallowsqus,qforqexample,qtoqcompareqtheqbundleq 
(Q 1b ,Q 1a )qtoqbundleq(Q 2b ,qQ 2a )qinqqFigureq83,qwhichqareqequallyqpreferred.qqq
q

Indifference curves maps q representq severalq indifferencesq curves,q eachq forq aq differentq 
levelq ofq utility.q Indifferenceq curvesq thatq areq moreq distanceq fromq theq originq representq 
combinationsq ofq twoq productsq thatq provideq higherq levelsq ofq utilityq thanq thoseq curvesq 
closerq toq theq origin.q Economistsq assumeq thatq peopleq wantq toq maximizeq utility,q whileq 
priceqandqincomeqvaluesqareqbudgetqconstraintsqgivenqinqadvance,qwhichqmeansqthatqtheq 
maximizationqproblemqisqaq constrained maximization problem q(Frank,q1991,qpp.q91R92).q 
Theqsolutionqtoqthisqproblemqofqutilityqmaximizationqisqsolvedqwhenq isocosts qmaps areq 
takenqintoqconsideration.qAnqisocostqlineqrepresentsqaqcombinationqofqinputsqthatqcostqtheq 
sameq amount,q inq termsq ofq capitalq andq labour.q Theq axesq areq replacedq byq factorsq ofq 
production,q ratherq thanqconsumerq goodsq orq services.q Forq eachq givenq costq orq budgetq isq 
drawnqoneqisocostqline.qIsocostqmapsqplotqparallelqlinesqthatqrepresentqdifferentqbudgetsq 
orqcosts.qThequseqofqtheqisocostqpertainsqtoqcostRminimizationqinqproduction,qasqopposedq 
toq utilityRmaximization.q Equilibriumq isq aq tangentialq solutionq whereq eachq factorq ofq 
productionqisqemployedqinqsuchqwayqthatqtheqratioqofqmarginalqproductqtoqpriceqofqtheq 
factorq isq equalized.q Thatq is,q itq costsq theq sameq toqproduceq oneq extraq unitq ofq outputq byq 
employingqonequnitqofqlabourqorqonequnitqofqcapitalq(marginalqcostsqandqmarginalqutilityq 
areqequal).qJustqasqinqindifferenceqcurveqanalysis,qanyqchangeqinqpricesqaffectsqtheqslopeq 
ofq theq isocost,q and,q hence,q theq allocationq ofq resourcesq amongq theq twoq factorsq andq theq 
finalqequilibrium.q
q
3.  Utility and the Demand for Attributes 
q
Theq demandq theoryq isq sometimesq analyzedq inq termsq ofq demand for attributes . Forq 
instance,q beerq isq demandedq becauseq isq freshq (beingqfreshnessq theq attribute),q sparkling,q 
andq aq complementq ofq socialq gathering.q Asq Jonesq (1998)q refers,q “developedq byq Kelvinq 
Lancasterq(1971),qtheqproductqattributesqmodelqsetsqoutqtoqexplainqconsumerqbehaviourq 
asq aq processq ofq choosingq bundlesq ofq productq characteristicsq orq attributesq inherentq inq 
goodsq andq services,q ratherq thanq simplyq choosingq bundlesq ofq goodsq orq servicesq 
themselves.qTheqbasicqassumptionqofqtheqmodelqisqthatqtheqconsumer'sqchoiceqisqbasedqonq 
maximizingqutilityqfromqtheqproductqattributesqsubjectqtoqaqbudgetqconstraintq(…).qTheq 
modelq isq particularlyq usefulq inq analyzingq differentiatedq productq markets,q inq whichq 
specificq productsq thatq areq substitutesq forq eachq otherq areq distinguishedq byq theirq 
embodimentqofqaqspecificqsetqofqcharacteristics”.qqAqtwo ‐dimensionalqgraphqrevealsqtheq 
model'sqmainqfeaturesqandqlinksqitqtoqtheqtraditionalqbudgetqconstraintqandqindifferenceq
